..........Na + ..........O<sub>2</sub> → ..........Na<sub>2</sub>O
parts.solutionMd:
The complete equation for the reaction of sodium burning in oxygen is:

The completed equation is:

4Na + O<sub>2</sub> →2Na<sub>2</sub>O

- **4**Na
**AND**
**2**Na<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Balance the oxygen atoms first; there are 2 on the left-hand side, so you need to put a 2 in front of Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*O to give 2 oxygen atoms on the right-hand side:*

  - *Na + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* →**2**Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Now there are 4 atoms of Na on the right-hand side, which can be balanced by putting a 4 in front of the Na on the left-hand side:*

  - *4**Na + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* →**2**Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd:
The position of an element in the Periodic Table can be used to predict its properties.

Which of the following statements could **not** be predicted using the trends in Group 1?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B.**

- Group 1 metals are soft and easy to cut, getting softer as you move down the group
- Lithium is further up the group than potassium, therefore is harder to cut
- **A** is incorrect as melting point decreases as you move down the group, due to decreasing attractive forces between outer electrons and positive ions
- **C** is incorrect as Group 1 metals react with oxygen in the air forming metal oxides, which is why they tarnish when exposed to the air. The metals tarnish more rapidly as you go down the group
- **D** is incorrect as the reactivity of the Group 1 metals increases as you descend the group

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Rubidium has a lower melting point than lithium

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: Sodium will tarnish more quickly than lithium

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Caesium is more reactive than potassium

parts.problemMd:
This question is about sodium and potassium.

A trough is filled with water and a few drops of phenolphthalein indicator are added.

A small piece of sodium is dropped into the water. One of the products of the reaction is an alkali.

i) Complete the chemical equation for the reaction of sodium with water.

(2)

___Na (.......) + ___H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → ___NaOH (........) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

ii) Identify the ion that causes the solution to become alkaline.

(1)

iii) Give three observations that would be made when sodium reacts with water.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The chemical equation for the reaction of sodium with water is:

**   2**Na (**s**) + **2**H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → **2**NaOH (**aq**) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

- Correct balancing number;** [1 mark]**
- (s) **AND **(aq) for state symbols;** [1 mark]**

ii) The ion that causes the solution to become alkaline is:

- Hydroxide / OH<sup>-</sup>; **[1 mark]**

iii) Three observations that would be made when sodium reacts with water are:

Any three from:

- Sodium moves / floats (on the surface); **[1 mark]**
- Effervescence / bubbling;** [1 mark]**
- (Indicator / phenolphthalein / water) turns pink; **[1 mark]**
- The sodium gets smaller / disappears / (appears to) dissolve;** [1 mark]**
- The sodium melts / turns into a ball;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Observations of Group 1 metals with water are frequently asked for, so make sure you know these*
- *You are expected to be able to give the chemical equation for any of the Group 1 elements with water*
- *The equations are all the same, it is just the symbol for the Group1 element that changes*

parts.problemMd: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium. Refer to the electronic configurations of the atoms in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Potassium is more reactive than sodium because:

- The electron configuration of sodium is 2,8,1
**AND **
The electron configuration of potassium is 2,8,8,1 / potassium has more shells / potassium has a larger atomic radius / the outer shell of potassium is further from the nucleus; **[1 mark]**
- The outer electron is less attracted to the nucleus (of potassium)
**OR**
There is more shielding between the outer electron and the nucleus; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, the outer electron is lost more easily / less energy is required to overcome the attraction; **[1 mark]**

The reverse argument for sodium is accepted, e.g. outer electron is more attracted to nucleus and is less easily lost

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When a question says "refer to electronic configurations," either write them out (2,8,1 and 2,8,8,1) or clearly state that potassium has more electron shells. Missing this loses you the first mark.
> 
> You must say "outer electron," not just "electron." Talking generally about "electrons being lost" without specifying the outer electron caps you at 2 marks.
> 
> Do not write "more outer shells." An atom only has one outer shell. Write "more shells" or "the outer shell is further from the nucleus."
> 
> Structure your answer as a chain where each step is a separate mark:
> 
> 1. Configuration difference
> 2. Weaker attraction
> 3. Easier loss

parts.problemMd:
This question is about some of the alkali metals and their compounds.

When a teacher drops a small piece of sodium into a trough of cold water, she observes bubbles of gas.

Give two other observations that would be made when sodium reacts with cold water.
parts.solutionMd:
Two other observations that can be made are:

Any **two** of the following observations:

- (Sodium) floats / moves on surface (of water);** [1 mark]**
- (Sodium) melts / forms a ball; **[1 mark]**
- (Sodium) gets smaller / disappears / dissolves; **[1 mark]**
- (Sodium) forms a white trail; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember: **Sodium does not react with a flame*

  - *This is why references to a yellow flame are ignored*
- *The question also asks for observations so saying that the reaction heats up will not gain marks as it is not something you can see*
- *Even though hydrogen is produced there is no visible fizzing / effervescence, so that is why these are not allowed as observations*

parts.problemMd:
Lithium reacts with fluorine to form the compound lithium fluoride.

i) Give a chemical equation for this reaction.

(1)

ii) Give a test to show that lithium fluoride contains lithium ions.

(2)

iii) Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of the electrons in a lithium ion and in a fluoride ion.

Include the charge on each ion.

(3)

| Lithium ion | Fluoride ion |
|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced equation for the reaction of lithium and fluorine is:

2Li + F<sub>2</sub> → 2LiF

- Correct species and balancing, multiples allowed; **[1 mark]**

ii) A test to show that lithium fluoride contains lithium ions is:

- (Perform a) flame test; **[1 mark]**
- (Flame is) (crimson / scarlet) red;** [1 mark]**

iii) The dot-and-cross diagrams showing the electron arrangements for the lithium and fluoride ions are:

- Correct electron arrangement of lithium ion; **[1 mark]**

**   **

- Correct electron arrangement of fluoride ion (including the inner shell); **[1 mark]**
- Correct charges on both ions (with or without brackets);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *You are expected to know the formula of:*

  - *Metals - represented by the unit formula of one atom*
  - *Halogens - which are all diatomic molecules*
- *The reactions between Group 1 metals (M) and the Group 7 halogens (X) follow the same equation pattern regardless of which metal or halogen is used:*

  - *2M + X*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2MX*
- *The question asks for the electronic configuration, so unless you are told otherwise assume that this means the full electronic configuration, including full inner shells*

  - *When this is required the examiners will ask you to draw small atoms or ions to minimise the time needed*
  - *You are allowed to use dots or crosses unless the exam question tells you what to use*

parts.problemMd:
The table shows the electronic configurations of sodium and potassium.

| **Element** | ** Electronic configurations** |
|---|---|
| sodium | 2.8.1 |
| potassium | 2.8.8.1 |

Explain, in terms of their electronic configurations, why potassium is more reactive than sodium.
parts.solutionMd:
Potassium is more reactive than sodium because:

An explanation that links **three** of the following four points:

- The outer electron is further from the nucleus in potassium **OR **Potassium has more shells  **OR **Potassium has a larger atomic radius; **[1 mark]**
- There is more shielding (by the inner shells) in potassium;** [1 mark]**
- Therefore, there is less attraction between the outer electron and the nucleus in potassium; **[1 mark]**
- (So the outer) electron (in potassium) is more easily lost; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The reverse argument for sodium having fewer shells and less shielding resulting in a stronger attraction and the outer electron being harder to remove is accepted*
- *The question gives you a big hint that you need to refer to the electronic configurations by including them in a table*
- *Some of the marks are even available for stating information from this table (that potassium has more shells of electrons)*
- *The question is asking for a comparison, so make sure you use comparative language (potassium has more shielding instead of potassium has lots of shielding)*
- *The shielding is from the inner shells of electrons*

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the temperature change in the reaction between dilute acids and solutions of Group 1 hydroxides.

He uses this apparatus.

![temperature-change-apparatus](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-1-group-1-alkali-metals/assets/004-temperature-change-apparatus.png)

This is the student’s method:

- Measure the temperature of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrochloric acid
- Pour the acid into a polystyrene cup
- Add 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of sodium hydroxide solution to the acid
- Measure the maximum temperature of the mixture

i) Suggest what could be added to the apparatus to improve the experiment.

(1)

ii) Explain a change to the method that would improve the accuracy of the experiment.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i)  What could be added to the apparatus to improve the experiment:

- A lid / cover; **[1 mark]**

ii)  A change to the method that would improve the accuracy of the experiment is:

Any **one **of the following pairs:

Pair 1:

Pair 2:

parts.problemMd:
These are the student’s results:

Temperature of hydrochloric acid = 19.9 °C

Maximum temperature of mixture = 26.5 °C

i) Calculate the energy change, Q, in joules for this reaction.

[mass of 1.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of mixture = 1.0 g]

[for the mixture, c = 4.2 J / g / °C]

Q = .............................................. J

(3)

ii) In the student’s reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, 0.050 mol of water forms.

Calculate the molar enthalpy change, Δ*H*, in kJ / mol for this reaction.

Δ*H* = .............................................. kJ / mol

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i)   The energy change, Q, in joules for this reaction is:

- Correct temperature change / Δ*T*; **[1 mark]**
- Correct substitution into Q = m x c x Δ*T*; **[1 mark]**
- Correct evaluation;** [1 mark]**

*Example calculation:*

- Δ*T* = (26.5 – 19.9) **OR** 6.6 - Q = 100 x 4.2 x 6.6 - Answer = 2800 (J)

ii)   The molar enthalpy change, Δ*H*, in kJ / mol for this reaction:

- Answer from (i) ÷ 0.05; **[1 mark]**
- Correct evaluation in kJ / mol with negative sign; **[1 mark]**

*Example calculation:*

- 2800 ÷ 0.05 **OR** 56000 (J) - Answer= - 56 (kJ / mol)

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *You can have full marks for correct answers in both parts even without workings*
- *In part i) credit can be given for 2770 or 2772 to allow for less rounding*
- *You must have the correct sign for Δ**H** in order to get the mark*
- *Depending on rounding, your answer could be -55, -55.4 or -55.44 to get the mark*

parts.problemMd:
The diagram represents an atom of lithium and an atom of sodium.

| ![li](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-1-group-1-alkali-metals/assets/006-li.png) | ![na](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-1-group-1-alkali-metals/assets/007-na.png) |
|---|---|
| lithium | sodium |

i) Give a reason why lithium and sodium have similar reactions with water.

(1)

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) One reason why lithium and sodium have similar reactions with water is:

- They have the same number of outer / valence electrons **OR **They both have one outer / valence electron; **[1 mark]**

ii) Lithium is less reactive than sodium because:

- Lithium has a smaller atomic radius / is smaller **OR **Lithium has less shells / energy levels / orbitals; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
The teacher adds 0.150 g of lithium to an excess of water and collects the hydrogen gas produced.

The equation for the reaction is

2Li (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

The teacher collects 254 cm<sup>3</sup> of hydrogen gas at room temperature and pressure (rtp).

Show by calculation that 1 mol of hydrogen gas has a volume of approximately 24000 cm<sup>3</sup> at rtp.
parts.solutionMd:
To show that 1 mole of hydrogen gas has a volume of approximately 24000 cm<sup>3</sup> at rtp:

- Amount of lithium = $\frac{0.150}{7}$ **OR **Amount of lithium = 0.0214 mol;** [1 mark]**
- Amount of hydrogen = 0.0107 mol; **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{254}{0.0107}$; **[1 mark]**
- 23,738; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You need to use the balanced equation to work out the number of moles of hydrogen from the number of moles of lithium*
- *Volume ÷ moles gives volume per mole*
- *Remember: **The question asks for this to be in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* not dm*<sup>*3*</sup>* so there is no need to convert volumes*

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
i) Give one observation that would be different if potassium is used instead of lithium.

(1)

ii) The diagram represents an atom of lithium and an atom of potassium.

![lithium-and-potassium-electron-structures](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-1-group-1-alkali-metals/assets/002-lithium-and-potassium-electron-structures.png)

Explain why potassium is more reactive than lithium.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) One observation that would be different if potassium is used instead of lithium is:

Any **one **from:

- More rapid bubbles / fizzing / effervescence;** [1 mark]**
- Melts / turns into a ball;  **[1 mark]**
- Moves more quickly; ** [1 mark]**
- Gets smaller more quickly;  **[1 mark]**
- Catches alight / burns / produces a flame; **[1 mark]**

ii) Potassium is more reactive than lithium because:

- Potassium has more shells / is bigger than lithium **OR **The outer shell / electron in potassium is further from the nucleus;  **[1 mark]**
- (Therefore) there is less attraction between the outer shell/electron and the nucleus **OR **There is more repulsion (from inner shells) **OR **There is more shielding (from the nuclear attraction) **OR **The nuclear pull for the outer shell / electron is weaker;** [1 mark]**
- So the electron in the outer shell is more easily lost; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (ii), the reverse argument for lithium will also score the marks*
- *Potassium is further down Group 1, so has a more vigorous reaction than lithium*
- *Make sure your answer is comparative, for example, it moves **more **quickly, not just it moves *
- *Group 1 reactivity is determined by how easily the element loses its outer electron to form a positive ion *
- *The further away the negative outer electron is from the positive nucleus, the weaker the attraction is and the more easily the electron is lost*
- *This is a common explanation you will be asked about, so make sure you learn the three points*

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction between lithium and water is:

2Li (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

i) A mass of 0.500 g of lithium reacts with an excess of water. Calculate the volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of hydrogen gas produced at rtp.

[molar volume of a gas at rtp = 24 000 cm<sup>3</sup>]

Give your answer to three significant figures.

(3)

volume = .......................................... cm<sup>3</sup>

ii) In a reaction between lithium and water, 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of lithium hydroxide solution is formed.

The lithium hydroxide solution is then completely neutralised by 24.85 cm<sup>3</sup> of 0.100 mol/dm<sup>3</sup> sulfuric acid. The equation for the neutralisation is

2LiOH (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) → Li<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4 </sub>(aq) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Calculate the concentration, in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>, of the lithium hydroxide solution.

(3)

concentration = .............................................................. mol/dm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
i) The volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of hydrogen gas produced at rtp is:

- Moles of Li= $\frac{0.500}{7}$ **OR** 0.0714;** [1 mark]**
- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>=$\frac{0.0714}{2}$ **OR** 0.0357; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of H<sub>2</sub> (= 0.0357 x 24000) = 857 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

ii) The concentration, in mol/dm<sup>3</sup>, of the lithium hydroxide solution is:

- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>= 0.02485 x 0.1 **OR** 0.002485;** [1 mark]**
- Moles of LiOH = 2 x 0.002485 **OR **0.00497; **[1 mark]**
- Concentration of LiOH = 0.0331 (mol/dm<sup>3</sup>);** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *To calculate the volume of gas *

  - *Find the number of moles of lithium using* $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass}}$
  - *The molar ratio of lithium to hydrogen gas is 2:1 so divide the number of moles of lithium by 2*
  - *Multiply the number of moles of hydrogen by 24 000 to find the volume it occupies *
  - *Make sure your answer is to three significant figures!*
- *To calculate the concentration of lithium hydroxide*

  - *You are able to calculate the moles of sulfuric acid using concentration x volume (making sure you have converted volume from cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* to dm*<sup>*3*</sup>*) so 0.02485 x 0.1 = 0.002485 mol*
  - *The equation tells you that the molar ratio of lithium hydroxide to sulfuric acid is 2:1 so you need to multiply the moles of sulfuric acid by 2 to give 0.00497 mol*
  - *Concentration can be found by using *$\frac{\mathrm{number} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{moles}}{\mathrm{volume}}$ *so *$\frac{0.00497}{0.150}$*=  0.0331 mol / dm*<sup>*3*</sup>

parts.problemMd: Suggest why the teacher does not repeat the experiment using hydrochloric acid instead of cold water.
parts.solutionMd:
The teacher does not repeat the experiment using hydrochloric acid instead of cold water because:

- The reaction (of potassium) with water is violent / vigorous **OR **The reaction (of potassium) with hydrochloric acid is too dangerous / violent / vigorous; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
i) Give the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of potassium with hydrochloric acid. State symbols are required.

(2)

ii) Draw diagrams to show the arrangement of the electrons in the product of this reaction.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced chemical equation including state symbols for the reaction of potassium with hydrochloric acid is:

2K (s) + 2HCl (aq) → 2KCl (aq) + H<sub>2</sub> (g)

- Correct chemical formulae **AND **Correct state symbols; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

ii) The diagrams to show the arrangement of the electrons in the product of this reaction are:

- Correct electron arrangement of the potassium ion  **AND **Correct electron arrangement of the chloride ion; **[1 mark]**
- Correct charges on <u>both</u> ions; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The reaction of potassium with hydrochloric acid is: Potassium + hydrochloric acid → potassium chloride + hydrogen*
  
    - *Potassium = K (s)*
    - *Hydrochloric acid = HCl (aq)*
    - *Potassium chloride = KCl (aq)*
    - *Hydrogen = H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *This gives the unbalanced chemical equation:*
  
    - *K (s) + HCl (aq) → KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *There are two hydrogen atoms on the right-hand side, so you need 2HCl on the left-hand side*
  
    - *K (s) + **2**HCl (aq) → KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *There are now two chlorine atoms on the left-hand side, so you need 2KCl on the right-hand side*
  
    - *K (s) + **2**HCl (aq) → **2**KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
  - *There are now two potassium atoms on the right-hand side, so you need 2K on the left-hand side*
  
    - *2**K (s) + **2**HCl (aq) → **2**KCl (aq) + H*<sub>*2*</sub>* (g)*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *Careful:** The question asks for the arrangement of the electrons in the product*
  
    - *This means that you need to draw how the electrons are arranged in the potassium and chloride ions that form potassium chloride*
    - *A common mistake is to draw how the electrons are arranged in **atoms** of potassium and chlorine*
  - *Unless you are told otherwise, the arrangement of electrons in an ion should include the electrons in the inner shells *
  - *The potassium ion and chloride ion have the same arrangement of electrons which is why they are both required for the mark to awarded*
  
    - *If the metal ion and non-metal ion had different electron arrangements, there would be one mark for the metal ion diagram and one mark for the non-metal ion diagram*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about some Group 1 metal oxides.

When lithium is exposed to oxygen, it is oxidised and traces of lithium peroxides are produced.

i) Explain why the formation of lithium oxide is a redox reaction.

(3)

ii) Lithium oxide and a gas are produced by the thermal decomposition of lithium peroxide, Li<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

Write the balanced chemical equation for this reaction. State symbols are not required.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The formation of lithium oxide from lithium and oxygen is a redox reaction because:

- Lithium is oxidised **AND **oxygen is reduced **OR **Both oxidation and reduction occur;** [1 mark]**
- Lithium gains oxygen **OR **Lithium loses electrons **OR **The oxidation number of lithium increases / changes from 0 to +1; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen gains electrons  **OR **The oxidation number of oxygen decreases from 0 to –2; **[1 mark]**

ii) The balanced chemical equation for the production of lithium oxide and a gas by the thermal decomposition of lithium peroxide, Li<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> is:

2Li<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> → 2Li<sub>2</sub>O + O<sub>2</sub>

- Correct chemical formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Redox reactions can be considered in terms of:*

  - *Oxygen *
  
    - *Oxidation is the gain of oxygen, which is what happens to the lithium*
    - *Reduction is the loss of oxygen, but this does not work for this reaction*
  - *Electrons (OILRIG)*
  
    - *Oxidation is the loss of electrons*
    - *The lithium loses one electron to become the Li*<sup>*+*</sup>* ion required to form lithium oxide*
    - *Reduction is the gain of electrons*
    - *Each oxygen atom gains 2 electrons to become the O*<sup>*2-*</sup>* ion required to form lithium oxide*
  - *Answers in terms of oxidation number are accepted although these are considered above the level of this course*
- *You are told that lithium peroxide decomposes to form lithium oxide and a gas*

  - *The gas must be oxygen, which gives the unbalanced equation:*
  
    - *Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *To get an even number of oxygen atoms on the right-hand side, you double the lithium oxide:*
  
    - *Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *There are now four lithium atoms and four oxygen atoms on the right-hand side, so you double the lithium peroxide*
  
    - *2**Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Li*<sub>*2*</sub>*O + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *The equation is now balanced*

parts.problemMd:
The oxidation of potassium can produce potassium oxide, K<sub>2</sub>O, and potassium superoxide, KO<sub>2</sub>.

Compare the oxidation of potassium with the combustion of carbon.
parts.solutionMd:
Comparing the oxidation of potassium with the combustion of carbon:

- Potassium reacts in excess oxygen / a plentiful supply of oxygen to form potassium superoxide / KO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- This is similar to the complete combustion of carbon to form carbon dioxide / CO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Potassium reacts in limited oxygen to form potassium oxide / K<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**
- This is similar to the incomplete combustion of carbon to form carbon monoxide / CO; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Answers in terms of carbon reacting with excess or limited oxygen and then the equivalent comparison to the oxidations of potassium will score the marks*
- *There are two oxidation of potassium reactions given in the question *

  - *Potassium + oxygen → potassium superoxide K + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → KO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Potassium + oxygen → potassium oxide 4K + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Carbon can undergo complete and incomplete combustion*

  - *Complete combustion Carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide C + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Incomplete combustion Carbon + oxygen → carbon monoxide 2C + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2CO*
- *The formation of potassium superoxide and the complete combustion of carbon both have one mole of reactant (potassium or carbon) reacting with one mole of oxygen to form the oxide*

  - *This suggests that they both require a plentiful supply of oxygen*
- *The formation of potassium oxide and the incomplete combustion of carbon both have multiple moles of reactant (potassium or carbon) reacting with one mole of oxygen to form the oxide*

  - *This suggests that they both have a limited supply of oxygen*

parts.problemMd:
Potassium superoxide is sometimes used as a water dehumidifier, carbon dioxide scrubber and oxygen generator on board space craft and submarines.

As it absorbs and reacts with carbon dioxide, it locks the carbon dioxide up as potassium carbonate and releases oxygen.

i) Write the balanced chemical equation for this chemical reaction. State symbols are not required.

(2)

ii) Determine the number of moles of carbon dioxide absorbed and the number of moles of oxygen released by one mole of potassium superoxide.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced chemical equation for potassium superoxide locking carbon dioxide up as potassium carbonate and releasing oxygen is:

4KO<sub>2</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub> → 2K<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> + 3O<sub>2</sub>

- Correct chemical formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing;** [1 mark] **

ii) The number of moles of carbon dioxide absorbed and the number of moles of oxygen released by one mole of potassium superoxide are:

- Carbon dioxide absorbed = 0.5 moles; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen released = 0.75 moles; [1 mark]

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *When potassium superoxide absorbs and reacts with carbon dioxide, it locks it up in the form of potassium carbonate*

  - *This is similar to carbon dioxide from the early atmosphere that was locked up in calcium carbonate *
- *The unbalanced chemical equation is:*

  - *KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *The three oxygen atoms in potassium carbonate make balancing the equation more challenging as there is an even number of oxygen atoms on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be resolved by producing 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  
    - *KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *This means that there are four potassium atoms on the right-hand side and only one potassium atom on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be resolved by using 4KO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *4**KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *There are also two carbon atoms on the right-hand side and only one carbon atom on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be resolved by using 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *4**KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **2**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *There are now 12 oxygen atoms on the left-hand side*

  - *There are six oxygen atoms in the 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>*, which leave 6 oxygen atoms*
  - *This imbalance can be resolved by producing 3O*<sub>*2*</sub>*  *
  - *4**KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **2**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *To determine the number of moles of carbon dioxide absorbed and the number of moles of oxygen released, you can use your chemical equation*

  - *4KO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2K*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + 3O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *4 moles of potassium superoxide react with 2 moles of carbon dioxide*
  
    - *Therefore, 1 mole of potassium superoxide will react with *$\frac{2}{4}$* or 0.5 moles of carbon dioxide*
  - *4 moles of potassium superoxide produce 3 moles of oxygen*
  
    - *Therefore, 1 mole of potassium superoxide will produce *$\frac{3}{4}$* or 0.75 moles of oxygen*

parts.problemMd:
The question is about Group 1 elements.

A small piece of a Group 1 element is added to some water in a large trough.

parts.problemMd:
In a further experiment, 0.225 g of sodium is added to an excess of water, and the hydrogen gas is collected.

The equation for the reaction is

2Na (s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → 2NaOH (aq) + H<sub>2 </sub>(g)

Calculate the volume of hydrogen gas collected at room temperature and pressure (rtp).

Give your answer to 2 significant figures.

(24,000 cm<sup>3</sup> at rtp)
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the volume of hydrogen:

- Convert the mass of Na into moles:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{A_{r}}$

amount of Na = $\frac{0.225}{23}$ = 0.00978 mol **[1 mark]**

- Deduce the mole ratio from the equation:

2 moles of Na $\Rightarrow$ 1 mol of H<sub>2</sub> gas

therefore, 0.00978 mol of Na $\Rightarrow$ $\left(\frac{0 . 00978}{2}\right)$ mol of H<sub>2 </sub>gas

= 0.0489 mol of H<sub>2 </sub>gas **[1 mark]**

- Convert the moles of H<sub>2</sub> into volume:

volume = moles x 24,000 cm<sup>3</sup>

volume of H<sub>2</sub> = 0.0489 x 24,000

volume of H<sub>2</sub> = 117.4 cm<sup>3</sup>

volume of H<sub>2</sub> = **120 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> A correct answer without workings also scores all three marks.

> **[exam-tip]**
> It is strongly advised that you show your workings! If you make a mistake, you may still pick up marks, even if you get the final answer wrong.
> 
> Examiner reports show that two common mistakes are made in this type of calculation:
> 
> 1. **Forgetting the mole ratio**
> 
>   - Students often forget to use the 2:1 ratio from the balanced equation.
>   - Always write it down as a separate step to remind yourself.
> 2. **Significant figures**
> 
>   - The question asks for the answer to 2 significant figures.
>   - Forgetting to round 117.39... to 120 would lose you the final mark.
>   - It is good practice to underline this instruction in the question when you first read it.

(1)

(1)
parts.solutionMd:

| ** bromine solution** | solution stays orange | not done | solution turns brown |

ii) The teacher does not add bromine solution to sodium bromide solution because:

- Bromine would not react with (sodium) bromide / bromine cannot displace itself / cannot react with itself **OR **Both solutions contain bromine / the same element / the same halogen **OR **No reaction would take place; **[1 mark] **

parts.problemMd:
A technician sees an unlabelled bottle containing a liquid. He knows that the liquid is a solution of one of these compounds.

- copper(II) bromide
- iron(II) chloride
- iron(II) bromide

parts.solutionMd:
The chemical tests that the technician could use to identify the compound in the solution are:

**Test for cation:**

- Add sodium hydroxide / ammonia (solution); **[1 mark]**
- If blue precipitate forms solution contains copper(II) ion(s) / contains Cu<sup>2+</sup> / is a copper compound;** [1 mark]**
- If green precipitate forms solution contains iron(II) ion(s) / contains Fe<sup>2+</sup> / is an iron compound; **[1 mark] ***If no reagent or incorrect reagent but correct results, award 1 mark*

**Alternative test 2 for cation:**

- Flame test **OR **description of flame test; **[1 mark]**
- If blue-green (flame) solution contains copper(II) ion(s) / contains Cu<sup>2+</sup> / is a copper compound; **[1 mark]** *No third mark available for this test*

**Alternative test 3 for cation:**

- Addition of suitable metal above Cu in reactivity series;** [1 mark]**
- Brown / pink / pink-brown solid forms; **[1 mark]** *No third mark available for this test*

**Test for anion:**

- Add silver nitrate (solution);** [1 mark]**
- If white precipitate forms solution contains chloride ion(s) / contains Cl<sup>-</sup> / is a chloride; **[1 mark]**
- If cream precipitate forms solution contains bromide ion(s) / contains Br<sup>- </sup>/ is a bromide; **[1 mark] ***If no reagent or incorrect reagent but correct results, award 1 mark*

**Alternative test 2 for anion:**

- Add chlorine water (to solution); **[1 mark]**
- If turns orange / yellow / brown solution contains bromide ion(s) / contains Br<sup>-</sup> / is a bromide; **[1 mark]** *No third mark available for this test*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *Make sure you learn the colours of the precipitates produced on the addition of sodium hydroxide solution to help you identify the ions present*

parts.problemMd: Give a chemical test for chlorine.

parts.problemMd: Give a test for bromide ions.

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of electron configuration, why fluorine is more reactive than chlorine.

>   - Explain that this results in a **stronger attraction** from the nucleus for an incoming electron.

parts.problemMd:
The table shows some physical properties of the halogens.

i) Complete the table by predicting a boiling point for chlorine, the state of fluorine at room temperature and the colour of astatine.

| **Halogen** | **Boiling point in °C** | **State at room temperature** | **Colour** |
|---|---|---|---|
| fluorine | -188 |   | yellow |
| chlorine |   | gas | green |
| bromine | 59 | liquid | red-brown |
| iodine | sublimes | solid | grey |
| astatine | 337 | solid |   |

(3)

ii) Why do the halogens have similar chemical properties?

(1)

| ☐ | **A** | they are non-metals |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **B** | they are molecules |
| ☐ | **C** | they have the same number of outer shell electrons |
| ☐ | **D** | they are in the same period of the Periodic Table |
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed table should contain the following information:

- (Fluorine) gas / vapour;** [1 mark]**
- (Chlorine) range between -150°C to 10°C inclusive; **[1 mark]**
- (Astatine) dark grey / black; **[1 mark]**

ii) The halogens have similar chemical properties as:

- **C** / the halogens have the same number of outer shell electrons;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i), blue-black is not an accepted answer for the colour of astatine*
- *You need to be able to recall the basic physical properties and colours of the halogens*

  - *You do not need to remember melting and boiling points but you are expected to know the trend, so chlorine should have a boiling point spaced out between those of fluorine and bromine*
- *The only correct answer is **C** because the halogens are in group 7 and have similar reactions because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shells.*

  - *A** is not correct because the fact halogens are non-metals does not make them react in a similar way.*
  - *B** is not correct because the fact halogens are molecules does not make them react in a similar way.*
  - *D** is not correct because elements in the same period have different numbers of outer shell electrons and react differently.*

parts.problemMd:
Sea water contains bromide ions.

Bromine can be obtained by bubbling chlorine through a sample of sea water.

The ionic equation for the reaction is

Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2Br<sub> </sub><sup>–</sup> (aq) → 2Cl<sup>–</sup> (aq) + Br<sub>2</sub> (aq)

i) Explain which species acts as an oxidising agent in this reaction.

(2)

ii) The reaction occurs because chlorine is more reactive than bromine. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 7. Explain the decrease in reactivity from chlorine to bromine.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The species acts as an oxidising agent in this reaction.

- Oxidising agent is chlorine / Cl<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark] **
- Because chlorine / Cl<sub>2</sub> gains electron(s) / is reduced; **[1 mark] **

ii) The decrease in reactivity from chlorine to bromine is due to :

Any** three** of the following points:

- Bromine and chlorine react by gaining electron / forming 1- or negative ion; **[1 mark] **
- Bromine atom larger (than chlorine atom); **[1 mark] **
- Bromine (atom) has smaller / weaker attraction (from nucleus) for (outer shell) electrons (than chlorine); **[1 mark] **
- So (bromine has) less tendency to gain electron / form negative ion (so less reactive than chlorine); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]  **

- **Remember**: The oxidising agent will itself be reduced

  - If the species has received electrons or the oxidation state has decreased, then it is the oxidising agent
- For part (ii), you could also say

  - Bromine has a larger atomic radius
  - Bromine outer (electron) shell is further from nucleus
  - Bromine atom has more (electron) shells (than chlorine)

parts.problemMd:
Elements in Group 7 react with elements in Group 1 to form ionic compounds.

Which pair of ions both have the electronic configuration 2.8.8?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D.**

- The correct answer is **D** / K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>–</sup> because both have electronic configuration of 2.8.8

  - A potassium atom has 19 electrons so when it loses an electron to form K<sup>+</sup>, it has 18 electrons which gives it the electronic configuration of 2.8.8
  - A chlorine atom has 17 electrons so when it gains an electron to form Cl<sup>-</sup>, it has 18 electrons which gives it the electronic configuration of 2.8.8
- **A** is not correct because Li<sup>+</sup> does not have electronic configuration of 2.8.8 (its electronic configuration is 2)
- **B** is not correct because F<sup>–</sup> does not have electronic configuration of 2.8.8 (its electronic configuration is 2.8)
- **C** is not correct because neither Li<sup>+</sup> nor F<sup>–</sup> have electronic configuration of 2.8.8

parts.problemMd:
The halogens are found in Group 7 of the Periodic Table.

Table 1 shows the melting point and boiling point of some of the halogens.

**Table 1**

| **Element** | **Melting Point in **<sup>**o**</sup>**C** | **Boiling Point in **<sup>**o**</sup>**C** |
|---|---|---|
| Fluorine | -220 | -188 |
| Chlorine | -101 | -25 |
| Bromine | -7 | 59 |
| Iodine | 114 | 184 |

What is the state of chlorine at -100 <sup>o</sup>C **and **at 0 <sup>o</sup>C?  State at -100 <sup>o</sup>C: ____________________ State at 0 <sup>o</sup>C: ____________________
parts.solutionMd:
The state of chlorine at -100 <sup>o</sup>C **and **at 0 <sup>o</sup>C is:

- -100 <sup>o</sup>C: liquid; **[1 mark]**
- 0 <sup>o</sup>C: gas; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *If the temperature is lower than the melting point, the element will be a solid*
- *If the temperature is between the melting point and boiling point then it will have melted but not boiled, i.e. it is a liquid*
- *If the temperature is higher than the boiling point, the element will be a gas*

parts.problemMd: Explain why the boiling point of the Group 7 elements increases as you go down the group as shown in Table 1.
parts.solutionMd:
The boiling point increases down Group 7 because:

- The size of the molecules increases **OR** The relative formula / molecular mass increases; **[1 mark]**
- The intermolecular force increases;** [1 mark]**
- More energy is needed to overcome the intermolecular forces;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Careful**: When referring to the melting/boiling point of covalent molecules, there are no covalent bonds broken*
- *The molecules are moving further apart from each other but the molecules themselves remain intact*
- *You would not gain the last mark if you made any references to breaking bonds*

parts.problemMd: The halogens all react with hydrogen to form the corresponding hydrogen halide. Explain why the halogens all react in a similar way.
parts.solutionMd:
The halogens all react similarly with hydrogen because:

- The reactivity with hydrogen depends on gaining/sharing electrons; **[1 mark]**
- They all have the same number / 7 electrons in their <u>outer</u> shell; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *It is not sufficient to say they all have the same number / 7 electrons as this is incorrect - you **must** specify that there have the same number of electrons in the outer shell to gain the mark*

parts.problemMd: Predict and explain the difference in the rate of the reaction between hydrogen with chlorine and between hydrogen and iodine.
parts.solutionMd:
The difference in rate of reaction is:

- Hydrogen with chlorine will have a quicker rate of reaction (than hydrogen with iodine); **[1 mark]**

The explanation for the difference is:

- Chlorine has fewer shells than iodine / less shielding; **[1 mark]**
- So chlorine gains electrons more easily / electrons are more easily attracted towards the nucleus; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Use the mark scheme to help you structure your answer*
- *3 marks are available so 1 mark will be to predict the difference in the rate of reaction and 2 marks to explain why*
- *This requires you to apply your knowledge about why Group 7 elements become less reactive as you go down the group*

parts.problemMd:
Chorine is a halogen.

Chlorine reacts with aqueous potassium iodide to form aqueous potassium chloride and iodine.

i) Give the balanced symbol equation for this reaction.

(2)

ii) State what would be seen when this reaction occurs.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The balanced symbol equation for this reaction is:

Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2KI → 2KCl + I<sub>2</sub>

- Correct reactants and products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing;** [1 mark]**

ii) When this reaction occurs, you would see:

- (Liquid changes from colourless to ) yellow / orange / brown / red;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You are expected to know the formulae for chlorine and potassium iodide and know the products formed from this displacement reaction*
- *Potassium iodide is colourless, when you add chlorine, the solution will turn brown due to the formation of iodine in the solution*
- *If potassium bromide had been used, the solution would have turned yellow-orange as bromine is formed*

parts.problemMd: This reaction is a redox reaction. Explain, using half equations, what is being oxidised and what is being reduced.
parts.solutionMd:
To explain what is being oxidised and what is being reduced:

- Iodine is oxidised **AND **as it / iodide ion loses an electron; **[1 mark]**
- 2I<sup>– </sup>→ I<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>– </sup>  ;** [1 mark]**
- Chlorine is reduced **AND **as it gains electrons; **[1 mark]**
- Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>– </sup>→ 2Cl<sup>–</sup>  ; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Remember**: **OIL RIG**: **O**xidation **I**s **L**oss, **R**eduction **I**s **G**ain of electrons*
- *You need to show, using half equations, what is gaining electrons and what is losing electrons*
- *Two iodide ions each lose one electron so are oxidised to form an iodine molecule*
- *Chlorine forms two chloride ions by gaining two electrons so is reduced *
- *You may not be used to using half equations in this context as you may have used them only when looking at the reactions that occur at each electrode in electrolysis, but the principle behind constructing them is exactly the same*

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of their electronic configuration, why chlorine is more reactive than iodine.
parts.solutionMd:
Chlorine is more reactive than iodine because:

- When they / chlorine and iodine react, they gain an electron / form a 1- ion / negative ion;** [1 mark]**
- An electron is more strongly attracted to a chlorine atom than to an iodine atom **OR** Chlorine has a greater tendency to gain an electron / form a 1- ion / negative ion; **[1 mark]**
- Because a chlorine atom is smaller  **OR** Outer electrons in a chlorine atom are closer to the nucleus **OR** More shielding between the nucleus of an iodine atom and outer electrons; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The reasons for the relative reactivity of the halogens are frequently examined, so this is an explanation well worth learning*
- *Remember**: Reactivity of the halogen is a measure of how easily it will gain an electron to complete its outer shell*
- *You need to show a clear understanding of why the electron is more easily gained by chlorine*

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine reacts with potassium to form the solid, potassium chloride.

Write the balanced symbol equation for this reaction, including state symbols.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation for this reaction, including state symbols is:

2K (s) + Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2KCl (s)

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**
- Correct state symbols;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You should know the formulae for the reactants and products in this equation, and it is a straightforward equation to balance*
- *Remember to include state symbols, as prompted in the question*
- *You are told that potassium chloride is a solid - often students overlook the information given in the question, leading them to give an incorrect state symbol, so make sure you read the question carefully*
- *You should know that chlorine is a gas and that potassium is a solid - think about the reactions of Group 1 metals!*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about gases in the atmosphere.

A teacher uses this apparatus to determine the percentage of oxygen in air.

![Diagram of a setup with two gas syringes connected to a tube containing pieces of copper wire. One gas syringe contains 50 cm³ of air, and the other is empty.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/001-diagram-of-a-setup-with-two-gas-syringes-connect.png)

The teacher heats the copper wire strongly and passes the air in the syringe from one side to the other.

She then lets the apparatus cool down and she measures the volume of air in the syringe.

i) State the appearance of the copper wire after heating.

[1]

ii) Write an equation for the reaction between copper and oxygen.

[1]

iii) Explain why the teacher leaves the apparatus to cool down before taking a reading of the volume.

[1]

iv) Explain why the teacher uses copper wire rather than a piece of copper.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) After heating, the copper wire is:
> 
> - Black (solid) **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The equation for the reaction between copper and oxygen is:
> 
> - 2Cu + O<sub>2</sub> → 2CuO **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The apparatus needs to cool down before taking a reading of the volume because:
> 
> - To allow the gas to cool to room temperature 
> **OR**
> Air expands when heated / contracts when cooled **[1 mark]**
> 
> iv) Copper wire is used rather than a piece of copper because:
> 
> - Copper wire has a larger surface area **[1 mark]**
> - So, the rate of reaction is faster **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) Examiner reports often show that students are uncertain about the colour changes for copper compounds. It is worth memorising the key ones:
> 
> - Copper metal: pink-brown / orange-brown

> iv) When a question asks "why" one form of a solid is used over another (e.g., wire vs. a lump, or powder vs. large chips), the answer is almost always about surface area and its effect on the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd: Calculate the expected volume of gas in the syringe at room temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the expected volume of gas in the syringe at room temperature:

**Method 1: Calculating the volume of gas that remains**

- Calculate the percentage of other gases in air:

% other gases = 100% - 21% = 79% **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume of these unreacted gases:

volume remaining = 50 cm<sup>3</sup> × $\frac{79}{100}$ **[1 mark]**

volume remaining = **39.5 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

**Method 2: Calculating the volume of oxygen that reacts**

- State the percentage of oxygen:

oxygen = 21% **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the volume of oxygen that reacts with the copper:

volume of oxygen = 50 cm<sup>3</sup> × $\frac{21}{100}$ = 10.5 cm<sup>3</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Subtract the volume of reacted oxygen from the initial volume:

final volume = 50 - 10.5

final volume = **39.5 cm**<sup>**3**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> A correct answer of 39.5 with no working scores 3 marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> To answer this question, you must recall the approximate percentage of oxygen in the air (~21%).
> 
> You can:
> 
> - Either calculate the volume of the gases that **do not react** (79% of the total)
> - Or calculate the volume of oxygen that **does react** (21% of the total) and subtract it from the starting volume
> 
> Both methods will give you the same correct answer.

parts.problemMd:

Give one reason why this was not the expected result.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> One reason why this was not the expected result is:
> 
> - The reaction was incomplete / did not go to completion **OR** Not all the oxygen was used up **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In this question, you have to use the answer to the previous part to come up with the correct explanation. If your previous answer was less than the expected volume, you might still get credit based on your answer.
> 
> To answer this question, you must first compare the experimental result with your calculated answer from part (b).
> 
> - **Experimental result:** 42 cm<sup>3</sup>
> - **Calculated (expected) result:** 39.5 cm<sup>3</sup>
> 
> The experimental volume is **higher** than expected. This means that **less oxygen was removed** from the air than predicted. The most likely reason for this is that the reaction was incomplete, and some of the oxygen did not react with the copper.
> 
> If the volume was less than expected, then you could say that air leaks were responsible.

parts.problemMd:
Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide are gases with simple molecular structures.

Explain why these substances have low melting and boiling points.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Sulfur dioxide and carbon dioxide have low melting and boiling points because:
> 
> - The molecules have <u>weak </u>intermolecular forces of attraction **[1 mark]**
> - A small amount of energy is needed to overcome them** [1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports show that the most common mistake is to say that "weak covalent bonds are broken". This is incorrect and will score zero marks.
> 
> Remember:
> 
> - **Covalent bonds** are the strong bonds **inside** the molecules (e.g., between the S and O atoms). These **do not break** when the substance melts or boils.
> - **Intermolecular forces** are the weak forces **between** the molecules. It is these weak forces that are overcome during melting and boiling.

**[2 marks]**

> To solve this, work out the electrons for each atom:

ii)  A chemical equation for this reaction of copper(II) carbonate:

- CuCO<sub>3</sub> →  CuO + CO<sub>2</sub> ; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You can be expected to know the colour of copper carbonate and copper oxide*

  - *Examiners often comment about how the colours of certain compounds are not well known*
- *Remember: **Metal carbonate → metal oxide + carbon dioxide*

  - *MCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → MO + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>

parts.problemMd:
There is a relationship between the position of a metal in the reactivity series and how easily the metal carbonate reacts when heated.

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
This question is about determining the percentage composition by volume of a mixture of three gases, oxygen, carbon dioxide and argon in air.

Two experiments are done to determine the percentage composition by volume of oxygen.

In experiment 1, a student connects a gas syringe to a conical flask filled with iron filings. The diagram shows the apparatus the student uses.

![2-3-3a-h-a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/012-2-3-3a-h-a.png)

i) Give two changes the student needs to make to the apparatus in experiment 1 to find the percentage by volume of oxygen in a sample of air.

(2)

In experiment 2, two 100 cm<sup>3</sup> gas syringes are connected to a reaction tube containing copper powder. The sample of air is passed over hot copper oxide. The diagram shows the apparatus that is used.

![2-3-3a-h-b](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/013-2-3-3a-h-b.png)

ii) Explain why both syringes should not be filled with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) Two changes that the student needs to make to the apparatus to find the percentage by volume of oxygen in a sample of air are:

- Use wet iron filings;** [1 mark]**
- Use a gas syringe filled with air / set to 100 cm<sup>3</sup>  **OR **Not use a gas syringe with no air inside / at 0 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

ii) Both syringes should not be filled with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of air because:

Any **one **of the following pairs:

Pair 1

- When the apparatus is heated, the air / gases will spread out; **[1 mark]**
- Which can cause the syringes to open; **[1 mark]**

Pair 2

- When the air / gas is pushed from one syringe to the other syringe, the syringe will open; **[1 mark]**
- As 100 cm<sup>3</sup> syringes cannot hold (over) 200 cm<sup>3</sup> of air; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *The reaction that will happen is the rusting of iron*
  - *The oxygen in the conical flask will react very slowly with the iron filings*
  
    - *Adding water / making the iron filings wet will make the reaction happen quicker / on a more appropriate timescale*
  - *To be able to calculate the percentage by volume of oxygen, you will need a measurement of how much oxygen has been removed from the air*
  
    - *This means that you need to have the gas syringe filled with 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of air*
    - *This allows you to see how much oxygen has reacted from the air*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *One syringe should be full and the other empty*
  - *This allows you to pass the air over the hot copper powder, from one syringe to the other*
  - *As the reaction proceeds, the total volume of air in the syringes will decrease as the oxygen reacts*

parts.problemMd:
When the apparatus in experiment 2 is set up correctly, the mixture of gases is passed over the hot copper powder.

The total volume of the mixture of gases in the syringes at the start is 76 cm<sup>3</sup>.

The total volume of the mixture of gases in the syringes at the end is 64 cm<sup>3</sup>.

i) Calculate the percentage by volume of oxygen in the mixture of gases.

(2)

ii) Explain how the answer to part (i) suggests that all of the oxygen has not reacted.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The percentage by volume of oxygen in the mixture of gases is:

- Volume of oxygen = 12 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Percentage of oxygen = 15.8%; **[1 mark]**

ii) The answer to part (i) suggests that all of the oxygen has not reacted because:

- The percentage of oxygen in the air is roughly 20 / 21%; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The volume of oxygen that reacts is 76 - 64 = 12 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *Therefore, the percentage of oxygen in the air is* $\frac{12}{76}\times100$* = 15.8%*
- *The percentage of oxygen in the air would be expected to be around 20 / 21%*
- *Since the percentage of oxygen in the air according to this experiment is less than 20 / 21%, it suggests that not all of the oxygen has reacted*

parts.problemMd:
To determine the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air, the student suggests adapting the apparatus in experiment 2.

They suggest replacing the reaction tube containing copper powder with a conical flask containing limewater, as shown.

![2-3-3c-h-per-cent-of-co2-in-air](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/014-2-3-3c-h-per-cent-of-co2-in-air.png)

Explain why this experiment will not show the presence of carbon dioxide and give two reasons why this experiment will not allow the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air to be determined.
parts.solutionMd:
This experiment will not show the presence of carbon dioxide and will not allow the percentage of carbon dioxide in the air to be determined because:

Not showing the presence of carbon dioxide:

- The air / gas is not bubbled through the limewater **OR **The air / gas does not pass through the limewater **OR **The left-hand tube is not in the limewater / does not reach the limewater; **[1 mark]**
- So, the limewater will not turn cloudy (to confirm the presence of carbon dioxide);** [1 mark]**

Not allowing the determination of the percentage of carbon dioxide: Any **two** of the following:

- The carbon dioxide (in the air / gas) is not removed / does not react with the limewater;** [1 mark]**
- The expected percentage of carbon dioxide (in the air / gas) is too small / only 0.04%;** [1 mark]**
- The divisions / scale on the gas syringes is too large (for meaningful results) **OR **The gas syringes are too big / large; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Remember:** The chemical test for carbon dioxide is that the gas is bubbled through limewater, which turns cloudy*

  - *The apparatus in this experiment does not allow the gas to bubble through the limewater*
  - *This means that the carbon dioxide does not react with the limewater*
  - *Therefore, there can be no positive test for carbon dioxide*
- *The syringes used in this experiment are 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* and the expected percentage of carbon dioxide in the air is around 0.04%*

  - *If the total volume of air in both gas syringes, the conical flask and the tubes was 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, then you would expect to see a decrease in the total volume of 0.04 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *The divisions / scale on the 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* gas syringes will be too large to accurately measure this change in volume *

Argon is extremely unreactive because:

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the combustion of fuels and atmospheric pollution.

Methane is a common fuel that can be combusted.

CH<sub>4</sub> (g) + 2O<sub>2</sub> (g) → CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Calculate the mass of methane that is required to produce 50.0 g of carbon dioxide.
parts.solutionMd:
The volume of methane required to produce 50.0 g of carbon dioxide is:

- Moles of carbon dioxide = 1.137 **AND **Moles of methane = 1.137;** [1 mark]**
- Mass of methane = 18.2 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *First, you need to calculate the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of carbon dioxide and methane*

  - *Carbon dioxide, CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* = 12 + (2 x 16) = 44*
  - *Methane, CH*<sub>*4*</sub>* = 12 + (4 x 1) = 16*
- *The main calculation part of this question uses variations of the moles =* $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$ *equation*
- *Then, you need to calculate the moles of carbon dioxide *

  - $\frac{50.0}{44}$ *= 1.137*
- *Since 1 mole of methane reacts to form 1 mole of carbon dioxide, the number of moles of methane is also 1.137*
- *Finally, you calculate the mass of methane*

  - *1.137 x 16 = 18.2 g*

parts.problemMd:
An experiment is set up to show the products of combustion for methane.

![2-3-4b-h-products-of-combustion-incorrect-set-up](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/004-2-3-4b-h-products-of-combustion-incorrect-set-up.png)

i) Write a chemical equation for the reaction that occurs in the limewater as it gives a positive test for one of the combustion products.

(1)

ii) The cobalt chloride paper tests for the other combustion product. Explain why the set-up of this apparatus does not prove that this combustion product is produced.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The chemical equation for the reaction that occurs in the limewater is:

- Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> → CaCO<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O;** [1 mark]**

ii) The set-up of this apparatus does not prove that this combustion product is produced because:

- Cobalt chloride tests for water **OR **Cobalt chloride changes <u>from blue to pink</u> with water; **[1 mark]**
- It can change due to the water from limewater / the limewater solution / Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq); **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Limewater is calcium hydroxide with the chemical formula Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq)*

  - *This reacts with carbon dioxide to give a cloudy / milky / white precipitate of calcium carbonate, CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* (s), and water*
  
    - *Ca(OH)*<sub>*2*</sub>* + CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CaCO*<sub>*3*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This equation requires no balancing, which explains why part (i) is only for one mark*
- *Cobalt chloride paper is blue when dry *

  - *This colour changes to pink when it is wet*
  - *The gases produced from the combustion of methane are carbon dioxide and water, which pass through the apparatus*
  - *Since the gases pass into the limewater first, it is likely that the water would condense inside the limewater solution*
  - *Even if the water did not condense in the limewater, the gases that pass through to the cobalt chloride paper have passed through the limewater solution*
  
    - *This means that the cobalt chloride paper could turn pink due to the combustion product **OR** due to the water from the limewater solution*

parts.problemMd:
Fossil fuels are burned in car engines releasing carbon dioxide and other gases. Rainwater is acidic because carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid along with other acidic pollutant gases, such as nitrogen dioxide, dissolving in the water.

i) Give the name of the acid that forms when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water.

(1)

ii) Explain how nitrogen dioxide is produced in a car engine if there are no nitrogen-based impurities in fossil fuels?

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The name of the acid that forms when nitrogen dioxide dissolves in water is:

- Nitric acid / HNO<sub>3</sub> **OR **Nitrous acid / HNO<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

ii) Nitrogen dioxide is produced in a car engine when there are no nitrogen-based impurities in fossil fuels because:

- Fossil fuels are burned / combusted at high temperatures (in a car engine); **[1 mark]**
- So, nitrogen (from the air) reacts with oxygen (from the air) **OR **N<sub>2</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub> **AND **the nitrogen comes from the air; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The most common answer to this question is nitric acid*

  - *NO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O → HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* (nitric acid)*
- *The atmosphere is approximately 78% nitrogen*

  - *This means that the air that is taken into a car engine during combustion can react*
  - *Although nitrogen is relatively unreactive, at the high temperatures inside a car engine it will react with oxygen to form nitrogen oxides which are also responsible for acid rain*

parts.problemMd: Explain how reducing the amount of sulfur in fossil fuels reduces the erosion of limestone.
parts.solutionMd:
Reducing the amount of sulfur in fossil fuels reduces the erosion of limestone because:

- Sulfur reacts with oxygen / burns / combusts to form sulfur dioxide / SO<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Reducing sulfur in fossil fuels means that less sulfur dioxide is emitted; **[1 mark]**
- Which means there is less acid rain to react with limestone; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *This question tests your knowledge of how the products of combustion of impurities cause pollution and the effects*
- *Sulfur forms sulfur dioxide, which is linked to acid rain*
- *The sulfurous / sulfuric acid formed reacts with limestone as it is a carbonate*

  - *Metal carbonate + acid → metal salt + carbon dioxide + water*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the percentage of oxygen in the air.

The percentage of oxygen in the air can be determined by observing the formation of hydrated iron(III) oxide.

Write the balanced chemical equation for the formation of iron(III) oxide from iron.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced chemical equation for the formation of iron(III) oxide from iron is:

4Fe + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

- Correct chemical formulae;** [1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Careful:** The question asks for the formation of iron(III) oxide, **not** hydrated iron(III) oxide*
- *The chemical formula of iron(III) oxide is Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>

  - *The Roman numeral tells you that the iron is Fe*<sup>*3+*</sup>
  - *Oxygen is O*<sup>*2–*</sup>
  - *To balance the charges, you need two irons and three oxygens *
  - *This gives the formula Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *Iron reacts with oxygen to form iron(III) oxide*

  - *Fe + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *There are two oxygen atoms on the left-hand side and three oxygen atoms on the right-hand side*

  - *So, working with six oxygen atoms on both sides will allow us to begin balancing the equation*
  - *Fe + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *There are now four iron atoms on the right-hand side and only one on the left-hand side*

  - *This can be solved by using four iron atoms on the left-hand side*
  - *4**Fe + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*<sub>*3*</sub>

parts.problemMd:
A student sets up this apparatus to observe the formation of hydrated iron(III) oxide.

![2-3-5b-h-per-cent-of-air-using-iron-filings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/006-2-3-5b-h-per-cent-of-air-using-iron-filings.png)

The reading on the syringe is recorded at the start of the experiment. The apparatus is then left for a week before the reading on the syringe is recorded again.

The table shows the initial reading of the syringe.

| syringe reading at start / cm<sup>3</sup> | 100 |
|---|---|
| syringe reading at end / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |
| volume of oxygen used / cm<sup>3</sup> |   |

The atmosphere is comprised of 20% oxygen. Complete the table to show the expected results.
parts.solutionMd:
To complete the table for the expected results:

| syringe reading at start / cm<sup>3</sup> | 100 |
|---|---|
| syringe reading at end / cm<sup>3</sup> | 59 |
| volume of oxygen used / cm<sup>3</sup> | 41 |

- Total volume of air = 205 (cm<sup>3</sup>) **AND **Volume of oxygen used = 41 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- Syringe reading at end = 59 cm<sup>3</sup>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Careful:** The table and gas syringe in the diagram are actually distractions to the main calculation*

  - *Many students will try to read the value from the gas syringe*
  
    - *It does appear to be around 52 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* which would give a volume of 48 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen used*
    - *But, the image is not clear enough for you to be able to do this*
  - *Some students will rush to a final syringe reading of 80 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* and the volume of oxygen used as 20 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  
    - *This is because the initial syringe reading is 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
    - *If 20% of this is oxygen, then 20 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* will be used giving the final syringe reading as 80 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
    - *This is incorrect as it does not account for the air in the delivery tube and conical flask*
- *You have to calculate 20% of the **total** volume of air in the apparatus to work out how much oxygen will be used up*

  - *Total volume = 100 + 5 + 100 = 205 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *20% of the total volume =* $\frac{205}{100}\times20$ *OR **205 x 0.2 = 41 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *This is the volume of oxygen that is used up and will cause the reading on the syringe to decrease by 41 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>

  - *100 - 41 = 59 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>

parts.problemMd:
A student completes a second experiment.

The diagram shows the readings on the student's experiment.

![2-3-5c-h-syringe-readings](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-3-gases-in-the-atmosphere/assets/007-2-3-5c-h-syringe-readings.png)

The student completes their results table, as shown, to calculate that the percentage of oxygen in the air is 21.5%.

| syringe reading at start / cm<sup>3</sup> | 84 |
|---|---|
| syringe reading at end / cm<sup>3</sup> | 40 |
| volume of oxygen used / cm<sup>3</sup> | 44 |

Identify the error that the student has made and calculate the correct percentage of oxygen in the air.
parts.solutionMd:
The error that the student has made is:

- The syringe reading at the start is not 84 (cm<sup>3</sup>) **OR **The syringe reading at the start should be 76 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

To calculate the correct percentage of oxygen in the air:

- Volume of oxygen used = 36 (cm<sup>3</sup>);** [1 mark]**
- Percentage of oxygen in the air = 17.6(%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *It is not enough to say that the syringe reading at the start is wrong*

  - *You have the information available and should be giving an answer using the specific values shown*
- *The student has made the common mistake of misreading the value on the syringe at the start of the experiment *

  - *Each division on the syringe represents 2 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *But the scale is decreasing from left to right, so the reading should be 80 - 4 = 76 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *This mistake is even easier to make / miss, when you are given the values*
- *This means that the calculation for the percentage of oxygen in the air will be:*

  - $\frac{36}{205}\times100$ *= 17.6%*

parts.problemMd:
Another set of experiments featured changes to the apparatus.

i) Explain how the use of dry iron filings would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air.

(3)

ii) Explain how leaving the apparatus in a warm place for 1 week would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) How the use of dry iron filings would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air:

- The percentage (of oxygen in the air) would be lower / less / decrease; **[1 mark]**

Explanation:

- Rusting requires water; **[1 mark]**
- So, less / no oxygen would react **OR **So, the volume of oxygen used would decrease / be less; **[1 mark]**

ii) How leaving the apparatus in a warm place for 1 week would affect the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air:

- The percentage (of oxygen in the air) would not change **OR **There will be no effect;** [1 mark]**

Explanation:

- The reaction would proceed / happen quicker / faster; **[1 mark]**
- But, the overall volume of oxygen used up will still be the same as the iron filings are in excess; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *These explain the effect type questions are always considered more challenging, with examiners often commenting on how poor the general standard of answers was*
- *Take your time to identify what the change is, the immediate effect on the rusting reaction and then the effect on the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air*
- *For part (i)*

  - *The change is the lack of water*
  - *Water is required for rusting to happen*
  - *With dry iron filings, there will be less rusting*
  - *This means that less oxygen will be used up*
  - *Therefore, the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air will appear less than it is   *
- *For part (ii)*

  - *The change is the addition of heat*
  - *Heat does not affect the overall chemical reaction, it affects the rate*
  - *For this experiment, warmer conditions mean that the reaction will happen quicker*
  - *The volume of oxygen used must be the same as the iron filings are still wet and in excess*
  - *Therefore, there will be no change to the calculated percentage of oxygen in the air*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about rusting.

A simplified formula for rust is Fe<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>

i) Name the two substances needed for iron to rust.

(2)

ii) Give the chemical name for rust.

(1)

iii) What type of reaction occurs in the rusting of iron?

(1)

| **A** | combustion |
|---|---|
| **B** | neutralisation |
| **C** | oxidation |
| **D** | thermal decomposition |
parts.solutionMd:
i) The two substances needed for iron to rust are:

- Oxygen / O<sub>2</sub>  **OR **Air; **[1 mark]**
- Water / H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

ii) The chemical name for rust is:

- (Hydrated) iron(III) oxide; **[1 mark]**

iii) The type of reaction that occurs when iron rusts is:

- **C** / oxidation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Rusting is the reaction of iron with oxygen, which is oxidation*
- *The reaction / rusting requires both water and oxygen*
- *Most people think that rust is iron oxide but it is hydrated iron(III) oxide more specifically *

  - *This is why iron(II) oxide is not accepted*

parts.problemMd:
Some iron objects are coated with a layer of zinc to prevent rusting.

i) Name this type of rust prevention.

(1)

ii) Explain how this type of rust prevention continues to protect iron when the layer of zinc is damaged.

(2)

iii) Give two other methods used to prevent iron from rusting.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) This type of rust prevention is:

- Galvanising / galvanisation; **[1 mark]**

ii) This type of rust prevention continues to protect iron when the layer of zinc is damaged because:

- Zinc is more reactive than iron 
**OR **
Zinc is higher in the reactivity series than iron; **[1 mark]**
- So, zinc reacts / oxidised / corrodes before iron; **[1 mark]**

iii) Two other methods used to prevent iron from rusting are:

Any **two **of the following:

- Painting; **[1 mark]**
- Powder / plastic coating; **[1 mark]**
- Oiling / greasing; **[1 mark]**
- Chromium plating; **[1 mark]**
- Sacrificial protection; **[1 mark]**
- Cathodic protection; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *For part (ii), talking about zinc rusting loses this mark *
- *The most common methods to prevent iron from rusting are:*

  - *Painting*
  - *Oiling / greasing*
  
    - *Painting / oiling / greasing are barrier methods that prevent oxygen / water getting to the iron*
  - *Galvanising*
  
    - *This uses the higher reactivity of zinc to prevent iron from rusting*
    - *The oxygen will react preferentially with the zinc*

parts.problemMd: What type of reaction occurs when iron rusts?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The type of reaction which occurs when iron rusts is Oxidation.
- Iron reacts with oxygen and water to form hydrated iron (III) oxide
- The iron is oxidised so it is therefore an oxidation reaction

parts.problemMd: Which metal is most suitable for galvanizing iron?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The metal most suitable for galvanizing iron is Zinc.
- Zinc is used to galvanize iron because it is higher up in the reactivity series
- The iron is coated with a layer of zinc so that ZnCO<sub>3</sub> is formed when zinc reacts with oxygen and carbon dioxide in the air thereby protecting the iron
- If the coating is damaged or scratched, the iron is still protected from rusting because zinc preferentially corrodes
- **A** and **B** are incorrect as they are less reactive than iron
- **C** is incorrect as even though sodium is more reactive than iron, sodium reacts vigorously with water so cannot be used

Two substances that are needed to cause iron to rust are:

- Oxygen / O<sub>2</sub>
**OR**
Air; **[1 mark]**
- H<sub>2</sub>O / Water / water vapour 
**OR **
Moisture; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *It doesn't matter which way round you give the two substances*
- *Although, air and moisture are accepted answers, it is better to learn that the two substances needed for rusting are oxygen and water*

parts.problemMd:
The box gives the names of some substances.

| calcium | copper | gold |

parts.problemMd:
This question is about rusting.

When iron rusts, it reacts with oxygen in the air.

A student uses the rusting of iron to find the percentage of oxygen in a sample of air.

The diagram shows the apparatus.

![2021-ja1c-q4a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-4-reactivity-series/assets/002-2021-ja1c-q4a.png)

These are the student’s results.

volume of air in conical flask and connecting tube = 265 cm<sup>3</sup>

volume of air in gas syringe at start = 100 cm<sup>3</sup>

volume of air in gas syringe at end = 25 cm<sup>3</sup>

Calculate the percentage of oxygen in the sample of air using the student’s results.

percentage of oxygen = .............................................................. %
parts.solutionMd:
The percentage of oxygen in the sample of air is:

- (Volume of oxygen =) 100 – 25 
**OR **
75 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{75}{365}\times100$; **[1 mark]**
- = 20.5 (%); [1 mark]

**Alternative method:**

- (Volume of air left =) 265 + 25 
**OR** 
290 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{290}{365}\times100$ **OR** 79.5 (%); **[1 mark]**
- (100-79.5 =) 20.5 (%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *A correct answer of 20.5 % with or without working scores 3 marks*
- *Careful**: The total volume of air needs to take into account the volume of air in the syringe **and** the volume of air in the conical flask and connecting tube = 100 + 265 = 365 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *Oxygen is used as it reacts with iron as it rusts, removing the oxygen from the syringe*
- *The volume of oxygen in the air = 100 - 25 = 75 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
- *To calculate the percentage of oxygen in the air, use the equation:*

$\frac{volume of oxygen in the air}{volume of air} \times 100 = \frac{75}{365} \times 100 = 20 . 5 \%$

- *A common error would be to use the volume of gas in the conical flask and connecting tube instead of the total volume of gas, i.e. divide by 265 instead of 365*

  - *This would give you a final answer of 28.3% and you would be awarded 2 marks for this*
