parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- One mole of any gas occupies the same volume, 24 dm<sup>3</sup> at room temperature and pressure
- The balanced symbol equation shows for every 2 moles of SO<sub>2</sub>, 2 moles of SO<sub>3</sub> are produced (if it goes to completion)
- As the number of moles are the same, the volume of SO<sub>3</sub> produced from 750 cm<sup>3</sup> of SO<sub>2</sub> will be the same

volume of oxygen = .............................. dm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:

- 1⁄2 x 750 
**OR **
375 (dm<sup>3</sup>);** [1 mark]**

The mass, in kilograms, of 750 dm<sup>3</sup> of sulfur dioxide, measured at room temperature and pressure is:

  - *moles = *$\frac{volume \left(dm^{3}\right)}{24}$

parts.problemMd:
The reaction to produce sulfur trioxide reaches an equilibrium.

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

The forward reaction is exothermic. The rate of attainment of equilibrium and the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide are affected by pressure and temperature.

A manufacturer considered two sets of conditions, A and B, for this reaction.

In each case sulfur dioxide is mixed with excess oxygen.

The manufacturer changed the temperature and the pressure and only used a catalyst in B.

The sets of conditions A and B are shown in Figure 7.

| set of conditions | pressure in atm | temperature in °C | catalyst |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2 | 680 | no catalyst used |
| B | 4 | 425 | catalyst used |

**Figure 7**

The manufacturer chooses set of conditions B rather than set of conditions A.

Explain, by considering the effect of changing the conditions on the rate of attainment of equilibrium and on the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide, why the manufacturer chooses the set of conditions B rather than the set of conditions A.
parts.solutionMd:
The manufacturer chooses the set of conditions B rather than the set of conditions A because:

Chemical ideas expressed:

**Temperature**:

- The equilibrium is reached faster because of the higher temperature in set A 
**OR **
The equilibrium is reached slower because of the lower temperature in set B
- The higher temperature means that there are more frequent collisions because molecules have more energy in set A 
**OR **
The lower temperature means that there are less frequent collisions because molecules have less energy in set B
- The decrease in temperature increases the equilibrium yield but the system takes longer to reach equilibrium
- The temperature chosen for optimum conditions
- The yield lowers / decreases as the forward reaction is exothermic
- A high temperature favours the backwards reaction, which is endothermic
- The equilibrium is reached faster because of the higher pressure in set B 
**OR **
The equilibrium is reached slower because of the lower pressure in set A

**Pressure:**

- Higher pressure causes molecules to be closer together so there are more frequent collisions in set B 
**OR **
Lower pressure causes molecules to be further apart so there are less frequent collisions in set A
- The yield is higher because the products occupy a smaller volume than reactants for set B

**Catalyst:**

- The catalyst used in set B causes the equilibrium to be reached faster
- A catalyst increases the rate of both forward and backward reactions
- The equilibrium position is not affected so the catalyst does not affect the yield

**Level 1:** **(1−2 marks)**

- A basic answer with some chemical ideas, missing information, using simple language and not presented in a logical order

**Level 2:**** ****(3−4 marks)**

- A relevant answer with confidently expressed chemical ideas, a few details missing and some chemical terms included

**Level 3:** **(5−6 marks)**

- A well developed answer that covers chemical ideas in a detailed and logical way, using a wide range of chemical terms

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> * Level 1 answer could be:*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 2 conditions*
- *A detailed explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 1 condition but may lack a full explanation*

> *An example of a Level 1 answer scoring 2 marks would be:*

> *A lower temperature is used as the forward reaction is exothermic.  A catalyst speeds up the rate of the reaction.*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of temperature and use of a catalyst (2)*

> *Level 2 answer could be:*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 3 conditions*
- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 1 condition **AND **a detailed explanation in terms of 1 other condition*

> *An example of a Level 2 answer scoring 4 marks would be:*

> *Higher pressure is favoured because the rate of reaction is quicker. A catalyst would not affect the yield but it speeds up the time taken to reach equilibrium as it increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reaction, so it reduces the need for higher temperatures.*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of pressure and** **a detailed explanation in terms of the use of a catalyst (4)*

> *Level 3 answer could be:*

- *A detailed explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 2 or more conditions*

> *An example of a Level 3 answer scoring 6 marks would be:*

> *A lower temperature gives a higher yield because the forward reaction is exothermic, so decreasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium position to the right.*

> *A higher pressure gives a higher yield because there are fewer gas molecules on the product side, so increasing pressure favours the forward reaction.*

> *Although a lower temperature would reduce the rate of reaction, a catalyst is used to speed up the rate and allow equilibrium to be reached more quickly.*

> *So condition B is chosen because it increases both the yield (by favouring the forward reaction) and the rate (due to the catalyst and higher pressure).*

- *A detailed explanation of why B was chosen in terms of temperature and pressure and a simple explanation in terms of a catalyst (6)*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about equilibrium.

An ionic equation for the reaction between iron (III), Fe<sup>3+</sup> and thiocyanate ions, SCN<sup>2+</sup> is shown below:

At room temperature, the mixture of the equilibrium solution is orange.

|   | Fe<sup>3+</sup> (aq)      + | SCN<sup>-</sup> (aq)       ⇌ | FeSCN<sup>2+ </sup>(aq) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Colour of solution | yellow | colourless | red |

Which solvent would be used to dissolve the ions in this reaction?

parts.problemMd: Explain the effect, if any, of changing pressure on the colour of the equilibrium mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
The effect of pressure will be:

- No effect on the change of colour; **[1 mark]**
- The position of equilibrium does not change; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) there are no gases present 
**OR** 
There are only ions in aqueous solutions present; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember:** pressure will only affect reactions that involve gases so look carefully at the equation *
- *Look at the number of marks to help you*

  - *What is the effect on the colour? There is no effect on the colour*
  - *Why is there no effect? Because the position of the equilibrium doesn't change*

parts.problemMd:
A few drops of a colourless solution containing a high concentration of Fe<sup>3+</sup> ions are added to the orange equilibrium mixture.

Explain the colour change observed.
parts.solutionMd:
The colour change observed is:

- The mixture becomes (more) red; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) the position of) equilibrium moves to the right 
**OR** 
(Because) the concentration of Fe<sup>3+</sup> increases 
**OR** 
(Because) the forward reaction is favoured; **[1 mark]**
- (So that) the concentration of Fe<sup>3+</sup> is reduced / so that the increase in Fe<sup>3+</sup> is counteracted;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember: **When a condition is changed (temperature, pressure, concentration), the system will oppose the change made*
- *So if the concentration of Fe*<sup>*3+ *</sup>*is increased then the system will try and reduce the concentration*
- *In order to do this, the rate of the forward reaction will increase and more  FeSCN*<sup>*2+ *</sup>*will be produced which is red*

parts.problemMd:
A water bath is set up at a temperature below room temperature.

When a test tube containing the orange equilibrium mixture is placed in the water bath, the mixture becomes more red.

Explain what this shows about the energy change for the forward reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The forward reaction is:

- Exothermic 
**OR** 
The forward reaction releases energy;** [1 mark]**
- (Because) the equilibrium moves to the right 
**OR** 
The forward reaction is favoured; **[1 mark]**
- So that the reduction in temperature is increased 
**OR** 
So that the reduction in temperature is counteracted; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *If the solution is placed in a water bath below room temperature, the temperature of the reaction has been decreased*
- *The reaction will oppose this change and attempt to increase the temperature *
- *A red solution is observed*

  - *The forward reaction produces a red solution so the rate of the forward reaction must have increased *
- *The forward reaction must therefore be exothermic *

parts.solutionMd:
The completed chemical equation for this reaction is:

*Multiples and fractions are accepted*

- *Remember: **You can put a big number in front of the chemical to say how many of that chemical there are, but you cannot add small numbers to the chemicals *

  - *e.g. 2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* means that you have 2 x C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* molecules*
  - *e.g. changing HCl to H*<sub>*2*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* might help with balancing the equation but it has changed the chemical*
- *One possible way to balance this equation is:*

  - *Double the HCl to balance the chlorine atoms on either side, which actually balances the carbons and hydrogens as well C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + **2**HCl + .......... O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + .......... H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *You can balance the one oxygen on the right-hand side by using half an oxygen molecule C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + 2HCl + **½**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This can be doubled to work with whole numbers 2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + 4HCl + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 2H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd:

(1)

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The chemical equation for the reaction where propene is bubbled through bromine water until there is no further colour change is:

- C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>  
**OR **
CH<sub>3</sub>CHCH<sub>2</sub> + Br<sub>2</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CHBrCH<sub>2</sub>Br; **[1 mark]**

ii) The observation supports that this is an addition reaction because:

- Bromine water is orange / brown; **[1 mark]**
- The bromine colour disappears / fades as it is added to propene / used up;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *When orange / brown bromine water is added to an alkene, it will decolourise or go colourless*

  - *Examiners are quite specific about colours, especially in relation to bromine*
  - *Orange / brown / orange-brown are all generally acceptable colours for bromine water but any mention of red will lose the mark*
  - *Clear is never an acceptable colour - you should be using the word colourless*
- *The question also tells you that this is an addition reaction which makes the chemical equation easier*

  - *Propene + bromine → a product*
  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* → a product*
  - *Since you know this is an addition reaction, you can simply add the Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* on the end of C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>*  *
  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>*Br*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *The bromine water (Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* (aq)) is responsible for an initial orange / brown colour*

  - *As the bromine reacts, it is added to the propene and removed from the bromine water*
  - *When you remove the bromine from bromine water, you are left with water *
  - *This means that the reaction will turn from orange / brown to colourless and will remain colourless once all of the bromine had reacted / been used up*

parts.problemMd:
An alcohol has this percentage composition by mass.

C = 60.0%       H = 13.3%       O = 26.7%

i) Show by calculation that the molecular formula of the alcohol could be C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O.

(3)

ii) Explain why the empirical formula is also the molecular formula of the alcohol.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) To show that the molecular formula of the alcohol could be C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O:

**Method 1**:

- Carbon = $\frac{60.0}{12}$ 
**AND **
Hydrogen = $\frac{13.3}{1}$ 
**AND **
Oxygen = $\frac{26.7}{16}$; **[1 mark]**
- Carbon = 5 
**AND **
Hydrogen = 13.3  
**AND **
Oxygen = 1.67;** [1 mark]**
- Divide by 1.67 to get 3 : 8 : 1; **[1 mark]**

**Method 2:**

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O = 60;** [1 mark]**
- Carbon = $\frac{36}{60}\times100$ 
**AND **
Hydrogen = $\frac{8}{60}\times100$ 
**AND **
Oxygen = $\frac{16}{60}\times100$; **[1 mark]**
- Carbon = 60.0 % 
**AND **
Hydrogen = 13.3% 
**AND **
Oxygen = 26.7%**[1 mark]**

ii) The empirical formula is also the molecular formula of the alcohol because:

- C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O has the simplest whole number ratio of atoms;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Make sure you know how to calculate empirical and molecular formulae from given data *
- *There is a single, consistent method that you can use:*

  - *Elements, values, atomic mass, divide, ratio, answer*
  - *Elements* |   | > *Carbon* | > *Hydrogen* | > *Oxygen* |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | > *Value from the question* | > *60.0 %* | > *13.3 %* | > *26.7 %* |
  | > *Atomic mass* | > *12* | > *1* | > *16* |
  | > *Divide * | > $\frac{60.0}{12}$* = 5* | > $\frac{13.3}{1}$*= 13.3* | > $\frac{26.7}{16}$* = 1.67* |
  | > *Ratio (divide by the smallest)* | > $\frac{5}{1.67}$* = 3* | > $\frac{13.3}{1.67}$* = 8* | > $\frac{1.67}{1.67}$* = 1* |
  | > *Answer* | > *C*<sub>*3*</sub> | > *H*<sub>*8*</sub> | > *O* |

> - (and the) same functional group
> - (and) similar chemical properties
> - where successive members differ by a -CH<sub>2</sub>- group
> 
> **[2 marks]**
> 
> ii) Functional group means:
> 
> - An atom or group of atoms that determine the chemical properties / reactions of a molecule **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These are key definitions you need to memorise for the organic chemistry topic.
> 
> For homologous series, there are four key features. A 2-mark question will usually require you to state any two of them. It's a good idea to learn all four:
> 
> 1. Same general formula (e.g., C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> for alkanes).
> 2. Same functional group (e.g., the C=C double bond for alkenes).
> 3. Similar chemical properties.
> 4. Each member differs from the next by a -CH<sub>2</sub>- group.
> 
> For functional group, think of it as the 'interesting' part of the molecule where reactions happen. For example, in an alcohol, the -OH group is the functional group.

parts.problemMd:
Pentane, C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, is a hydrocarbon used as a solvent and a blowing agent to create the bubbles in polystyrene.

The polystyrene packaging for a television has a volume of 12,500 cm<sup>3</sup>.

i) Assuming the pentane vapour occupies 90% of the volume of the packaging at rtp, calculate the amount of pentane, in moles, needed to create the packaging.

(rtp = 24,000 cm<sup>3</sup>)

[1]

ii) Calculate the mass of pentane in the packaging.

[2]

iii) Explain a problem in the disposal of addition polymers such as polystyrene.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To find the amount of pentane in the packaging:

- Calculate the volume of pentane vapour in the packaging:

volume of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12 </sub>= 12,500 cm<sup>3</sup> x 90%

volume of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> = 11,250 cm<sup>3</sup>

- Calculate the moles of pentane:

moles of a gas = $\frac{\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{in} \mathrm{cm}^{3}}{24,000\mathrm{cm}^{3}}$

moles of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> = $\frac{11,250}{24,000}$

moles of C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> = **0.468 mol** **[1 mark]**

ii) To find the mass of pentane in the packaging:

- Calculate the *M*<sub>*r*</sub> of pentane:

*M*<sub>*r*</sub><sub> </sub>= (12 x 5) + (1 x 12) = 72 g/mol<sup> </sup>**[1 mark]**

- Convert the moles of pentane into mass:

mass = moles x *M*<sub>*r*</sub><sub> </sub>

mass of pentane = 0.468 x 72

mass of pentane = **33.8 g** **[1 mark]**

iii) Problems disposing of addition polymers such as polystyrene are:

Any two from:

- Addition polymers like polystyrene are inert / unreactive 
**AND**
They are not biodegradable **[1 mark]**
- Therefore, they take up space in landfill sites for a very long time**[1 mark]**
- When burned, they can release toxic gases (such as carbon monoxide or hydrogen cyanide) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For multi-step calculations:
> 
> - Lay out your working clearly, step-by-step.
> - Don't round your answers too early.
> - Use the full value from your calculator in the next step of the calculation to ensure your final answer is accurate.
> 
> For the environmental question, you are asked for problems with addition polymers. The two main problems you need to remember are:
> 
> 1. They are non-biodegradable (so fill up landfill)
> 2. They can produce toxic gases when burned.

parts.problemMd: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH undergoes a combustion reaction in excess oxygen. Write a balanced symbol equation for this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation is:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + 4½O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O  **   **
**OR **   
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH + 4½O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 2 marks] **

- *To construct this equation start with the information you are given*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → *
- *This reaction is therefore combustion- the two products are carbon dioxide and water*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Then you can balance this equation*

  - *Start with the carbon atoms CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 3CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Then balance the hydrogen atoms CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 3CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 4H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Then balance the oxygen atoms CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + 4½O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 3CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 4H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *You would also be awarded the mark for any correct multiples of this, e.g.:*

  - *2CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*OH + 9O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 6CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 8H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the percentage by mass of carbon:

**[Total: 2 marks] **

- *To answer this question, use the clues given to you*

  - *The functional group will be OH, which has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 17 (16 + 1)*
  
    - *Therefore the remaining **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* is 85 (102 - 17)*
  - *You know that this must contain carbon and hydrogen atoms*
  
    - *The compound must contain a CH*<sub>*3*</sub>* group and CH*<sub>*2*</sub>* groups*
    - *The CH*<sub>*3*</sub>* group has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 15 leaving a mass of 70*
    - *Therefore there must be C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>* in the remaining part of the compound*
    - *C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*14*</sub>*O*
  - *Now you know you have 6 carbon atoms in compound A you can work out the percentage by mass*

parts.problemMd:
Compound X is a hydrocarbon with an *M*<sub>r</sub> of 70 that contains 85.7% by mass of carbon. When bromine water is added to compound X it remains orange.

Calculate the molecular formula of compound X
parts.solutionMd:
To determine the molecular formula of compound X - Carbon = $\frac{85.7}{12}$ = 7.14 Hydrogen = $\frac{14.3}{1}$= 14.3; **[1 mark] ** - Ratio Carbon = $\frac{7.14}{7.14}$ = 1 Hydrogen = $\frac{14.3}{7.14}$ = 2; **[1 mark] ** - Molecular formula = $\frac{\mathrm{CH}_{2}}{70}=\frac{14}{70}$= 5 CH2 x 5 = C5H10 ; **[1 mark] ** **[Total: 3 marks] ** - *Empirical formula calculations follow the same steps regardless of the compound* - *To calculate the empirical formula, it can be helpful to use the following table:* | > *1* | > *Write the elements* | > *C* | > *H* | |---|---|---|---| | > *2* | > *Write the values from the question*
*(can be % or g)* | > *85.7* | > *14.3* | | > *3* | > *Write the atomic mass* | > *12* | > *1* | | > *4* | $\frac{\mathrm{Value}}{\mathrm{Atomic} \mathrm{mass}}$ | > *7.14* | > *14.3* | | > *5* | > *Ratio (divide the answers by the smallest value)* | > $\frac{7.14}{7.14}$* = 1* | > $\frac{14.3}{7.14}$* = 2* | | > *6* | > *Write the empirical formula* | > *C* | > *H**2* | - *Using the empirical formula the next step is to determine the molecular formula* - *This can be done by:* | > *M**r** of empirical formula* | > *CH**2** = 12 + 1*

*M**r** **= 14* | |---|---| | *Divide **M**r** of molecular formula by **M**r** **of empirical formula* | > * *$\frac{70}{14}$* = 5* | | > *Multiply empirical formula by answer* | > *5 x CH**2** = C**5**H**10* |

parts.problemMd:
A compound X contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen only.

X contains 54.54% of carbon by mass, 9.09% of hydrogen by mass and 36.37% of oxygen by mass.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of compound X.

(2)

ii) Compound X has a relative molecular mass of 88.

Deduce the molecular formula of compound X.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The empirical formula of compound X is found by:

- (Moles of) C = 54.54/12 **OR **4.5 
**AND** 
(Moles of) H = 9.09/1 **OR **9.09 
**AND** (Moles of) O = 36.37/16 **OR **2.27;** [1 mark]**
- Empirical formula: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O;** [1 mark]**

ii) The molecular formula of compound X is found by:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O = 44; **[1 mark]**
- (88/44 = 2 therefore molecular formula is) C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula when given percentages, it is easiest to assume that you have 100 g of the sample, then you can work out the number of moles of each element in 100 g by using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

|   | **C** | **H** | **O** |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element in 100g (%/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{54.54}{12}\,=4.5$ | $\frac{9.09}{1}\,=9.09$ | $\frac{36.37}{16}\,=2.27$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * 4.5/2.27 = 2* | > * 9.09/2.27 = 4* | > * 2.27/2.27 = 1* |

- *The empirical formula is therefore C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*O*
- *Compound X has twice the** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula, therefore compound X must contain twice the number of atoms that appears in the empirical formula*

parts.problemMd:
Compound **D** undergoes combustion to form a toxic colourless gas, a brown gas and one other product.

i) Give a chemical equation for this reaction.

(2)

ii) Explain how the toxic colourless gas affects the respiratory system.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The chemical equation for the combustion of compound **D** to form a toxic colourless gas, a brown gas and one other product is:

2CH<sub>3</sub>Br + 2.5O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO + Br<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O **   **
**OR **   
4CH<sub>3</sub>Br + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 4CO + 2Br<sub>2</sub> + 6H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

ii) How the toxic colourless gas affects the respiratory system:

- It reduces the ability of blood / red blood cells / haemoglobin to carry oxygen 
**OR **
It prevents blood / red blood cells / haemoglobin from carrying oxygen; **[1 mark]**
- (Because,) it binds tightly / strongly / irreversibly (to blood / red blood cells / haemoglobin) 
**OR **
(Because,) it causes haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part (i)*

  - *Compound **D** is CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br*
  - *It undergoes combustion which means it is reacting with oxygen*
  
    - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → *
  - *The toxic colourless gas is carbon monoxide*
  - *The brown gas is bromine*
  - *The other product is water, since this is a combustion reaction*
  
    - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO + Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Two bromine atoms on the right-hand side mean that you need 2CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br*
  
    - *2**CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO + Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *This now means that there are two carbon atoms on the left-hand side, which will make 2CO*
  - *This also means that there are six hydrogen atoms on the left-hand side, which will make 3H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  
    - *2**CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**CO + Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *There are now five oxygen atoms on the right-hand side, which require 2.5O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  
    - *2**CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br + **2.5**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**CO + Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *You can also double all of the numbers if you prefer equations with whole number coefficients*
  
    - *4**CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*Br + **5**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **4**CO + **2**Br*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **6**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *For part (ii)*

  - *The toxic colourless gas is carbon monoxide*
  - *You should know that carbon monoxide binds strongly / irreversibly to haemoglobin in the blood / red blood cells*
  - *This means that less oxygen can be carried around the body*
  - *Answers in terms of haemoglobin are not expected but are often seen in exam answers*

parts.problemMd:
Compound **H** belongs to the same homologous series as compound **A**.

The complete combustion of one mole of compound **H** burns is represented by the equation

compound **H** + *x* O<sub>2</sub> → *y* CO<sub>2</sub> + *z* H<sub>2</sub>O

The numbers *x*, *y* and *z* are used to balance the equation.

i) One mole of compound **H** burning completely in oxygen produces 308 g of carbon dioxide and 144 g of water.

Calculate the values of *y* and *z*.

[*M*<sub>r</sub> of CO<sub>2</sub> = 44, *M*<sub>r</sub> of H<sub>2</sub>O = 18]

(2)

*y* = ..........

*z* = ..........

ii) Determine the molecular formula of the compound **H** and the value of *x*.

(2)

molecular formula = ..........

*x* = ..........
parts.solutionMd:
i) The values of *y* and *z* are:

- *y* = $\frac{308}{44}$ = 7; **[1 mark]**
- *z* = $\frac{144}{18}$ = 8; **[1 mark]**

ii) The molecular formula of the compound **H** and the value of *x* are:

- Molecular formula = C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>16</sub>;** [1 mark]**/li>
- *x* = 11;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The question tells you that one mole of compound **H** forms 308 g of carbon monoxide and 144 g of water*

  - *This means that you can use these values to calculate the number of moles of each product, using the equation:*
  *Moles = *$\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$
  - *y** = *$\frac{308}{44}$* = 7*
  - *z** = *$\frac{144}{18}$* = 8*
- *This means that the chemical equation can be updated to:*

  - *Compound **H** + **x** O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **7**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **8**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *The question also tells you that compound **H** is in the same homologous series as compound **A*

  - *This means that it is an alkane*
  - *It must contain seven carbon atoms to form seven carbon monoxide molecules*
  - *It must also contain 16 hydrogen atoms to form eight water molecules*
  - *Therefore, the molecular formula is C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>
- *This means that the chemical equation can be updated to:*

  - *C*<sub>*7*</sub>*H*<sub>*16*</sub>* + **x** O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **7**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **8**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *There are (7 x 2) + (8 x 1) = 22 oxygen atoms on the right-hand side of the equation*

  - *This will require eleven oxygen molecules on the left-hand side*
  - *Therefore, **x** = 11*

parts.problemMd:
Incomplete combustion occurs when there is insufficient oxygen for a reaction.

Which are the **two** main substances formed during incomplete combustion, aside from water?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The **two** main substances formed during incomplete combustion, aside from water are: A / Particulates and carbon monoxide

- During incomplete combustion, there is insufficient oxygen for the fuel to burn in
- Instead of carbon dioxide and water (formed during complete combustion) you can form either particulates (a mixture of solid carbon particles and unburnt hydrocarbons) or carbon monoxide, CO, with minimal or no CO<sub>2</sub>
- B is incorrect because, although soot is produced by incomplete combustion, sulfur dioxide is not — it forms when fuels containing sulfur impurities are burned, not from the combustion of the hydrocarbon itself
- **C** is incorrect as carbon dioxide is a main product made by complete combustion
- D is incorrect as neither is a product of incomplete combustion — oxides of nitrogen form when nitrogen and oxygen in the air react at high temperatures inside engines, and sulfur dioxide forms from sulfur impurities in the fuel

choices.label: D

parts.problemMd:
Fractional distillation is the process by which crude oil is separated into simpler, more useful fractions.

Which of the following statements about the process of fractional distillation is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The correct statement about the process of fractional distillation is: C / The molecules in each fraction have a similar boiling point and carbon chain length

- The boiling point of hydrocarbons depends on the number of carbon atoms in the chain

  - Each fraction consists of groups of hydrocarbons of** similar** chain lengths
  - Therefore each fraction will have **similar **boiling points
- **A** & **B** are incorrect as fractional distillation is carried out in a fractionating column which is very hot at the **bottom **and cool at the **top**

  - Crude oil enters the fractionating column and is heated so vapours rise
  - Vapours of hydrocarbons with **low** boiling points will rise up the column and condense at the top to be tapped off
- **D ** is incorrect as viscosity refers to the ease of flow of a liquid. Viscosity increases with increasing chain length as the intermolecular forces of attraction increase with molecular size. Fractions collected at the bottom of the column have longer chain lengths and therefore have a **high **viscosity

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: The fractionating column is cooler at the bottom than at the top

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The fractions collected at the top of the fractionating column have a high boiling point

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: The molecules in each fraction have a similar boiling point and carbon chain length

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: The fractions collected at the bottom of the fractionating column have a low viscosity

parts.problemMd: Describe how long-chain alkanes are converted into short-chain alkanes and alkenes.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Long-chain alkanes are converted into short-chain alkanes and alkenes by:
> 
> - (Catalytic) cracking **[1 mark]**
> - Using a catalyst of silica (SiO<sub>2</sub>) or alumina (Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - Using a temperature range of 600 - 700 <sup>o</sup>C **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports often show that students confuse **cracking** with **fractional distillation**. It is essential to remember the difference:
> 
> - Fractional distillation is a **physical separation **process that separates the hydrocarbons already present in crude oil.
> - Cracking is a **chemical reaction **(thermal decomposition) that breaks down large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones.
> 
> You are expected to memorise the specific conditions for catalytic cracking: the **catalyst** (silica or alumina) and the **temperature** (600-700 °C).

parts.problemMd: Explain why it is necessary to convert long-chain alkanes into short-chain alkanes and alkenes.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason long-chain alkanes are converted into short-chain alkanes and alkenes:
> 
> Any **two **from (1 mark for each):
> 
> - There is a surplus of long-chain alkanes **OR** There is a low demand for long-chain alkanes
> - There is a low supply of short-chain alkanes **OR** There is a high demand for short-chain alkanes
> - Short-chain alkanes are useful as fuels / petrol
> - Short-chain alkenes are used to make polymers / alcohols
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To get full marks for explaining why cracking is important, you need to discuss the uses of **both** types of products formed:
> 
> 1. **Short-chain alkanes**
> 
>   - These are in high demand for use as high-quality fuels, such as petrol for cars.
> 2. **Alkenes**
> 
>   - These are essential for the chemical industry, primarily as monomers to make polymers (plastics).
> 
> A complete answer should also mention the economic reason for this:
> 
> - Fractional distillation produces more long-chain alkanes than we need, and not enough short-chain alkanes to meet demand.
> - Cracking solves this problem.

parts.problemMd:
A car is driven at constant speed for 4.00 km.

The exhaust gases are collected and their volume at room temperature and pressure (rtp) is 5.02 × 10<sup>5</sup> cm<sup>3</sup>.

The exhaust gases include carbon dioxide and oxides of nitrogen.

The carbon dioxide is removed from the exhaust gases. The volume of the remaining gases at rtp is 2.96 × 10<sup>5 </sup>cm<sup>3</sup>.

i) Explain how oxides of nitrogen form in a car engine.

(2)

ii) Give a reason why oxides of nitrogen should not be released into the atmosphere.

(1)

iii) Show that the car produces less than 100 g of carbon dioxide per km. [molar volume of carbon dioxide at rtp = 24 000 cm<sup>3</sup>]

(5)
parts.solutionMd:
i) Oxides of nitrogen form in a car engine because:

- Nitrogen (from the air) reacts / combines with oxygen (from the air); **[1 mark]**
- At high temperatures (in the car engine); **[1 mark]**

ii) A reason why oxides of nitrogen should not be released into the atmosphere is:

Any **one** from:

- Acid rain; **[1 mark]**
- Respiratory problems; **[1 mark]**

iii) Showing that the car produces less than 100 g of carbon dioxide per km:

- Volume of carbon dioxide = 206 000 cm<sup>3</sup> / 2.06 × 10<sup>5</sup> cm<sup>3</sup> / 206 dm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of carbon dioxide per km = 51 500 cm<sup>3</sup> / 5.15 × 10<sup>4</sup> cm<sup>3</sup> / 51.5 dm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of carbon dioxide (51 500 ÷ 24 000) = 2.15 moles; **[1 mark]**
- *M*<sub>r</sub> of carbon dioxide = (12 + (2 x 16) =) 44;** [1 mark]**
- Mass of carbon dioxide per km = 94.4 g; **[1 mark] ***Correct answer of 94 to 95 scores 5 marks*

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *The volume of carbon dioxide is calculated from the total volume of exhaust gases minus the volume of exhaust gases after carbon dioxide has been removed:*

  - *5.02 x 10*<sup>*5*</sup>* - 2.96 x 10*<sup>*5*</sup>* = 2.06 x 10*<sup>*5*</sup>
- *This volume of carbon dioxide was released during a 4.0 km journey, so to work out the volume of carbon dioxide released per km, divide this by 4:*

  - *2.06 x 10*<sup>*5 *</sup>*÷ 4 = 5.15 x 10*<sup>*4*</sup>
- *1 mole of any gas occupies 24 000 cm3, so the number of moles of carbon dioxide present is calculated by:*

  - *moles ÷ 24 000 = 5.15 x 10*<sup>*4 *</sup>*÷ 24 000 = 2.15 moles*
- *The mass of carbon dioxide is calculated by moles x **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 2.15 x 44 = 94.4 g*
- *Make sure that you show your working clearly, if you make a mistake you will be allowed error carried forward meaning you only get penalised once*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about pollutants.

Fossil fuels, such as coal, are burned to release energy.

Hydrogen, sulfur, and carbon are all elements found in coal.

Name two products released when coal burns that have a negative effect on the environment.

State the impact each of the products you have named have.
parts.solutionMd:
The products of burning coal containing carbon, sulfur and hydrogen that affect the environment are:

Any **two** pairs from:

Pair 1:

- Carbon dioxide; **[1 mark]**
- Causes global warming; **[1 mark]**

Pair 2:

- Sulfur dioxide;** [1 mark]**
- Causes acid rain 
**OR**
** **kills plants / causes erosion / acidifies water; **[1 mark] **

Pair 3:

- Carbon monoxide;** [1 mark] **
- Is toxic / poisonous; **[1 mark]**

Pair 4:

- Carbon particles / soot / particulates;** [1 mark]**
- Cause global dimming / blocks out sunlight / smog / causes breathing difficulties; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Make sure you name the product **AND** give the effect *
- *You cannot get more than 2 marks if you name more products but give no effects*
- *You may not be aware of the effects of carbon particulates / soot although you should know that they are produced during the incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons*

parts.problemMd:
Another major source of pollutants is motor vehicles.

i) Nitrogen monoxide, NO, is released by motor vehicle exhausts. Explain how nitrogen monoxide is formed in motor vehicle engines.

(2)

ii) When nitrogen monoxide is released into the atmosphere, nitrogen dioxide, NO<sub>2</sub>, is formed. Suggest an explanation why this happens.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) Nitrogen monoxide is formed in motor vehicle engines because:

- Nitrogen and oxygen react or combine;** [1 mark]**
- At high temperatures / in presence of a spark; **[1 mark]**

ii) When nitrogen monoxide is released into the atmosphere, nitrogen dioxide / NO<sub>2</sub> is formed because:

- It reacts with oxygen 
**OR** 
NO + 1⁄2O<sub>2</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub> / 2NO + O<sub>2</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub>;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Do not be thrown by part i) asking you how nitrogen monoxide is formed, this is an oxide of nitrogen that is formed by the high temperatures in a car engine allowing nitrogen and oxygen from the air to react*
- *You can tell from the formula of nitrogen dioxide, NO*<sub>*2,*</sub>* compared to nitrogen monoxide, NO, that additional oxygen has been added which helps answer part iv)*

parts.problemMd: Describe two effects of oxides of nitrogen being released into the atmosphere.
parts.solutionMd:
Two effects of oxides of nitrogen are:

Any **two** from:

- Acid rain;** [1 mark]**
- Production of (photochemical) smog; **[1 mark] **

parts.problemMd:
How are the amounts of carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emitted by modern motor vehicles reduced?

Include an equation in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The amounts of carbon monoxide and nitrogen monoxide emitted by modern motor vehicles are reduced by:

- The use of a catalytic converter; **[1 mark]**

2NO + 2CO → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + N<sub>2</sub>

- Correct species; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *In a catalytic converter *

  - *Carbon monoxide is oxidised to carbon dioxide: 2CO + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Oxides of nitrogen are reduced to N*<sub>*2*</sub>* gas: 2NO → N*<sub>*2*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *This gives the overall equation: 2NO + 2CO → 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + N*<sub>*2*</sub>
  - *Oxygen does not need to be included *

Which two are **not **classed as alkanes?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D.**

- Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons

  - This means they contain only hydrogen and carbon atoms only, joined together with single bonds
- Compound P - contains C, H and only single bonds

  - This is an alkane
- Compound Q - contains C, H and only single bonds

  - This is an alkane
- Compound R - contains C, H but has a double bond

  - This is not an alkane, it is an alkene
- Compound S - contains C, H and only single bonds

  - This is an alkane
- Compound T - contains C, H and Br

  - This is not alkane, it is a haloalkane
- Compound U - contains C, H but has a double bond

  - This is not an alkane, it is an alkene
- The compounds that are not alkanes are compounds R, T and U

  - The only answer option that contains two non-alkane compounds is option D (R and T)

parts.problemMd: What is the correct chemical formula of butane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D.**

- The correct formula of butane is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>
- The names of organic compounds have two parts: the prefix or stem and the end part (or suffix)
- The prefix tells you how many carbon atoms are present in the longest continuous chain in the compound
- But- indicates that four carbon atoms are present
- Alkanes have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>
- C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10 </sub>is therefore the formula of butane

parts.problemMd: Which of the following is the formula of an alkane?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The formula of an alkane is CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>
- Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons so they only contain hydrogen and carbon atoms, and the carbon-carbon bonds are single bonds
- Alkanes have the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>
- **B** has the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> which obeys the general formula for alkanes
- **A** can be eliminated as it contains an oxygen atom
- **C** can be eliminated as it has a C=C double bond, and is an alkene
- **D** can be eliminated as it is an alkene because it obeys the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>

parts.problemMd:
Ethane can react with chlorine in a substitution reaction where one of the hydrogen atoms in ethane is replaced by a chlorine atom.

| ☐ | **A** | a catalyst |
|---|---|---|
| ☐ | **B** | 30 °C and no oxygen |
| ☐ | **C** | ultraviolet radiaton |
| ☐ | **D** | none - it will occur at room temperature and pressure |
parts.solutionMd:
i) The correct equation for the reaction is:

ethane + chlorine → chloroethane + hydrogen chloride

- Chlorine identified as the missing reactant; **[1 mark]**
- Chloroethane identified as the missing product; **[1 mark]**

ii) The necessary condition for the reaction is:

- C / ultraviolet radiation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *When chlorine reacts with ethane, C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>*, one of the hydrogen atoms on the ethane molecule is replaced with a chlorine atom to form C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*Cl, chloroethane*
- *The hydrogen that was replaced reacts with the other chlorine atom to form hydrogen chloride, HCl:*

  - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*Cl + HCl*

parts.problemMd:
The alkanes are generally unreactive. Their reactions include combustion and substitution.

The complete combustion of an alkane gives carbon dioxide and water.

i) 10 cm<sup>3</sup> of butane is mixed with 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of oxygen, which is an excess. The mixture is ignited. What is the volume of unreacted oxygen left and what is the volume of carbon dioxide formed?

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (g) + 6.5O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 4CO<sub>2</sub> (g) + 5H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

Volume of oxygen left = .................................................. cm<sup>3</sup>

Volume of carbon dioxide formed = .................................................. cm<sup>3</sup>

(2)

ii) Why is the incomplete combustion of any alkane dangerous, particularly in an enclosed space?

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The volumes are:

- Volume of oxygen left = 35 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**
- Volume of carbon dioxide formed = 40 cm<sup>3</sup>; **[1 mark]**

ii) Incomplete combustion of any alkane, particularly in an enclosed space, is dangerous because:

- It forms carbon monoxide; **[1 mark]**
- Which is poisonous / toxic / lethal 
**OR **
Which prevents blood carrying oxygen / effect(s) on haemoglobin; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *There are two ways of calculating the volume of oxygen and carbon dioxide, one is more complicated than the other*
- *Method 1:*

  - *This uses the concept that equal volumes of gases will occupy the same volume, regardless of what type of gaseous species it is*
  - *So, 10 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of butane contains the same number of moles as 10 cm*<sup>*3 *</sup>*of carbon dioxide or 10 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen*
  - *Using the balanced symbol equation, you can see that 1 mole of butane will react with 6.5 moles of oxygen, therefore 10cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of butane will react with 10 x 6.5 = 65 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen*
  - *Initially, there was 100 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen, therefore the volume of oxygen remaining = 100 - 65 = 35 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>
  - *Also, 1 mole of butane will form 4 moles of carbon dioxide, therefore 10 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of butane forms 10 x 4 = 40 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of carbon dioxide*
- **Method 2:**

  - *This involves calculating the number of moles of butane*
  - *In both cases, you have to determine the number of moles of butane and then apply that to determine the volumes of oxygen remaining and carbon dioxide formed*
  - *Moles of butane = *$\frac{10}{24000}$* = 0.000417 mol*
  - *Oxygen remaining*
  
    - *There are 6.5 times more moles of oxygen used in the reaction *$\frac{10}{24000}\times6.5$* = 0.0027803 moles*
    - *This corresponds to 0.0027803 x 24 000 = 65 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen that are consumed in the reaction*
    - *Therefore, there are 100 - 65 = 35 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of oxygen remaining*
  - *Carbon dioxide formed*
  
    - *There are 4 times more moles of carbon dioxide formed in the reaction *$\frac{10}{24000}\times4$* = 0.00167 moles*
    - *This corresponds to 0.00167 x 24 000 = 40 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* of carbon dioxide are formed in the reaction*
- *Incomplete combustion of hydrocarbons releases carbon monoxide (and carbon particulates) *

  - *Carbon monoxide is harmful to the human body but, nowadays, the word harmful is insufficient for any marks, so you have to be more specific by saying that it is poisonous / toxic / lethal or describe the effects that it has on haemoglobin and the blood's ability to transport oxygen*

Cyclohexane will also react with chlorine in the presence of ultraviolet to form hydrogen chloride and compound **Y. **When heated with sodium hydroxide solution, compound **Y** will undergo a further substitution reaction to form sodium chloride and another product, **Z**. Give the names of compounds **X**, **Y** and **Z**.

| Compound **X** | ................................................. |
|---|---|
| Compound **Y** | ................................................. |
| Compound **Z** | ................................................. |
parts.solutionMd:
The names of compounds **X**, **Y** and **Z** are:

- Compound **X**: (1-)chlorohexane; **[1 mark]**
- Compound **Y**: Chlorocyclohexane; **[1 mark]**
- Compound **X**: Cyclohexanol;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *This question requires you to apply your knowledge and use the information provided as the reaction between chloroalkanes and sodium hydroxide solution is not a reaction that you will have studied*
- *For compound X:*

  - *A hydrogen atom is substituted by a chlorine atom when alkanes react with chlorine in the presence of UV radiation*
  - *The products are hydrogen chloride and a chloroalkane*
  - *To name chloroalkanes, simply use 'chloro-' as a prefix in front of the alkane name *
- *For compound Y:*

  - *This is the same reaction as compound X, but using cyclohexane*
  - *Again, the product should have the 'chloro-' as a prefix in front of the alkane name*
- *For compound Z:*

  - *The chlorine atom is replaced by an OH group when chloroalkanes are heated with sodium hydroxide solution*
  - *The products are sodium chloride and an alcohol*
  - *To name alcohols, remove the 'e' from the alkane name and add the suffix '-ol'*

parts.problemMd:
Alkynes are hydrocarbons with the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n-2</sub>. The alkyne containing 2 carbon atoms is ethyne, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>.

State, with a reason, whether the boiling point of ethyne would be expected to be higher or lower than the boiling point of ethane, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
The boiling point of ethyne:

Would be expected to be lower than ethane as:

- Ethyne has fewer (atoms and) electrons than ethane 
**OR** 
Ethyne has a lower relative molecular mass than ethane; **[1 mark] **
- The intermolecular forces would be weaker (so the boiling point should be lower); **[1 mark] **

**OR**

Would be expected to be higher than ethane as:

- Ethyne is a linear molecule / only 1 hydrogen on each carbon atom;** [1 mark] **
- The molecules can pack together more closely increasing the strength of the intermolecular forces; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 2 marks]     **

- *In this question, you do not get a mark for stating whether the boiling point of ethyne is higher or lower than ethane, the marks are for the explanation*
- *The expected response is the first option as you will have learnt that the boiling point of a substance will increase with relative molecular mass*
- *Sometimes predictions in chemistry are not always straightforward, as more than one factor can be involved.*
- *In reality, ethyne has a higher boiling point than ethane*
- *Ethyne does not have as many hydrogen atoms and the molecules can pack more closely together*
- *This means there are more surface area points of contact and the intermolecular forces are slightly stronger than in ethane, leading to a higher boiling point*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactions of the gas ethane, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>.

Write the equation which represents the complete combustion of 1 mole of ethane.
parts.solutionMd:
The equation which represents the complete combustion of 1 mole of ethane is:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> +3½O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *You should know that the complete combustion of alkanes produces carbon dioxide and water, so the unbalanced equation is:*

  - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* +O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *When balancing combustion reactions, balance the carbon atoms first:*

  - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **2**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Then balance the hydrogen atoms:*

  - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Finally, balance the oxygen atoms, there are 7 on the right-hand side so on the left-hand side, you need 3½ molecules of oxygen to provide 7 oxygen atoms:*

  - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + **3½**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Often in a balanced equation where fractions exist, the whole equation is multiplied to give a whole number ratio, to show 2 moles of ethane combusting:*

  - * 2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* +7O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 4CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + 6H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *However, in this question, you are asked to give the equation for the complete combustion of **one mole** of ethane, so it needs to be left with 3½ moles of O*<sub>*2*</sub>* and 1 mole of ethane*

parts.problemMd:
The enthalpy change of this reaction is -122 kJ/mol.

Use the bond energy data in the table below to calculate the bond energy of the C-Cl bond.

| **Bond** | **Bond energy (kJ/mol)** |
|---|---|
| C – H | 413 |
| C – C | 347 |
| H – Cl | 432 |
| Cl – Cl | 243 |

bond energy ........................................................ kJ / mol
parts.solutionMd:
The bond energy of the C-Cl bond is calculated by:

- Sum of bond broken = 3068 (kJ/mol); **[1 mark]**
- Sum of bonds formed = 2844 (+ C-Cl); **[1 mark]**
- Bond energy = (+)346 (kJ/mol); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The most common type of question involving bond energies is to calculate the enthalpy change of reaction*
- *This question gives you the enthalpy change of the reaction, and you need to use this and the bond energies to calculate the bond energy of the C-Cl bond*
- *The sum of the bonds broken, Σ(bonds broken), are:*

  - *(6 x C-H) + (1 x C-C) + (1 x C-Cl) = (6 x 413) + (1 x 347) + (1 x 243) = 3068*
- *The sum of the bonds formed, Σ(bonds made), are:*

  - *(5 x C-H) + (1 x C-C) + (1 x C-Cl) + (1 x H-Cl) = (5 x 413) + (1 x 347) + (1 x C-Cl) + (1 x 432) = 2844 + C-Cl*
- *The enthalpy change is calculated by:*

  - *Enthalpy change = Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds made)*
- *Substituting the values known gives:*

  - *-122 = 3068 - (2844 + C-Cl)*
- *Rearranging gives:*

  - *C-Cl = 3068 - 2844 + 122 = (+)346 kJ/mol*
- *You would score the full three marks for a final answer of 346, but only two marks if your final answer is -346, so take care when rearranging*
- *Remember**: Bond energies will always be positive as they give the energy required to break bonds, which is an endothermic process*

parts.problemMd: Use your answer from part c) to suggest which compound, ethane or chloroethane, is the more reactive. Explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The compound which is the most reactive is:

- Chloroethane;** [1 mark]**
- (Because) a C-Cl bond requires less energy to break than C-H;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *As the question contains the command word 'suggest' you should expect that you will need to apply your knowledge *
- *The only structural difference between ethane and chloroethane is that chloroethane contains a C–Cl bond whereas ethane contains a C–H bond*
- *As the bond energy of the C–Cl bond is 346 kJ/mol but the bond energy is 413 kJ/mol for the C–H bond, the C-–Cl bond will break more easily, making it more reactive*

i) Another compound, G, has this percentage composition by mass.

C = 37.8%   H = 6.3%   Cl = 55.9%

Show by calculation that the empirical formula of compound G is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl

ii) The relative formula mass (*M*<sub>r</sub>) of G is 127

parts.solutionMd:
i) To show by calculation that the empirical formula of compound G is C2H4Cl: Method 1: - Carbon: $\frac{37.8}{12}$ **AND ** Hydrogen: $\frac{6.3}{1}$ **AND ** Chlorine: $\frac{55.9}{35.5}$; **[1 mark]** - Carbon: 3.15 **AND** ** **Hydrogen: 6.3 **AND ** Chlorine: 1.575; **[1 mark]** - Carbon: $\frac{3.15}{1.575}$ = 2 **AND ** Hydrogen: $\frac{6.3}{1.575}$ = 4 **AND ** Chlorine: $\frac{1.575}{1.575}$ = 1; **[1 mark]** Method 2: - *M*r of C2H4Cl = 63.5;** [1 mark]** - Mass of carbon in compound G = 2 x 12 = 24 **AND ** Mass of hydrogen in compound G = 4 x 1 = 4 **AND ** Mass of chlorine in compound G = 1 x 35.5 = 35.5; **[1 mark]** - Carbon: $\frac{24}{63.5}\times100$ = 37.8% **AND ** Hydrogen: $\frac{4}{63.5}\times100$= 6.3% **AND ** Chlorine: $\frac{35.5}{63.5}\times100$ = 55.9%; **[1 mark]** ii) The molecular formula of G is: - $\frac{127}{63.5}$ = 2;** [1 mark]** - Molecular formula = C4H8Cl2; **[1 mark]** **[Total: 5 marks]** - *Empirical formula calculations follow the same steps regardless of the compound* - | 1 | > *Write the elements* | > *C* | > *H* | > *Cl* | |---|---|---|---|---| | > *2* | > *Write the values from the question*
*(can be % or g)* | > *37.8* | > *6.3* | > *55.9* | | > *3* | > *Write the atomic mass* | > *12* | > *1* | > *35.5* | | > *4* | $\frac{\mathrm{Value}}{\mathrm{Atomic} \mathrm{mass}}$ | > *3.15* | > *6.3* | > *1.575* | | > *5* | > *Ratio (divide the answers by the smallest value)* | > $\frac{3.15}{1.575}$* = 2* | > $\frac{6.3}{1.575}$* = 4* | > $\frac{1.575}{1.575}$* = 1* | | > *6* | > *Write the empirical formula* | > *C**2* | > *H**4* | > *Cl* | - *Edexcel like to give questions asking you to prove an empirical formula and these are answered surprisingly badly, even though you have the final answer to work towards* - *Once you have calculated the empirical formula, you calculate its mass* - *C**2**H**4**Cl = (2 x 12) + (4 x 1) + 35.5 = 63.5* - *To determine the molecular formula, you divide the molecular mass by the mass of the empirical formula* - $\frac{127}{63.5}$* = 2* - *Then you apply this number to the empirical formula* - *C**2**H**4**Cl x 1 = C**4**H**8**Cl**2*

parts.problemMd:
0.01 moles of an alkene needed 2.4 g of oxygen for complete combustion. 2.2 g of carbon dioxide were formed.

i) Determine the following mole ratio.

From this ratio determine the formula of the alkene.

(3)

ii) Write an equation for the complete combustion of this alkene.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) To determine the formula of the alkene:

- Moles of O<sub>2 </sub>(= 2.4 / 32 =) 0.075 mol 
**AND** moles of CO<sub>2</sub> (= 2.2 / 44 =) 0.05 mol; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of alkene : moles of O<sub>2</sub> : moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 1 : 7.5 : 5 **OR** 
2 : 15 : 10; **[1 mark]**
- Formula of alkene = C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>; **[1 mark]**

ii) The equation for the complete combustion of this alkene is:

- C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + 7.5O<sub>2</sub> → 5CO<sub>2</sub> + 5H<sub>2</sub>O 
**OR **
2C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10 </sub>+ 15O<sub>2</sub> → 10CO<sub>2 </sub>+ 10H<sub>2</sub>O;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Complete combustion occurs when a fuel reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water *
- *The word equation would be:*

  - *Alkene + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water *
- *You are given the number of moles of the alkene = **0.01 mol*
- *You are given the mass of oxygen and carbon dioxide so can use these to find the moles of the oxygen and carbon dioxide (as shown in the mark scheme) *

  - *Oxygen 2.4 ÷ 32 = **0.075 mol*
  - *Carbon dioxide = 2.2 ÷ 4 4=** 0.05 mol*
- *You, therefore, have: 0.01 : 0.075 : 0.05 *
- *To calculate the ratio divide each of these by the smallest number which is 0.01*

  - *This gives you the ratio of 1 : 7.5 : 5 or if you double it 2 : 15 : 10*
- *From this, you know that you have five moles of carbon dioxide*

  - *Therefore, the alkene must have five carbons*
- *The general formula for alkenes is C*<sub>*n*</sub>*H*<sub>*2n*</sub>* so if you have 5 carbons you have 10 hydrogen atoms *
- *Put this information into the equation  *

  - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>* + 7.5O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Balance the rest of the equation*

  - *C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>* + 7.5O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 5CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **5**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *This answer is accepted or you could double the 7.5 to achieve a whole number 15, but remember to double the other substances too*

  - *2**C*<sub>*5*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>* + **15**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **10**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **10**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd: Write a balanced symbol equation for the incomplete combustion of propene to form carbon monoxide and water.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation is:

- Correct formulae; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → CO + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Balance the carbon atoms first*

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **3**CO + H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Balance the hydrogen atoms second *

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **3**CO + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *Balance the oxygen atoms last *

  - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*6*</sub>* + **3**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → **3**CO + **3**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd:
When ethanol is heated with potassium dichromate(VI) and one other reagent, a reaction occurs.

Which statement about the reaction is correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B.**

- Alcohols will undergo oxidation when heated with an oxidising agent.
- Acidified potassium dichromate(VI) is an oxidising agent (represented in equations by [O]); potassium dichromate(VI) is acidified using dilute sulfuric acid:

CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH + [O]  →  CH<sub>3</sub>COOH + H<sub>2</sub>O

- **A** is incorrect as the colour change is from orange to green
- **C** is incorrect as the product is ethanoic acid
- **D** is incorrect as it is an example of an oxidation reaction

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: The colour change that occurs during the reaction is from green to orange

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The other reagent is sulfuric acid

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: The product of the reaction is ethene

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: This is an example of a displacement reaction

parts.problemMd: Which is of these is true about the manufacture of ethanol?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The hydration of ethene has only one product, ethanol, so it has a 100% atom economy

ethene + steam → ethanol

- **A** is incorrect as fermentation produces ethanol and carbon dioxide. Since the question is about the manufacture of ethanol, which is the desired product, then we cannot say the process has 100% atom economy
- **C** is incorrect as the ethanol produced by fermentation is very impure as it contains a lot of water
- **D** is incorrect as alkenes are reactive and will undergo some reactions at room temperature. However, the hydration of ethene requires steam and a catalyst, so does not occur at room temperature

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: The hydration of ethene has a 100% atom economy

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Alkenes are reactive so the hydration of ethene occurs readily at room temperature

parts.problemMd:
Ethanol is produced by fermentation.

Which of the following conditions is **not **required to produce ethanol by fermentation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Fermentation is an anaerobic process

  - Oxygen is not required for ethanol to be produced by fermentation
  - If oxygen is present, further oxidation of the ethanol would occur forming ethanoic acid (a carboxylic acid)

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: Sugar or starch dissolved in water

parts.problemMd:
#### Separate: Chemistry Only

Methanol and ethanol are both members of the same homologous series.

Which of the following is the functional group of this homologous series?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Methanol and ethanol are both alcohols
- The functional group of alcohols is –OH

  - **A** is incorrect as this is the functional group of alkenes
  - **B** is incorrect as this is the functional group of carboxylic acids
  - **D** is incorrect as this shows a carbon-carbon single bond

parts.problemMd: Which of the following is **not** a feature of a homologous series?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Options **A**, **B** and **C** are all features of a homologous series
- **D** is not a feature of a homologous series as they do not have the **same **physical properties, but they do share **similar **physical properties
- You need to know these features that are characteristic of homologous series and you could be asked to list some of these features in an exam

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: the compounds differ by CH<sub>2 </sub>in molecular formula from neighbouring compounds

choices.label: C
choices.textMd: they have the same general formula

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: they have the same physical properties

parts.solutionMd:
The correct sentences are:

- Ethanol can be **oxidised **to form ethanoic acid; **[1 mark]**
- The functional group of ethanoic acid is **–COOH**; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Alcohols undergo oxidation to produce carboxylic acids*
- *You need to know about three different ways in which ethanol can be oxidised to form ethanoic acid:*

  - *By burning in excess oxygen*
  - *Reacting with the oxygen in air - this is known as microbial oxidation *
  - *Heating with acidified potassium(VI) dichromate solution*
- *Alcohols will oxidise when left standing in the air due to the oxygen present*
- *Wine that has been left open for a few days will have a vinegary taste as the ethanol in the wine oxidises to ethanoic acid, which is the main component of vinegar *

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
Alcohols can be oxidised to form organic compounds from a different homologous series.

Place ticks (✔) in boxes by the two statements that are correct

| Alkenes are formed when alcohols are oxidised |   |
|---|---|
| Ethanol oxidises to form ethanoic acid |   |
| Alcohols can be oxidised by heating with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid |   |
| Alcohols are oxidised by fermenting at 30 °C with the absence of oxygen |   |
| When ethanol oxidises in air, carbon dioxide is produced |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The two correct statements are:

| Alkenes are formed when alcohols are oxidised |   |
|---|---|
| Ethanol oxidises to form ethanoic acid | ✔; **[1 mark]** |
| Alcohols can be oxidised by heating with potassium dichromate(VI) in dilute sulfuric acid | ✔;** [1 mark]** |
| Alcohols are oxidised by fermenting at 30 °C with the absence of oxygen |   |
| When ethanol oxidises in air, carbon dioxide is produced |   |

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Alcohol can be oxidised by complete combustion, in air by microbial oxidation or by heating with potassium dichromate(VI)*

  - *When oxidised by complete combustion, water and carbon dioxide are formed*
  - *When oxidised in air or by potassium dichromate(VI), a carboxylic acid and water are formed*
  - *Ethanol will oxidise to produce ethanoic acid*
- *Alkenes are not formed when alcohols are oxidised*

  - *The hydration of alkenes is used to manufacture alcohols, e.g. ethene reacts with steam to form ethanol*
- *Alcohols are also produced (and not oxidised) by the fermentation process*

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

parts.problemMd:

![screen-shot-2022-10-12-at-22-00-46](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/4-organic-chemistry/4-5-alcohols/assets/011-screen-shot-2022-10-12-at-22-00-46.png)

The grapes are collected and crushed to produce an aqueous solution containing glucose. Yeast is added to the solution and the mixture is left to ferment at a temperature of about 30 °C in the absence of air.

ii) Explain why another organic compound may also be formed if fermentation is carried out in the presence of air.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:

parts.solutionMd:

ii) This process is carried out in the absence of air and at a temperature below 40 °C because:

Explanation including **four** from:

**[Total: 5 marks] **

- *You need to know both fermentation and hydration of ethene in the production of ethanol *

**Advantages of fermentation / disadvantages of hydration:**

- Sugar cane can be re-grown / is renewable; **[1 mark] **
- Crude oil is finite/cannot be replaced/is non-renewable; **[1 mark] **

- Fermentation uses lower pressure so energy costs are lower/ hydration uses higher pressure, so energy costs are higher;** [1 mark] **
- Yeast is a natural substance and not harmful / phosphoric acid is corrosive; **[1 mark] **

**Advantages of hydration / disadvantages of fermentation:**

- Hydration is a faster process / fermentation is a slower process; **[1 mark] **
- Hydration gives pure ethanol / fermentation gives impure ethanol; **[1 mark] **

i) This reaction is in dynamic equilibrium. Give two features of a reaction in dynamic equilibrium.

(2)

ii) When the equilibrium mixture is heated, the yield of ethanol decreases. Explain whether the forward reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) Two features of a reaction in dynamic equilibrium are:

- Rate of the forwards reaction = the rate of the backwards reaction;** [1 mark]**
- The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant; ** [1 mark]**

ii) The forward reaction is:

- Exothermic;  **[1 mark]**
- (Because) an increase in temperature shifts the (position of) equilibrium in the endothermic direction (so backwards reaction is endothermic); ** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *According to Le Chatelier's principle, whenever a change is made to a system, the system will shift the position of the equilibrium in order to oppose the change *
- *So when temperature increases, the system opposes the change and decreases the temperature *
- *To do this, it will favour the endothermic reaction which is the reverse reaction, shifting the equilibrium to the left and reducing the yield of ethanol*

  - *Zymase / enzymes*
  - *A sensible method of warming e.g. water bath, but not boiling as this will denature the enzymes present *
  - *‘Heat’ but only if the temperature specified is within the range 20-45 °C*
- *A fractional distillation column will increase the concentration*
- *Ethanol has a boiling point of 78 °C and water of 100 °C*
- *The mixture is heated until it reaches 78 °C, at which point the ethanol boils and distills out of the mixture and condenses into the beaker*

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the fermentation of the carbohydrate glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, is

C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2CO<sub>2</sub>

Calculate the maximum mass of carbon dioxide that could be produced if 135 g of this carbohydrate is fully fermented

(*M*<sub>r</sub>:    CO<sub>2 </sub>= 44;    C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6 </sub>= 180)

mass of carbon dioxide = ............................... g
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the mass of carbon dioxide:

Method 1

- Moles of carbohydrate = $\frac{135}{180}$ = 0.75 mol; **[1 mark] **
- Moles of carbon dioxide = 0.75 x 2 = 1.5 mol;**[1 mark] **
- Mass = 1.5 x 44 = 66 (g); **[1 mark]**

Method 2

- 180 g carbohydrate → 2 x 44 g (= 88 g) carbon dioxide; **[1 mark] **
- 135 g carbohydrate → $\frac{135}{180}$ x 2 x 44 g carbon dioxide; **[1 mark] **
- = 66 (g); **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 3 marks] **

- *The two methods shown above are both accepted so use whichever method works for you*
- *Method 1 uses the equations: moles = *$\frac{mass \left(g\right)}{relative formula mass}$* and mass = moles x relative formula mass*

  - *With method 1, don't forget to take into account the ratio of C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*12*</sub>*O*<sub>*6*</sub>* to CO*<sub>*2*</sub>
- *Method 2 uses reacting masses which involves using the relative formula masses *

|   | > *C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*12*</sub>*O*<sub>*6*</sub> | > *→* | > *2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*5*</sub>*OH * | > *2CO*<sub>*2*</sub> |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| > *Write down mass given* | > *135 * |   | > *?* |   |
| > *Write in **M*<sub>*r*</sub> | > *180* |   | > *44 x 2 = 88 (due to ratio)* |   |
| > *Divide by 180* | > *1* |   | > *0.48* |   |
| > *Multiply by 135* | > *= 135 g* |   | > *= 66 g* |   |

- *66 (g) as the final answer with or without working scores 3 marks*

parts.problemMd:
Sucrose is another type of carbohydrate that can be used to produce alcohols. Calculate the total number of atoms in 10.0 g of sucrose, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub>. 
(*M*<sub>r</sub>: C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub> = 342; Avogadro constant = 6.02 × 10<sup>23</sup>)

number of atoms = ......................................
parts.solutionMd:
The total number of atoms in 10.0 g of sucrose, C<sub>12</sub>H<sub>22</sub>O<sub>11</sub> is:

- Moles of sucrose in 10.0 g = $\frac{mass}{M_{r}} = \frac{10 . 0}{342} \left(= 0 . 029\right)$;** [1 mark]**
- Number of atoms = moles x number of atoms in 1 molecule x Avogardo constant = 0.029 x 45 x 6.02 x 10<sup>23 </sup>
**OR** 
7.92 x 10<sup>23</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Ensure your answer makes sense - the number of atoms in 10 g will be very large, so if you don't get an answer which is very big or you get a number with a negative power of 10, you have gone wrong somewhere!*
- *Careful**: The question asks you for the number of **atoms**, not molecules, so you need to work out how many molecules there are in 10 g by multiplying the number of moles by the Avogadro constant*
- *You then need to calculate how many atoms there are in each molecule (12 + 22 + 11 = 45) and multiply by this*

parts.problemMd:
Alcohols can be produced in a number of different ways.

Methanol can be made from a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen.

CO (g) + 2H<sub>2 </sub>(g)<sub> </sub>$\rightleftharpoons$ CH<sub>3</sub>OH (g)

The forward reaction is exothermic.

i)  Explain why the concentration of methanol at equilibrium does not change.

(2)

ii)  Suggest conditions, in terms of temperature and pressure, which would give a high yield of methanol.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The concentration of methanol at equilibrium does not change because:

- The rate at which methanol is formed by the forward reaction; **[1 mark]**
- Equals the rate it is reacting in the backward / reverse reaction;  **[1 mark]**

ii) The temperature and pressure which would give a high yield of methanol are:

- Low / lower / decreased temperature; **[1 mark]**
- High / higher / increased pressure;  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *For part i), you would gain a mark if you stated that the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of backwards reaction*
- *Whilst you have not studied the conditions for this reaction, you can apply Le Chatelier's principle to predict what conditions would increase the yield of methanol*

  - *High pressures will favour the side with the fewest number of moles which is the product side of this reaction, therefore high pressures will increase the yield of methanol*
  - *A decrease in temperature will favour the forward reaction as it is exothermic, therefore lower temperatures will increase the yield of methanol*
- *You do not need to give an explanation, however, if you do, it must be correct otherwise you will not gain the mark*

parts.problemMd: Deduce the molecular formula of the alcohol that has a relatvie molecular mass of 102.
parts.solutionMd:
The molecular formula of the alcohol that has the relative molecular mass of 102 is:

- C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>OH; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *There are a number of different ways to approach this question:*

  - *Trial and error:*
  
    - *Choose any alcohol using the general equation to give its formula, e.g. C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*9*</sub>*OH and work out is **M*<sub>*r*</sub>
    - *If it is too low, choose an alcohol that contains more carbons atoms and repeat*
    - *If it is too high, choose an alcohol that contains fewer carbon atoms and repeat*
    - *Carry on like this until the alcohol that you choose has a **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 102*
  - *A more logical approach:*
  
    - *You should be aware that each consecutive member of a homologous series, such as the alcohols, differs in formula by CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*, which has a **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 12 + (2 x 1) = 14*
    - *The first alcohol of the series, methanol, CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH has a **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 12 + (3 x 1) + 16 + 1 = 32*
    - *So the 2nd alcohol will have a **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 32 + 14 = 46*
    - *The 3rd alcohol will have a **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 32 + (2 x 14) = 60*
    - *And so on, until you get to the 6th alcohol which will have an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 32 + (5 x 14) = 102*
  - *A more mathematical approach - if this does not make sense, do not worry, you can ignore it and use the other methods:*
  
    - *You can use an equation to solve this*
    - *We can write an expression for the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of any alcohol, using n to represent the number of carbons atoms and using the general equation for alcohols:*
    - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 12 x n + ((2n + 2) x 1) + (1 x 16) + (1 x 1)*
    - *Which simplifies to *
    - *M*<sub>*r*</sub>* = 14n + 18*
    - *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of our alcohol is 102 so:*
    - *102 = 14n + 18*
    - *n = 84/14 = 6*
    - *So the number of carbons is 6*
- *Do not get caught up with this question - it is only worth one mark, so in an exam situation if you were spending too long on it, you would be best to leave it and come back to it if you have time at the end of the exam*

parts.problemMd:
Alcohols undergo combustion reactions.

Write a balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of butanol.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation for the complete combustion of butanol is:

C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH   +  **6**O<sub>2</sub>   →   **4**CO<sub>2</sub>   +  **5**H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct formulae of all reactants and products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing LHS;** [1 mark]**
- Correct balancing RHS; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *You should be able to use the general formula for alcohols given in part (a) to work out the chemical formula of butanol as C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*9*</sub>*OH, you would gain credit if you used C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*10*</sub>*O in place of C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*9*</sub>*OH*
- *Complete combustion indicates there is a plentiful supply of oxygen so carbon dioxide and water are produced *
- *Remember: **When balancing combustion equations: *

  - *Balance the carbon atoms first *
  
    - *C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*9*</sub>*OH  +  O*<sub>*2*</sub>*   →   **4**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>*   +  H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Then balance the hydrogen atoms*
  
    - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*7*</sub>*OH   +  O*<sub>*2*</sub>*   →   **4**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>*   +  **5**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
  - *Calculate the total number of oxygen atoms on the right-hand side and balance these last *
  
    - *C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*7*</sub>*OH   +  **6**O*<sub>*2*</sub>*   →   **4**CO*<sub>*2*</sub>*   +  **5**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*

parts.problemMd: Describe the conditions needed to convert ethene to ethanol.
parts.solutionMd:
The conditions needed to convert ethene to ethanol are:

- Steam; **[1 mark]**

Any **two** from:

- High temperature / temperature of approximately 300 to 330 <sup>o</sup>C; **[1 mark]**
- High pressure / pressure of 60 to 70 atm; **[1 mark]**
- (Concentrated phosphoric) <u>acid</u> catalyst;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Ethanol is produced from ethene via an addition reaction*

  - *The steam, H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O, adds across the double bond -H on one carbon atom and -OH on another*
- *This method of producing ethanol uses non-renewable raw materials, as the ethene for the reaction is produced by cracking the hydrocarbons in crude oil*
