zinc + methanoic acid → ............................................ + ............................................

(2)

iii) Aluminium is also above hydrogen in the reactivity series. Why does methanoic acid not react with an aluminium kettle?

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The completed equation is:

**2**HCOOH + CaCO<sub>3</sub> → Ca(HCOO)<sub>2</sub> + **CO**<sub>**2**</sub> + **H**<sub>**2**</sub>**O**

- Correct species; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

ii) The completed word equation is:

zinc + methanoic acid → **zinc methanoate** +** hydrogen**

- Zinc methanoate; **[1 mark]**
- Hydrogen; **[1 mark]**

iii) Methanoic acid does not react with an aluminium kettle because:

- (Aluminium is) protected by <u>oxide</u> layer;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *Carboxylic acids will undergo typical acidic reactions, so the general equations for acids will apply*

  - *metal carbonate + acid → salt + carbon dioxide + water*
  - *metal + acid → salt + hydrogen*
- *Carboxylic acids form salts which end in '-anoate'*
- *Aluminium will not react despite it being high in the reactivity series because it reacts readily with oxygen, forming a protective layer of aluminium oxide which is very thin *
- *This layer prevents reaction with water and dilute acids, so aluminium can behave as if it is unreactive*

parts.problemMd:
This question is about carboxylic acids and esters.

A carboxylic acid has the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O.

The relative formula mass of the acid is *M*<sub>*r *</sub>= 88.

[2]

[1]

[1]

iii) Draw a ring around the functional group.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To determine the molecular formula of the acid:

- Calculate the empirical mass:

empirical formula mass = (12 x 2) + (1 x 4) + 16

empirical formula mass = 44 **[1 mark]**

- Determine the multiple of the empirical mass:

multiple = $\frac{\mathrm{empirical} \mathrm{formula} \mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{relative} \mathrm{formula} \mathrm{mass}}$

multiple= $\frac{88}{44}$= 2

- Deduce the molecular formula:

molecular formula = 2 x empirical formula

molecular formula = 2 x C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O

molecular formula = **C**<sub>**4**</sub>**H**<sub>**8**</sub>**O**<sub>**2**</sub> **[1 mark]**

![Structural formula of butyl acetate, showing a carbon chain with a terminal ester group. The molecule consists of carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and oxygen (O).](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/4-organic-chemistry/4-6-carboxylic-acids/assets/001-structural-formula-of-butyl-acetate-showing-a-ca.png)

**[1 mark]**

**[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A **displayed formula** must show every single bond. If you write the alcohol group as -OH, instead of -O-H, it will cost you the mark.
> 
> The acids are all named according to the stem **alkanoic acid**. You need to learn the formulas of methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, and butanoic acid.

parts.problemMd:
i) Describe what you would see when a small piece of magnesium ribbon is added to a solution of the carboxylic acid.

[2]

ii) Describe how you would identify any gaseous products.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) When a small piece of magnesium ribbon is added to the carboxylic acid:
> 
> - The magnesium would dissolve / disappear
> **OR**
> The magnesium would get smaller **[1 mark]**
> - Bubbles are produced
> **OR**
> Fizzing / effervescence is seen** [1 mark]**
> 
> ii) To identify the gaseous product:
> 
> - Place a lighted / burning splint into the gas** [1 mark]**
> - The gas will burn with a 'squeaky pop'
> **OR**
> The gas makes a popping sound **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiners will look for descriptions of what can be directly seen happening to the metal and the solution.
> 
> For example:
> 
> 1. "Hydrogen gas is produced"
> 
>   - This is an inference, not an observation.
>   - The observation is **bubbles of gas** are produced.
> 2. "The magnesium reacts"
> 
>   - You can't physically see the reaction, only signs of the chemical reaction.
>   - So, the observation would be that the magnesium is getting smaller / disappearing / dissolving.
> 
> Examiner reports consistently show that students lose marks by not describing the full test for a gas.
> 
> For example:
> 
> - "The squeaky pop test tests for hydrogen"
> 
>   - This does not describe how to do the test.
>   - It does not truly describe the positive outcome, it assumes that hydrogen creates the squeaky pop.
> - So, you must state both the method and the result:
> 
>   - **Method**
>   
>     - Use a **lighted** splint.
>     - A common mistake is to say "glowing splint", which is the test for oxygen.
>   - **Result**
>   
>     - You hear a **'squeaky pop'**.
> 
> Part (i) is worth two marks, so give two separate observations: mentioning only the bubbles and forgetting the magnesium getting smaller costs an easy mark.

|---|---|
| Structural formula | ............................................................................ |

- Name: Ethyl propanoate; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *During esterification, the OH from the carboxylic acid is removed, leaving CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*

parts.problemMd:
Propanoic acid reacts with sodium carbonate.

Write the balanced symbol equation for the reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced symbol equation for the reaction between propanoic acid and sodium carbonate is:

2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> → 2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa + H<sub>2</sub>O + CO<sub>2</sub>

- Correct reactants;** [1 mark]**
- Correct products; **[1 mark]**
- Correct balancing; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Remember: **Acids (including carboxylic acids) react with metal carbonates to form a salt, water and carbon dioxide*
- *You should be able to deduce the formula of sodium carbonate:*

  - *Sodium has a 1+ charge and the carbonate ion, CO*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>*, has a 2- charge*
  - *For the charge on the compound to be neutral overall, 2 sodium ions are needed for every 1 carbonate ion*
  - *This gives the formula Na*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *In the reaction, the acid loses the H from the –COOH group, leaving the ethanoate ion, CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*COO*<sup>*–*</sup>*, which has a 1- charge*

  - *Sodium has a 1+ charge, which means that 1 sodium is needed for every 1 ethanoate ion*
  - *This gives the formula CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*COONa*

The volume, in cm<sup>3</sup>, of hydrogen gas produced in this reaction is:

- Moles of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH = 1.0 x $\frac{50}{1000}$ = 0.05 (mol);** [1 mark]**
- Moles of hydrogen produced = $\frac{0.05}{2}$ = 0.025 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Volume of hydrogen gas produced = 0.025 x 24 000 = 600 (cm<sup>3</sup>); **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
A piece of magnesium was added to 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of an aqueous acid. The time taken for the metal to react completely was measured.

This experiment was repeated using different aqueous acids. The same volume of acid was used in each experiment and the pieces of magnesium used were identical.

In one experiment the reaction was carried out at a different temperature.

| **experiment** | **acid** | **concentration in mol/dm**<sup>**3**</sup> | **temperature / °C** | **time / seconds** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | propanoic | 1.0 | 20 | 300 |
| **B** | propanoic | 1.0 | 30 | 180 |
| **C** | propanoic | 0.5 | 20 | 480 |
| **D** | hydrochloric | 1.0 | 20 | 60 |

Explain the following in terms of collision rate between reacting particles.

i) Why is the rate in experiment **C** slower than the rate in experiment **A**?

(2)

ii) Why is the rate in experiment **B** faster than the rate in experiment **A**?

(2)

iii) Why is the rate in experiment **D** faster than the rate in experiment **A**?

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The rate in experiment **C** is slower than the rate in experiment **A** as:

- Concentration (of acid in **C**) is less / halved or concentration of **A** is more / doubled; **[1 mark]**
- Less frequent collisions in **C** / more frequent collisions in **A** (than in **C**);** [1 mark]**

ii) The rate in experiment **B** is faster than the rate in experiment **A **as:

- Higher temperature in **B** particles / molecules / atoms move faster/ have more energy / more have E<sub>a </sub>**OR** Particles / molecules / atoms in **A** move slower / have less energy / less have E<sub>a</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- More frequent collisions in reaction **B** / less frequent collisions in **A** (than in** B**); **[1 mark]**

iii) The rate in experiment **D** is faster than the rate in experiment **A** as:

- It (**D**) has strong (acid) and **A** has weak acid / (**D**) stronger / (**D**) ionises more / (**D**) dissociates more **OR** **A** is weaker / **A** ionises less / **A** dissociates less; **[1 mark]**
- It (**D**) has a higher concentration of hydrogen ions / **A** has a lower concentration of hydrogen ions; **[1 mark]**
- More frequent collisions (in **D**) or fewer collisions in **A**; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 7 marks]**

- *The frequency of the collisions is key to rate; more frequent collisions that arise as a result of increased concentration, surface area, temperature or pressure will all increase the rate*
- *Temperature also increases the energy of the particles and therefore the number of collisions that has enough energy to successfully react*
- *Stronger acids have greater concentrations of H*<sup>*+*</sup>* available, and therefore this acts in the same way as increasing the concentration of any other reactant*

parts.problemMd:
Maleic acid is an unsaturated acid. 5.8 g of this acid contained 2.4 g of carbon, 0.2 g of hydrogen and 3.2 g of oxygen.

i) How do you know that the acid contained only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen?

(1)

ii) Calculate the empirical formula of maleic acid.   Number of moles of carbon atoms = ................................

Number of moles of hydrogen atoms = ................................

Number of moles of oxygen atoms = ................................

The empirical formula is ......................................................................................

(3)

iii) The mass of one mole of maleic acid is 116 g. What is its molecular formula?

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) You know that the acid contained only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen because:

- Their masses add up to 5.8 g; **[1 mark]**

ii) The empirical formula of maleic acid is calculated by:

Calculations:

Number of moles of carbon atoms = 0.2    Number of moles of hydrogen atoms = 0.2    Number of moles of oxygen atoms = 0.2

- All three moles calculations correct; **[2 marks]**
- Two moles calculations correct; **[1 mark]**

Empirical formula:

- CHO; **[1 mark]**

iii) To determine the molecular formula of maleic acid:

- Mass of CHO = 29 **AND **$\frac{116}{29}$ = 4; **[1 mark]**
- So, the molecular formula is C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>4</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* | > *O* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element (mass/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{2.4}{12}=0.2$ | $\frac{0.2}{1}=0.2$ | $\frac{3.2}{16}=0.2$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * *$\frac{0.2}{0.2}$* = 1* | > $\frac{0.2}{0.2}$* = 1 * | > $\frac{0.2}{0.2}$* = 1 * |

- *The empirical formula is therefore CHO*
- *The **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the empirical formula is 12 + 1 + 16 = 29*
- *The** M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of the compound is 116 ÷29 = 4 *

  - *This means that there are 4 CHO fragments in the overall compound *
  - *Therefore, the molecular formula of maleic acid must contain 4 times the number of atoms than appears in the empirical formula*

parts.problemMd: Maleic acid is dibasic. One mole of acid produces two moles of H<sup>+</sup>. Deduce its structural formula.
parts.solutionMd:
The structural formula of maleic acid is:

HOOCCH=CHCOOH / CH<sub>2</sub>=C(COOH)<sub>2</sub>

- Double bond present; **[1 mark]**
- Correct number of C, H and O atoms **AND **The rest of the structural formula correct;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *As maleic acid is dibasic, it must contain 2 -COOH groups so that it can donate 2 moles of H*<sup>*+*</sup>* ions for every 1 mole of acid*
- *The **M*<sub>*r *</sub>* of the two  -COOH groups is 2 x (12 + (2 x 16) + 1) = 90*
- *This leaves 116 - 90 = 26*
- *This value must come from C and H atoms*
- *This must be from 2 C atoms and 2 H atoms: (2 x 12) + (2 x 1) = 26*
- *This means that maleic acid must contain a double bond*

  - *Otherwise there would be 2 more hydrogen atoms present*

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the ester produced is:
> 
> - Ethyl propanoate **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Two characteristics of a dynamic equilibrium are:
> 
> - The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate **[1 mark]**
> - The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The name of an ester has two parts. A good way to remember the rule is:
> 
> 1. The **first part** of the name comes from the **alcohol**.
> 
>   - Change the "-anol" ending to "-yl".
>   - e.g., ethan**ol** → eth**yl**
> 2. The **second part** of the name comes from the **carboxylic acid**.
> 
>   - Change the "-oic acid" ending to "-oate".
>   - e.g., propan**oic acid** → propan**oate**
> 
> **Dynamic equilibrium**
> 
> Remember that "dynamic" means the forward and reverse reactions are still happening, but **at the same rate**, so there is no overall change. A common mistake is to think the reaction has stopped.
> 
> Another common error is to state that the amounts of reactants and products are equal; they are **not equal**, they are just **constant**.
> 
> You might get credit for saying that a dynamic equilibrium occurs in a **closed system**, but this is not in the specification.

parts.problemMd: Which structure represents part of an ester molecule but **not** part of a carboxylic acid molecule?

**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C **

- An ester has the functional group RCOOR
- A carboxylic acid has the functional group -COOH

**A** is incorrect as this group (sometimes called an ester link) is present in both esters and carboxylic acids

**B** is incorrect as the carbonyl group (C=O) is present in both esters and carboxylic acids

**D** is incorrect as this piece can appear in a number of organic molecules including esters and ethers

> **[exam-tip]**
> It's important to distinguish between a **functional group** and a specific example of a molecule containing that group.
> 
> - The **ester functional group** is the RCOOR arrangement of atoms that is common to all esters.
> - A specific ester, like methyl ethanoate, contains this group but also has specific alkyl groups (e.g., -C<sub>3</sub>) attached.
> 
> This question asks for the functional group itself, which is represented by structure **C**.

- Visual pollution / litter; **[1 mark]**
- Danger to animals; **[1 mark]**
- Produce poisonous gases when burnt;  **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *To draw the structural formula of the polyester, remove the OH from either end of the carboxylic acid and the H from either end of the alcohol:*

  - *—OC—C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*—CO— and —O—CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*—CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*—O—*
- *Now join them together by an ester linkage —COO—:*

  - *—OC—C*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*—COO—CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*—CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*—O—*
- *Usually in structural formula, most of the covalent bonds are omitted but it is important that you keep the bonds at either end, to show that this is a repeating unit:*

  - *—OCC*<sub>*6*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*COOCH*<sub>*2*</sub>*CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*O—*

parts.problemMd:
Ethanoic acid and methanol will react to form a different ester.

i) Name the catalyst needed to form an ester from ethanoic acid and methanol.

(1)

ii) Name the ester formed when ethanoic acid reacts with methanol.

(1)

iii) Give the structural formula of the ester formed when ethanoic acid reacts with methanol.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The catalyst needed to form an ester from ethanoic acid and methanol is:

- (Concentration) sulfuric acid; **[1 mark]**

ii) The ester formed when ethanoic acid reacts with methanol is:

- Methyl ethanoate; **[1 mark]**

iii) The structural formula of the ester formed when ethanoic acid reacts with methanol is:

- CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Esters are formed from alcohols and carboxylic acids *
- *The first part of the name indicates the length of the carbon chain in the alcohol, and it ends with the letters ‘- yl’*
- *The second part of the name indicates the length of the carbon chain in the carboxylic acid, and it ends with the letters ‘- oate’*
- *So. the ester formed from** meth**anol and ***ethan***oic acid is called **meth**yl ***ethan***oate*
- *When giving the structural formula of an ester- the methyl part is given after the COO group, and the carboxylic acid before it*

parts.problemMd:
The ester methyl butanoate is found in apples. It can be made from butanoic acid and methanol. Their structural formulae are given below.

| ![butanoic-acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/4-organic-chemistry/4-7-esters/assets/008-butanoic-acid.png) | ![methanol](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/4-organic-chemistry/4-7-esters/assets/009-methanol.png) |
|---|---|
| butanoic acid | methanol |

Calculate the relative molecular mass of methyl butanoate.

(*A*<sub>r</sub>: C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)

Relative molecular mass .....................................................
parts.solutionMd:
The relative molecular mass of methyl butanoate is:

- (5 x 12) + (10 x 1) + (2 x 16); **[1 mark]**
- = 102; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *A correct answer of 90 scores 2 marks, with or without working*
- *Be careful in this question as you need to first work out the number of each element in methyl butanoate *
- *When methanol, CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH, and butanoic acid, C*<sub>*3*</sub>*H*<sub>*7*</sub>*COOH react*

  - *Butanoic acid loses the OH group leaving C*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*7*</sub>*O*
  - *Methanol loses the H from the OH group leaving CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*O*
- *So the resulting ester will contain:*

  - *5 carbon atoms (4 from butanoic acid and 1 from methanol)*
  - *10 hydrogen atoms (7 from butanoic acid and 3 from methanol)*
  - *2 oxygen atoms (1 from butanoic acid and 1 from methanol)*
- *Then you need to multiply the** A*<sub>*r*</sub>* of each element by the number of atoms of that element and add these together:*

  - *(5 x 12) + (10 x 1) + (2 x 16) = 102*

parts.problemMd:
An ester has the structural formula CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.

i) Draw out the displayed formula and circle the functional group.

(2)

ii) State the name of the alcohol used to make this ester.

parts.solutionMd:

- Correct displayed formula: **[1 mark]**
- -COO- circled; **[1 mark]**

ii) The name of the alcohol used to make this ester is:

- Propanol; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 mark]**

- *Make sure you show all of the bonds when drawing the displayed formula*
- *The functional group of an ester is COO so you need to make sure that these 3 atoms - and these only- are circled*
- *Careful**: The question in part ii) asks you to identify the name of the alcohol used to prepare this ester NOT the name of the ester, sometimes students misread and incorrectly give propyl ethanoate as their answer*
- *The alcohol part of the ester is the part to the right of the COO group*

parts.problemMd:
The ester CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> is an ester found in apples and contributes to their smell.

This ester can be prepared in the laboratory from a carboxylic acid and an alcohol.

Write a balanced equation for the production of CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
The balanced equation for the production of CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> is:

CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOH<sub> </sub>+ CH<sub>3</sub>OH → CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3 </sub>+ H<sub>2</sub>O

- Correct formula for the reactants; **[1 mark]**
- Rest of the equation correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Don't be put off by the more complicated formula of the ester *
- *To deduce the formula of the carboxylic acid and alcohol, work backwards from the formula of the ester*
- *During esterification, the carboxylic acid loses OH and the alcohol loses the H from the OH group, so split the ester between the two O atoms:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*(CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO and OCH*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *Add an OH to the carboxylic acid part:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*(CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*COOH*
- *Add an H to the alcohol part:*

  - *CH*<sub>*3*</sub>*OH*
- *So these are the reactants*
- *Don't forget that the OH and H that are removed join together to form a water molecule - students often forget to include the water molecule in equations showing esterification*

parts.problemMd:
An ester, **X**, was found to contain 39.98% carbon and 6.65% hydrogen.

Show that ester **X** is not the ester with the formula CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>.
parts.solutionMd:
To show that ester **X** is not the ester with the formula CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub>:

- Percentage of oxygen = 53.37%; **[1 mark]**
- Divide percentages by relative atomic masses: 
C = $\frac{39.98}{12}$ **OR **3.33(167) 
**AND** 
H = $\frac{6.65}{1}$ **OR **6.65 
**AND** 
O = $\frac{53.37}{16}$ **OR **3.34 **OR **3.3356(25); **[1 mark]**
- Divide results by the smallest value to obtain the ratio, C:H:O = 1:2:1; **[1 mark]**
- The empirical formula of ester **X **is CH<sub>2</sub>O **AND** The (empirical formula of the) other ester CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>3</sub> is C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub> (so they cannot be the same esters); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *You are only given the percentages of carbon and hydrogen but esters also contain oxygen*
- *You, therefore, need to work out the percentage of oxygen present:*

  - *100 - 39.98 - 6.65 = 53.37%*
- *To show that they are not the same ester, you need to compare their empirical formulae*

  - *So, you must give both empirical formulae to be awarded the final mark*

parts.problemMd:
The molecular mass of ester **X** is 60.

Deduce the molecular formula of ester **X**.
parts.solutionMd:
The molecular formula of ester **X** is:

- Relative molecular mass of CH<sub>2</sub>O = 12 + (2 x 1) + 16 = 30; **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{60}{30}$ = 2; **[1 mark]**
- Molecular formula of ester **X** = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *If the mass of the CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*O is 30 and the mass of the ester is twice this, then there must be 2 x CH*<sub>*2*</sub>*O within the molecule*
- *Ester **X** is methyl methanoate*

parts.problemMd:
A sweet-smelling ester with the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O was produced.

Which of the following reactants could not have been used to produce this ester?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- For this question, you needed to work out the resulting ester from the reactants given and then deduce whether it had the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O
- The reactants in option **D** will form butyl methanoate:

  - Butanol, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH, would have the H removed from the OH group - leaving C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>O
  - Methanoic acid, HCOOH, would have the OH removed, leaving HCO
  - Combining these, the resulting ester, butyl methanoate, would have the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, this is the simplest ratio so is also its empirical formula
- Working through the other reactants in a similar way will show that they have the empirical formula C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O:

  - The reactants in option **A** will form methyl propanoate:
  
    - Methanol, CH<sub>3</sub>OH, would have the H removed from the OH group - leaving CH<sub>3</sub>O
    - Propanoic acid, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH, would have the OH removed, leaving C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CO
    - Combining these, the resulting ester, methyl propanoate, would have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, and its empirical formula is therefore C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O
  - The reactants in option **B** will form ethyl ethanoate:
  
    - Ethanol, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH, would have the H removed from the OH group - leaving C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>O
    - Ethanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>COOH, would have the OH removed, leaving CH<sub>3</sub>CO
    - Combining these, the resulting ester, ethyl ethanoate, would have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, and its empirical formula is therefore C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O
  - The reactants in option **C** will form propyl methanoate:
  
    - Propanol, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>OH, would have the H removed from the OH group - leaving C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>O
    - Methanoic acid, HCOOH, would have the OH removed, leaving HCO
    - Combining these, the resulting ester, propyl methanoate, would have the molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, and its empirical formula is therefore C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O

parts.problemMd:
During the preparation of an ester, the reactants are added to a flask and heated using a water bath.

Explain how and why the ester is separated from the reaction mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
The ester is separated from the reaction mixture by:

- (Fractional) distillation;** [1 mark]**
- The ester distils first because it has a lower boiling point;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Fractional distillation is used to separate two or more liquids that are miscible (i.e. mix with each other)*
- *The mixture should be heated until it reaches the temperature that corresponds to the lowest boiling point in the mixture which will cause all of that substance to evaporate and condense in the condenser so it can be collected*
- *This question is worth 2 marks, so it is a safe assumption that 1 mark is to explain how the ester is separated, i.e. what method is used and 1 mark to explain why it is separated, i.e. it has the lowest boiling point of the substances in the reaction mixture*

parts.problemMd:
A carboxylic acid, **Y**, was used to form a polyester. The relative formula mass of the carboxylic acid was found to be 90 and its empirical formula is CHO<sub>2</sub>.

i) Deduce the molecular formula of carboxylic acid **Y**.

(2)

ii) Draw the displayed formula of the carboxylic acid, **Y**.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
The molecular formula of **Y** is:

- Relative mass of CHO<sub>2</sub> = 12 + 1 + (2 x 16) = 45;** [1 mark]**
- ($\frac{90}{45}$ = 2), so molecular formula = C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>;** [1 mark]**

ii) The displayed formula of the carboxylic acid, **Y** is:

![ethandioic-acid](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/4-organic-chemistry/4-7-esters/assets/012-ethandioic-acid.png)

- Two -COOH groups;** [1 mark]**
- The rest of the structure correct;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *The carboxylic functional group is -COOH, which contains the same number of atoms of each element as the empirical formula of **Y*
- *Combining the fact that the molecular formula contains 4 oxygen atoms with your knowledge that polyesters can be formed from the reaction between a diol and dicarboxylic acid should lead you to deduce **Y** is a dicarboxylic acid*
- *Make sure you show the bond in the OH groups*

parts.problemMd:
Carboxylic acid **Y** reacted with alcohol **Z** to form a polyester.

Give the formula of the other product in this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The formula of the other product in this reaction is:

- H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The reaction between a carboxylic acid and alcohol is a condensation reaction in which a small molecule of water is also produced*
- *You must give the formula, as specified in the question, stating water would not gain the mark*

parts.problemMd:
An ester was produced in the following reaction between methanoic acid and butanol.

HCOOH + C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH $\rightleftharpoons$ HCOOC<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O

After a period of time, the reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium.

Explain what is meant by the term **dynamic equilibrium**.
parts.solutionMd:
The term **dynamic equilibrium **means:

- A reaction is taking place in both directions (at the same time) 
**OR **
Forward and backwards reactions are taking place (at the same time); **[1 mark]**
- At an equal rate 
**OR**
** **The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the backward reaction 
**OR **
The concentrations of the reactants and products remain constant;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *This is a key definition that you need to know*
- *The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction would gain 2 marks*
- *Careful: **You would gain the second mark by stating that the concentration of the reactants and products remains **constant*

  - *You would not be awarded this mark for stating that the concentrations of the reactants / products are **the same** or **equal*

parts.problemMd:
i) Give the name of the ester produced during the reaction between methanoic acid and butanol.

(1)

ii) State the necessary catalyst for the reaction.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The name of the ester produced during the reaction between methanoic acid and butanol is:

- Butyl methanoate;** [1 mark]**

ii) The necessary catalyst for the reaction is:

- <u>Concentrated</u> (sulfuric) acid;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *The first part of the name indicates the length of the carbon chain in the alcohol, and it ends with the letters ‘- yl’*
- *The second part of the name indicates the length of the carbon chain in the carboxylic acid, and it ends with the letters ‘- oate’*

  - *e.g. the ester formed from** but**anol and ***methan***oic acid is called **but**yl ***methan***oate*
- *You must state that the acid is concentrated to get the second mark but you do not need to specify which acid*

  - *Concentrated sulfuric acid is the common acid used in esterification*

parts.problemMd:
4.60 g of methanoic acid was added to 9.62 g of butanol.

Calculate the maximum mass of ester that could be produced from this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
The maximum mass of ester that could be produced from this reaction is:

- *M*<sub>r</sub> of HCOOH =  46 
**AND **
*M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH = 74 
**AND** 
*M*<sub>r</sub> of HCOOC<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub> = 102; **[1 mark]**
- Moles of HCOOH = $\frac{4.60}{46}$ = 0.10 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Moles of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>OH = $\frac{9.62}{74}$ = 0.13 (mol);** [1 mark]**
- Moles of HCOOC<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub> = 0.10 (mol); **[1 mark]**
- Maximum mass of HCOOC<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub> = 0.10 x 102 = 10.2 (g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *You need to use the equation moles = mass ÷ **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* to find the number of moles of methanoic acid and butanol used in the reaction*
- *The balanced symbol equation shows that 1 mole of methanoic acid reacts with 1 mole of butanol to form 1 mole of the ester, HCOOC*<sub>*4*</sub>*H*<sub>*9*</sub>
- *As there are more moles of butanol than methanoic acid, butanol is in excess and methanoic acid is the limiting reactant *
- *The number of moles of limiting reactant determines the number of moles of product formed, therefore 0.10 moles of the ester is formed*

parts.problemMd:
The percentage yield of the reaction was found to be 68.6%.

Determine the mass of ester produced.

Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The mass of ester produced is:

- Actual yield = $\frac{68.6}{100}$ x 10.2; **[1 mark]**
- = 7.00 g;** [1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Percentage yield = *$\frac{\mathrm{actual} \mathrm{yield}}{\mathrm{theoretical} \mathrm{yield}}\times100$
- *You need to rearrange this equation to give you the actual yield*
- *You must give your answer to 3 significant figures to be awarded the second mark*
- *Careful**: The calculator value of 6.9972 should be rounded to 7.00, not 6.99, and you must give the two 0's after the decimal place*

parts.problemMd: Why do addition polymers not biodegrade easily?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The  correct answer is A**

- Addition polymers contain strong covalent bonds and are essentially inert at ordinary temperatures
- They cannot be broken down by bacteria so are not biodegradable
- They are usually sent to landfill or incinerated which both negatively impact the environment

parts.problemMd: Which of the following statements about polymers is **NOT **correct?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Addition polymers are formed by the joining up of many monomers and only occurs in monomers that contain C=C bonds

  - One of the bonds in each C=C bond breaks and forms a bond with the adjacent monomer with the polymer being formed containing single bonds only
  - Compounds containing single bonds only are saturated compounds

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: Polymers can be recycled but it is a difficult and expensive process

choices.label: B
choices.textMd: Addition polymers are unsaturated as they are made by combining molecules which contain a carbon double bond

choices.label: C

parts.problemMd:
Poly(ethene) is an addition polymer. Polyesters are a different type of polymer that form from two monomers and produce water.

|---|---|
| Addition |   |
| Substitution |   |
parts.solutionMd:
The type of polymer formed is:

- Condensation; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *Addition polymers are formed from monomers that have a double bond *
- *Condensation polymers are formed from either:*

  - *One type of monomer that has different functional groups*
  - *Two different monomers that have the same functional group on either end capable of reacting together *

parts.problemMd:
Biopolyesters are a specific type of polyester that are synthesised from sugar and plant oils.

Give an advantage of using biopolyesters instead of synthetic polyesters.
parts.solutionMd:
An advantage of using biopolyesters instead of synthetic polyesters is:

- Biopolyesters / they biodegrade easily / naturally; **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Poly(chloroethene) is a polymer.

It is made from its monomer, chloroethene.

Chloroethene has the percentage composition by mass

C = 38.4%      H = 4.8%      Cl = 56.8%

Show, by calculation, that the empirical formula of chloroethene is C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>Cl
parts.solutionMd:
The empirical formula of chloroethene can be shown to be C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>Cl as follows:

- Dividing percentages by atomic masses: C: 38.4/12 **AND **H: 4.8/1 **AND **Cl: 56.8/35.5; **[1 mark]**
- Correct results of divisions: C: 3.2 **AND **H: 4.8 **AND** Cl: 1.6; **[1 mark]**
- Obtaining ratio by dividing results by smallest value: C: 3.2/1.6 (= 2) **AND **H: 4.8/1.6 (= 3) **AND** Cl: 1.6/1.6 (= 1); **[1 mark]**

**Alternative method**

- Calculating *M*<sub>r</sub> of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>Cl:  C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>3</sub>Cl (= 24 + 3 + 35.5) = 62.5; **[1 mark]**
- Working for finding ratio of each element: C: 24/62.5 **AND **H: 3/62.5 **AND **Cl: 35.5/62.5; **[1 mark]**
- Evaluation of correct percentages: all x 100 C = 38.4(%) **AND **H = 4.8(%) **AND **Cl = 56.8(%); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *To calculate the empirical formula when given percentages, it is easiest to assume that you have 100 g of the sample, then you can workout the number of moles of each element in 100 g by using the **M*<sub>*r*</sub>*:*

|   | > *C* | > *H* | > *Cl* |
|---|---|---|---|
| > *Calculate the number of moles of each element in 100 g (%/**M*<sub>*r*</sub>*)* | $\frac{38.4}{12}\,=3.2$ | $\frac{4.8}{1}\,=4.8$ | $\frac{56.8}{35.5}\,=1.6$ |
| > *Divide by the smallest number to find the smallest ratio* | > * 3.2/1.6 = 2* | > * 4.8/1.6 = 3* | > * 1.6/1.6 = 1* |

- *The empirical formula is therefore C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*3*</sub>*Cl*

parts.problemMd:
Ethene can be used as a starting point in the manufacture of poly(chloroethene).

Stage 1 involves the formation of 1,2-dichloroethane and can happen by two different methods.

- Both methods form 1,2-dichloroethane
- Method 1 involves the reaction of chlorine with ethene.
- Method 2 reacts ethene with hydrogen chloride and oxygen and forms a second product.

Use chemical equations to compare the two methods.
parts.solutionMd:
The equations for both methods are:

- Method 1: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- Method 2: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + 2HCl + ½O<sub>2</sub> → C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O
**OR**
2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + 4HCl + O<sub>2</sub> → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O; **[1 mark]**

Plus any **one **of the following:

- Method 1 uses one mole of ethene
**AND**
Method 2 uses 2 moles of ethene;** [1 mark]**
- Method 1 only forms 1,2-dichloroethane / C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> 
**AND**
Method 2 forms 1,2-dichloroethane / C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub> and water / H<sub>2</sub>O **OR **method 2 forms a second / more than one product; **[1 mark]**
- Method 1 is more efficient than method 2; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Since the question asks you to use chemical equations, you should give the equations for both reactions*

  - *Method 1*
  
    - *Involves the reaction of chlorine with ethene to form 1,2-dichloroethane*
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>
    - *This equation does not require balancing*
  - *Method 2*
  
    - *Involves the reaction of hydrogen chloride and oxygen with ethene to form 1,2-dichloroethane and a second product*
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + HCl +O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + ?*
  - *To balance this equation:*
  
    - *There are two chlorine atoms on the right-hand side, which will require 2HCl on the left-hand side*
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + 2HCl +O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **?*
    - *The carbon atoms, some hydrogen atoms and the chlorine atoms are accounted for on both sides of the equation. *
    - *This leaves some hydrogen atoms and the oxygen atoms unaccounted for, so it is likely that the second product is water*
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + 2HCl +O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
    - *There are two oxygen atoms on the left-hand side but only one on the right-hand side, so we can use ½O*<sub>*2*</sub>* to form the H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
    - *C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + 2HCl +**½**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* + **H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
    - *You can also double the entire equation to remove the **½**O*<sub>*2*</sub>* and write your equation with whole numbers*
    - *2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>* + 4HCl +O*<sub>*2*</sub>* → 2C*<sub>*2*</sub>*H*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl*<sub>*2*</sub>* +2**H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O*
- *When you are comparing the two methods, ensure that you say about both methods*

  - *This may seem obvious but mark schemes often expect both sides of the comparison and examiner's reports frequently comment on the lack of balance*
  - *For example, method 1 only makes 1,2-dichloroethane*
  
    - *It may seem obvious to you that this means method 2 makes another product*
    - *But without clearly stating method 2 creates water as well, the examiner will not award the mark for the actual comparison*

The compounds that cannot form polymers are:

- (Because,) they do not have alcohol / hydroxyl / OH groups **OR **they are not diols

parts.problemMd:
Potassium permanganate is a purple solid that is soluble in water. A crystal of potassium permanganate is placed in a beaker containing water

After a short time, the crystal becomes smaller and the liquid at the bottom of the beaker becomes purple. Which statement explains this observation?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — the crystal dissolves in the water.**

The purple colour spreads because the potassium permanganate crystal dissolves in the water at the bottom of the beaker, putting coloured particles into solution that then move around. parts.problemMd:
A student uses this apparatus to investigate the temperature change that occurs when ammonium nitrate dissolves in water.

The student's results:

- Starting temperature of water: 20.0 °C
- Lowest temperature of solution: 14.2 °C

Use the results of the experiment to explain what type of reaction is taking place when ammonium nitrate is added to water.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the reaction is endothermic — it takes in energy, because the temperature fell.**

*M1:* the reaction is **endothermic** (the mark is lost if you write exothermic).

*M2:* evidence from the results: the temperature of the solution **decreased** when the ammonium nitrate dissolved (20.0 °C → 14.2 °C). A fall in temperature means the mixture took in heat energy from its surroundings — the defining sign of an endothermic change.

parts.problemMd: Show that the heat energy change, Q, is about 2400 J. [mass of 1.00 cm3 of solution = 1.00 g] [for the solution, c = 4.18 J/g/ °C ] Q = J
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Q ≈ 2400 J (calculation gives −2420 J).**

*Step 1 — temperature change:* ΔT = 14.2 − 20.0 = −5.8 °C.

*Step 2 — substitute into Q = mcΔT:* the solution's mass is 100 cm³ × 1.00 g/cm³ = 100 g, so
Q = 100 × 4.18 × (−5.8) = −2420 J.

*Step 3:* −2420 J is "about 2400 J", as the question asks. The negative sign shows the energy came *out of* the surroundings — consistent with the endothermic dissolution.

parts.problemMd: Use your answer to part (b) to calculate the enthalpy change, ∆H, in kilojoules per mole of ammonium nitrate. [Mr of ammonium nitrate = 80.0] Include a sign in your answer. ∆H = kJ/mol
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = +24.2 kJ/mol.**

*Step 1 — moles of ammonium nitrate:* n = 8.00 ÷ 80.0 = 0.100 mol.

*Step 2 — energy per mole:* 2420 J ÷ 0.100 mol = 24200 J/mol = 24.2 kJ/mol (any number of significant figures accepted).

*Step 3 — sign:* the mixture cooled, so the dissolving is endothermic and ΔH is **positive: ΔH = +24.2 kJ/mol**. (A correct answer with no working and no/incorrect sign scores 3 of the 4 marks.)

parts.problemMd: Explain why the reaction between aluminium and iron(III) oxide is a redox reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: aluminium is oxidised and iron oxide is reduced — both happen, so it is redox.**

*M1:* aluminium is oxidised **and** iron(III) oxide is reduced — oxidation and reduction occur together.

- *M2:* in a giant, rigid **tetrahedral lattice** (3D network).
- *M3:* the covalent bonds are **very strong** (lots of them, lots of energy to break).

- *M7:* there are only **weak forces between the layers**.
- *M8:* the **layers can slide over each other** — so graphite rubs off onto paper and makes marks — which is why it suits pencils.

parts.problemMd: Which group contains elements that are all unreactive?
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: D — Group 0.** The Group 0 noble gases (helium, neon, argon and the rest) have full outer shells, so every element in the group is unreactive. parts.problemMd: Which of these is the least reactive element in Group 1?
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: B — lithium.** Reactivity increases down Group 1: the atoms get bigger, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and is lost more easily. So of the four elements listed, caesium (A) is the most reactive, and potassium (C) and sodium (D) both react more vigorously than lithium — potassium melts into a ball and lights the hydrogen it makes. Lithium is nearest the top of the group, so it is the least reactive of the four.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the chemical formula of ammonium sulfate is (NH4)2SO4 Refer to the charges on the ions in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because the charges must cancel — two 1+ ammonium ions balance one 2− sulfate ion.**
The ammonium ion, NH₄⁺, carries a single positive charge, while the sulfate ion, SO₄²⁻, carries two negative charges. An ionic compound is neutral overall, so the formula needs enough ammonium ions for their positive charges to balance the sulfate's negative charge: two charges of 1+ give 2+, which cancels the 2− exactly. That is why the formula is (NH₄)₂SO₄, with brackets round the NH₄ to show two whole ammonium ions for every sulfate ion.

parts.problemMd: Describe how compound D can be obtained from crude oil using the industrial process of fractional distillation.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: heat the crude oil until it vaporises, pass the vapour into a fractionating column, let the fractions separate by boiling point, and collect compound D at the top of the column in the refinery gas fraction.**
*Step 1.* The crude oil is heated in a furnace so that it boils and vaporises.
*Step 2.* The hot vapour passes into the fractionating column (tower), which is hottest at the bottom and cooler towards the top — a temperature gradient.
*Step 3.* The column separates the mixture: each hydrocarbon condenses (or stays as a gas) at the height where the temperature matches its own boiling point, so the compounds in crude oil separate because of their different boiling points.
*Step 4.* Compound D is propane (C₃H₈), whose molecules are small with very low boiling points, so it rises to the top without condensing and is collected there, in the refinery gas fraction.

parts.problemMd: A student is given a sample of solid red lead oxide and some dilute nitric acid. Describe how the student could obtain a pure dry sample of lead(II) nitrate crystals.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: warm the dilute nitric acid, add the red lead oxide and stir, filter off the insoluble solids, then crystallise the lead(II) nitrate from the filtrate by heating, cooling and filtering again, and dry the crystals gently.**
*Step 1 — react.* Warm the dilute nitric acid in a beaker (gently — it must not be boiled) and add the red lead oxide a little at a time, stirring so the acid reaches all of the solid. The reaction forms lead(II) nitrate, which dissolves, while the insoluble lead(IV) oxide and any unreacted red lead oxide stay solid.
*Step 2 — filter.* Filter the mixture. The filtrate is the lead(II) nitrate solution; the residue on the filter paper is the unwanted insoluble material.
*Step 3 — concentrate.* Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to boil off some of the water. Every so often dip a glass rod in and let a drop cool on it: when small crystals form on the glass rod, stop heating.
*Step 4 — crystallise.* Leave the concentrated solution to cool so more lead(II) nitrate crystals form as the solution becomes saturated, then filter the crystals off.
*Step 5 — dry.* Dry the crystals by pressing them between filter papers or leaving them somewhere warm — never over a hot Bunsen flame, which would spit the crystals away or scorch them. That leaves a pure, dry sample of lead(II) nitrate crystals.

parts.problemMd:
The table gives the melting and boiling points of four pure substances, W, X, Y and Z. Melting point in °C Boiling point in °C W –7 60 X 660 2500 Y 180 1330 Z 115 445 Use data from the table to answer the questions.

Which substance is a gas at 100 °C?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — W.**

A substance is a gas at any temperature above its boiling point. W boils at 60 °C, so at 100 °C it is well above its boiling point and is a gas. The other three are still below their melting points at 100 °C, so they are solids: X (B) does not melt until 660 °C, Y (C) not until 180 °C, and Z (D) not until 115 °C.

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: W

parts.problemMd: Which substance is a liquid for the largest range of temperature?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — X.**

A substance is liquid between its melting point and its boiling point, so the widest liquid range belongs to the biggest gap between those two values. X: 2500 − 660 = 1840 °C, far wider than any other. W (A): from −7 to 60 is only 67 °C. Y (C): 1330 − 180 = 1150 °C. Z (D): 445 − 115 = 330 °C. So X stays liquid over by far the largest range of temperature.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: X

parts.problemMd: Which substance is a liquid at 1000 °C and a gas at 2000 °C?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: C — Y.**

Y melts at 180 °C and boils at 1330 °C. At 1000 °C it sits between those two values, so it is a liquid; at 2000 °C it is above its boiling point, so it is a gas. The others fail one condition or the other: W (A) boils at only 60 °C, so it is a gas at 1000 °C and at 2000 °C; X (B) is liquid from 660 °C up to 2500 °C, so it is still a liquid at 2000 °C; Z (D) boils at 445 °C, so it is a gas at both 1000 °C and 2000 °C.

markPoints.textMd: Answer C: Y

parts.problemMd: Substance Y does not conduct electricity when solid but does conduct electricity when molten. Give the type of bonding in substance Y.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ionic (or electrovalent).**

Ionic compounds do not conduct electricity in the solid state because their ions are fixed in position within the crystal lattice. However, when molten, the ions become free to move and can carry electrical current. This property is characteristic of ionic bonding.

parts.problemMd: Suggest how the melting point of a pure substance changes when an impurity is added.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: The impure substance will melt over a range of temperatures and will have a lower melting point.**

This disruption weakens the forces between particles, requiring less energy to break them apart, resulting in a lower melting point. parts.problemMd: Explain why solid lead iodide takes less time to form when the reaction is repeated using water at a higher temperature.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: At higher temperatures, crystals dissolve faster and particles move faster, so lead and iodide ions meet after a shorter period of time.**

When the water temperature is higher, the lead nitrate and potassium iodide crystals dissolve more quickly, releasing the ions into solution. Additionally, all particles in the solution, including the lead ions, iodide ions, and water molecules, move faster due to having more kinetic energy. This increased movement means that the lead and iodide ions diffuse through the water more rapidly and collide with each other more frequently, resulting in the formation of solid lead iodide in less time.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:**

For ammonium carbonate solution mixed with magnesium sulfate solution: no precipitate

For ammonium carbonate solution mixed with calcium chloride solution: precipitate of calcium carbonate

For barium chloride solution mixed with magnesium sulfate solution: precipitate of barium sulfate

When solutions of salts are mixed together, precipitates form if the combination produces an insoluble compound. The solubility rules help us predict these outcomes:

- Ammonium carbonate and magnesium sulfate: Both ammonium and magnesium salts are generally soluble, while sulfate salts are soluble except for Ba²⁺, Ca²⁺, Pb²⁺, and Sr²⁺. Since magnesium sulfate is soluble and no insoluble combination is formed, no precipitate appears.

- Ammonium carbonate and calcium chloride: Calcium carbonate is insoluble, so when calcium ions from calcium chloride combine with carbonate ions from ammonium carbonate, a precipitate of calcium carbonate forms.

- Barium chloride and magnesium sulfate: Barium sulfate is insoluble, so when barium ions from barium chloride combine with sulfate ions from magnesium sulfate, a precipitate of barium sulfate forms.

parts.problemMd: A student has four unlabelled beakers, each containing a colourless solution of a different salt. The four solutions are • potassium carbonate • potassium chloride • potassium iodide • sodium chloride Describe a method to identify each solution. Do not refer to safety in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:**

To identify each solution, perform the following tests:

1. Begin with a flame test for each solution. The sodium chloride solution will produce a yellow-orange flame, distinguishing it from the potassium-containing solutions which produce a lilac flame (though this color might be masked by sodium contamination).

2. For the remaining solutions (potassium carbonate, potassium chloride, and potassium iodide), add dilute acid to each. The potassium carbonate solution will effervesce, producing carbon dioxide gas that turns limewater cloudy, confirming its presence.

3. To distinguish between potassium chloride and potassium iodide, add silver nitrate solution to the remaining two solutions. The potassium chloride solution will form a white precipitate of silver chloride, while the potassium iodide solution will form a yellow precipitate of silver iodide.

parts.problemMd: Deduce the molecular formula of this alkane.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: C4H10**

The molecular formula of an alkane follows the general formula CnH2n+2. Using the empirical formula C2H5:

*Step 1:* The empirical formula has 2 carbon atoms and 5 hydrogen atoms.
*Step 2:* For alkanes, the general formula is CnH2n+2. For n=2: C2H(2×2)+2 = C2H6
*Step 3:* Since C2H5 is not in the form CnH2n+2, we need to find a multiple that works.
*Step 4:* If we double the empirical formula (C2H5) × 2 = C4H10
*Step 5:* Check if C4H10 fits the alkane formula: CnH2n+2 = C4H(2×4)+2 = C4H10

Therefore, the molecular formula is C4H10 (butane).

parts.problemMd: The equation for the complete combustion of one mole of an alkane can be represented by alkane + ZO2 → XCO2 + YH2O Complete combustion of one mole of the alkane produces 308 g of carbon dioxide and 144 g of water. parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: X = 7, Y = 8, Z = 11**

*Step 1:* Calculate the moles of carbon dioxide produced:
- Moles of CO2 = mass ÷ Mr = 308g ÷ 44g/mol = 7 mol
- Since each CO2 molecule contains 1 carbon atom, X = 7

*Step 2:* Calculate the moles of water produced:
- Moles of H2O = mass ÷ Mr = 144g ÷ 18g/mol = 8 mol
- Since each H2O molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms, the alkane must have produced 16 hydrogen atoms
- Therefore, Y = 8

*Step 3:* Determine the molecular formula of the alkane:
- From CO2, we know the alkane contains 7 carbon atoms
- From H2O, we know the alkane contains 16 hydrogen atoms
- So the alkane is C7H16

*Step 4:* Balance the equation C7H16 + ZO2 → 7CO2 + 8H2O
- Carbon is balanced (7 on each side)
- Hydrogen is balanced (16 on each side)
- For oxygen: on the right side we have (7×2) + (8×1) = 14 + 8 = 22 oxygen atoms
- Therefore, Z = 11 (since 11 O2 molecules provide 22 oxygen atoms)

The balanced equation is: C7H16 + 11O2 → 7CO2 + 8H2O

parts.problemMd: Explain why ammonia has a low boiling point.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Ammonia has weak intermolecular forces, so little energy is required to overcome them.**

Ammonia is a simple molecular substance, so the forces between molecules (intermolecular forces) are weak. These weak forces require little energy to overcome, which is why ammonia has a low boiling point. It's important to note that these are the forces between molecules, not the covalent bonds within the ammonia molecules themselves, which are strong.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about barium chloride.

Barium chloride can be made by reacting barium carbonate with dilute hydrochloric acid. The chemical equation for the reaction is BaCO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → BaCl2(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) Describe a method to produce dry crystals of hydrated barium chloride, starting with barium carbonate powder and dilute hydrochloric acid.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: react the dilute hydrochloric acid with excess barium carbonate, filter, crystallise the filtrate, then dry the crystals gently.**

- Add the barium carbonate powder to the dilute hydrochloric acid in a beaker, one spatula-measure at a time, stirring between additions; the mixture fizzes as carbon dioxide is released.
- Keep adding until the fizzing stops and some solid barium carbonate is left on the bottom: the carbonate is now in excess, so every trace of acid has reacted and the crystals will not be contaminated with acid.
- Filter to remove the excess solid; the filtrate is a solution of barium chloride.
- Heat the filtrate in an evaporating basin to evaporate some of the water, stopping when crystals begin to form on a glass rod dipped into the solution — do not boil all the water away at this stage.
- Leave the hot, concentrated solution to cool slowly so that crystals of hydrated barium chloride form.
- Filter the crystals from the remaining solution, then leave them to dry in a warm place (on filter paper, in a warm oven or in a desiccator) to give dry hydrated crystals.

Evaporating only until crystallisation starts, then drying gently, keeps the water of crystallisation inside the crystals so they stay hydrated.

parts.problemMd: A colourless solution contains sodium carbonate and sodium sulfate. Describe a test using barium chloride to show that the colourless solution contains sulfate ions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Add dilute acid (like nitric acid) to the solution before adding barium chloride solution. A white precipitate will form, confirming the presence of sulfate ions.

First, add a dilute acid (any acid except sulfuric acid) to the solution. This step is important because carbonate ions would also form a white precipitate with barium chloride, which would interfere with the test. Adding acid converts any carbonate ions to carbon dioxide gas, removing them from the solution. Then, add barium chloride solution to the acidified mixture. The formation of a white precipitate indicates the presence of sulfate ions, as barium sulfate is insoluble. This test specifically identifies sulfate ions in the presence of carbonate ions.

parts.problemMd: The student adds 2.12 g of sodium carbonate to an excess of dilute hydrochloric acid. The chemical equation for the reaction is Na2CO3(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H2O(l) + CO2(g) Calculate the maximum mass, in g, of carbon dioxide formed in the reaction. mass = g
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.88 g.**

*Step 1 — formula mass.* The relative formula mass of sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃, is 106.

*Step 2 — moles of sodium carbonate.* 2.12 ÷ 106 = 0.02 mol.

*Step 3 — moles of carbon dioxide.* The equation Na₂CO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g) shows one mole of CO₂ forming for every one mole of Na₂CO₃, so n(CO₂) = 0.02 mol.

*Step 4 — mass of carbon dioxide.* mass = 0.02 × 44 = 0.88 g.

The acid is in excess, so the sodium carbonate is the limiting reactant and 0.88 g is the maximum mass the reaction can give.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the reactivity of metals.

Name the type of reaction that occurs between manganese and chromium sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** displacement

The reaction between manganese and chromium sulfate is a displacement reaction. In this type of reaction, a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound. parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Graphite has a giant covalent structure with strong covalent bonds throughout, requiring a lot of energy to break. C60 fullerene has a simple molecular structure with weaker intermolecular forces between molecules.

Graphite is a giant covalent structure where each carbon atom is bonded to three others in layers. To melt graphite, these strong covalent bonds must be broken, which requires a lot of energy. Volume of H₂O = 5.63 g ÷ 1.00 g/cm³ = 5.6 cm³ (to 1 decimal place)

parts.problemMd: Ethane (C2H6) and ethene (C2H4) both react with bromine. Describe the differences in the reactions of ethane and ethene with bromine. Refer to the conditions, the products and the types of reaction involved.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane reacts with bromine only in ultraviolet light, by substitution, making bromoethane and hydrogen bromide; ethene reacts readily without UV, by addition across its double bond, making dibromoethane.**

Ethane, C₂H₆, is saturated, so a C–H bond must break for anything to happen: ethane needs UV radiation as its condition, and a bromine atom swaps in for a hydrogen — C₂H₆ + Br₂ → C₂H₅Br + HBr. Swapping an atom in for another is substitution.

Ethene, C₂H₄, is unsaturated: its C=C bond opens and each carbon picks up a bromine atom — C₂H₄ + Br₂ → C₂H₄Br₂. Adding atoms across a double bond is addition, and it needs no UV at all.

That is five differences: the condition (UV for ethane only), the bond broken (a C–H bond in ethane, the C=C bond in ethene), the type of reaction (substitution versus addition) and the products (bromoethane + HBr versus dibromoethane) — any five of the following earn the full credit.

parts.problemMd:
Diamond and graphite are made of carbon atoms, joined together by covalent bonds. The diagram shows their structures.

![diagram — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.21)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2022-06/4CH1-1C/assets/asset_8_b_diagram.png)

Discuss the differences between diamond and graphite. Refer to structure and bonding, electrical conductivity and hardness in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond is hard and does not conduct electricity, while graphite is soft and conducts electricity — the differences come from how the carbon atoms are bonded and arranged.**

Structure and bonding: in diamond each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four other carbon atoms in a giant tetrahedral structure. In graphite each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms, forming hexagonal rings arranged in flat layers.

Electrical conductivity: diamond does not conduct electricity because all of its outer electrons are locked in covalent bonds — there are no delocalised electrons to move and carry charge. Graphite conducts electricity because each carbon atom has one electron not used in bonding; these delocalised electrons move along the layers when a voltage is applied.

Hardness: diamond is very hard — to scratch or cut it, many strong C–C covalent bonds need to be broken. Graphite is soft and slippery because the weak forces between its layers let the layers slide over each other, which is why graphite works as a lubricant and in pencils.

However, ammonia is a gas that is difficult to handle directly and must be dissolved in water before application, which can lead to wastage. Additionally, ammonia has a high pH of 11, which will make the soil alkaline and may damage plants or stunt their growth. Ammonium sulfate, with a pH of 5.5, is closer to the pH of rainwater (approximately 5.6) and will not significantly alter the soil pH, making it safer for plants. However, ammonium sulfate has a lower percentage of nitrogen, so larger amounts are needed to provide the same amount of nitrogen. Both compounds are soluble, which can lead to runoff, wastage of fertiliser, water pollution, and eutrophication if not properly managed.

parts.solutionMd:

Burying polymers in landfill sites causes environmental problems because polymers are inert and do not biodegrade, meaning they remain in the environment indefinitely. parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd: **Answer: fractional distillation.** Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons whose boiling points increase as their molecules get bigger. The oil is heated so most of it vaporises, and the vapours rise up a fractionating column that is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top. Each fraction, including gasoline, condenses at the height where the column temperature matches its boiling range, so the mixture is separated.

parts.problemMd: Give the best method for separating the dyes in black ink.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: chromatography.** A spot of black ink is put near the bottom of some absorbent paper and the paper is dipped in solvent. Each dye in the ink dissolves to a different extent and is attracted differently to the paper, so the dyes travel up the paper at different speeds and separate into distinct spots. This is exactly what chromatography is designed to do — separate the substances in a mixture so they can be identified.

parts.problemMd: Give the best method for obtaining pure water from seawater.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: simple distillation.** The seawater is heated in a flask until pure water boils off and evaporates. The vapour travels into a water-cooled condenser, where it turns back into liquid and is collected — that distillate is pure water, because the dissolved salt has a very high boiling point and stays behind in the flask. Distillation is the best choice whenever you need to obtain the solvent itself from a solution.

parts.problemMd: A student mixes the following pairs of solutions. Pair 1 bromine solution and potassium chloride solution Pair 2 bromine solution and potassium iodide solution Explain how the student can use the results of these experiments to show the order of reactivity of the three halogens, bromine, chlorine and iodine. **Answer: Pair 1 shows chlorine is more reactive than bromine, and Pair 2 shows bromine is more reactive than iodine — so the overall order of reactivity is chlorine > bromine > iodine.**

Pair 1: bromine solution mixed with potassium chloride solution. Nothing happens — there is no reaction and no change in colour; the mixture stays yellow/orange. A halogen can only displace the halogen beneath it in the reactivity order, and here the bromine does not react with the chloride ions to produce chlorine — which can only be because bromine is the less reactive of the two. So chlorine is more reactive than bromine.

Pair 2: bromine solution mixed with potassium iodide solution. This time the mixture turns brown (an orange-brown tinge counts too): the bromine has displaced iodine from its iodide ions, and the brown colour is the iodine released — Br₂ + 2KI → I₂ + 2KBr. Displacement only works when the halogen added is the more reactive one, so bromine is more reactive than iodine.

Combining the experiments: chlorine > bromine from Pair 1 and bromine > iodine from Pair 2, which fixes the order of reactivity as chlorine > bromine > iodine.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 7.2 × 10²⁴ electrons.**

parts.problemMd:
Calcium bromide is an ionic compound. The table shows the formulae and melting points of caffeine and calcium bromide. Name Formula Melting point in °C caffeine C8H10N4O2 235 calcium bromide CaBr2 730 The relative formula mass of calcium bromide is similar to the relative formula mass of caffeine. parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: calcium bromide is a giant ionic lattice held together by strong electrostatic attractions between oppositely charged ions, while caffeine is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular forces between its molecules — so far more energy is needed to melt calcium bromide (730 °C) than caffeine (235 °C).**

In solid calcium bromide, Ca²⁺ and Br⁻ ions are packed into a giant lattice. Every ion pulls electrostatically on all of its oppositely charged neighbours, and those strong attractions run throughout the whole structure, so a huge amount of energy is needed to separate the ions before the solid can melt.

Caffeine, C₈H₁₀N₄O₂, has a simple molecular structure: the atoms inside each molecule are joined by strong covalent bonds, but between neighbouring molecules there are only weak intermolecular forces. Melting only has to overcome those weak intermolecular forces — the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken — so much less energy is needed. That is why a similar relative formula mass still leaves the two melting points (730 °C and 235 °C) far apart: it is the structure and bonding that decide the melting point, not the Mr.

parts.problemMd: What is the formula of ammonium carbonate?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — (NH₄)₂CO₃.**

The ammonium ion is NH₄⁺ (charge 1+) and the carbonate ion is CO₃²⁻ (charge 2−), so two NH₄⁺ ions are needed to balance one CO₃²⁻ ion, giving (NH₄)₂CO₃. A, NH₃CO₃, is wrong because NH₃ is ammonia — an uncharged molecule, not the ammonium ion. B, (NH₃)₂CO₃, is wrong for the same reason: it uses ammonia instead of NH₄⁺. C, NH₄CO₃, is wrong because one 1+ charge cannot cancel one 2− charge.

parts.problemMd: A technician finds an unlabelled bottle on a shelf that could be ammonium carbonate solution. Describe tests that the technician should do to confirm that the solution contains ammonium ions and carbonate ions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ammonium ions — add sodium hydroxide solution and warm (heat) the mixture, then test the gas given off with damp red litmus paper: it turns blue. Carbonate ions — add dilute hydrochloric acid and test the gas given off with limewater: it turns cloudy/milky.**

For the ammonium test: adding sodium hydroxide and warming releases ammonia gas from the ammonium ions (NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O). Hold damp red litmus paper at the gas — ammonia is alkaline, so the paper turns blue. The litmus must test the gas coming off, not be dipped into the solution.

For the carbonate test: acid plus a carbonate gives carbon dioxide gas, so fizzing starts as soon as the hydrochloric acid is added. Bubble the gas into limewater: the CO₂ turns the limewater cloudy/milky because a white precipitate of insoluble calcium carbonate forms. Again, the limewater tests the gas escaping from the solution — it is never poured straight into the sample.

parts.problemMd: Explain how method B prevents iron from rusting even when the zinc coating is scratched.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: zinc is more reactive than iron, so the zinc reacts instead of the iron — it oxidises, forming zinc oxide, before the iron can react.**
Zinc is above iron in the reactivity series: it has a greater tendency to lose electrons than iron does. When the coating is scratched, both metals are exposed to oxygen and water, but the more reactive zinc atoms lose their electrons first — the zinc oxidises, forming zinc oxide, and reacts before any iron is attacked. **Answer: a catalyst provides an alternative pathway (an alternative route) for the reaction, with a lower activation energy.**

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: each magnesium atom loses its two outer electrons, and each of two chlorine atoms gains one of them, forming Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions.**
Magnesium has two electrons in its outermost shell. It gives away (transfers) those two electrons, leaving a full outer shell and a 2+ charge: the metal becomes Mg²⁺. parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the covalent bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between the shared pair of electrons and the nuclei of the two bonded atoms.**

**Answer: ethane is saturated — it contains single bonds only, with no double bond.**

parts.problemMd: Explain why hexane (C6H14) has a higher boiling point than butane (C4H10).
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: hexane has a higher boiling point because its molecules are larger with longer chains, so there are stronger intermolecular forces between the molecules and more energy is needed to overcome them.**

A C₆H₁₄ molecule is a longer chain than C₄H₁₀, giving more contact between neighbouring molecules, so the intermolecular forces of attraction are stronger in hexane than in butane. Boiling separates the molecules from one another — no covalent bonds are broken — so the stronger the intermolecular forces, the more energy is needed to overcome them and the higher the temperature at which the liquid boils. Butane has weaker intermolecular forces between its smaller molecules, so they are overcome at a lower temperature and it boils first.

parts.problemMd: Explain why this is a redox reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: it is a redox reaction because reduction and oxidation happen together — the iron(III) oxide loses oxygen (it is reduced) while the carbon monoxide gains oxygen (it is oxidised).**

In Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂, the Fe₂O₃ gives up its oxygen and ends as iron, so iron(III) oxide is reduced. The CO takes that oxygen and becomes CO₂, so carbon monoxide is oxidised. parts.problemMd:
Diamond and graphite are two naturally‑occurring forms of carbon. They both have giant covalent structures

![diamond and graphite structures — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.18)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2025-06/4CH1-1C/assets/asset_8_stem_structures.png)

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond has a high melting point because its atoms are held by strong covalent bonds — there are very many of them, and a large amount of energy is needed to break them.**

Diamond is a giant covalent structure: every carbon atom is covalently bonded to several others in a rigid 3D network. Because the structure is giant, melting is not a matter of freeing a molecule — strong covalent bonds throughout the whole lattice have to be broken, and there are enormous numbers of them. Overcoming that many strong bonds needs a large amount of thermal energy, which is why diamond melts only at a very high temperature. (This is about breaking covalent bonds in the giant lattice — diamond has no separate molecules between which weak forces could act.)

parts.problemMd: Explain why graphite is soft and is a conductor of electricity. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite is soft because it is layered — strong covalent bonds hold each carbon atom to three others within flat layers, but the weak forces between the layers let them slide over each other — and it conducts electricity because each carbon atom contributes one delocalised electron that is free to move through the solid.**

Structure: in graphite each carbon atom is joined to three other carbon atoms by covalent bonds, so the atoms form flat hexagonal sheets — a 2D layer structure — rather than the 3D network of diamond.

Why it is soft: within a layer the covalent bonds are strong, but the forces between neighbouring layers are weak. Little energy is needed to slide one layer over another, so the layers flake off easily — which is why a pencil leaves graphite on paper and why graphite feels soft.

Why it conducts: because each carbon is bonded to only three neighbours, one outer-shell electron per atom is left out of the bonding. These electrons become delocalised between the layers, and delocalised electrons are free to move through the whole solid. When a voltage is applied they drift along and carry charge, so graphite conducts electricity — unlike diamond, where every outer electron is locked into a covalent bond and nothing can move.

parts.problemMd: Ethane and ethene undergo different types of reaction with bromine. Describe the differences between these two reactions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane reacts by substitution only in ultraviolet light, decolourising the bromine very slowly (if at all) and making two products — bromoethane and hydrogen bromide; ethene reacts by addition immediately, even in the dark, decolourising the orange bromine straight away and making one product, dibromoethane.**

*Ethane (saturated):* its C−C single bonds are strong, so a substitution reaction happens only when ultraviolet (UV) radiation supplies the energy — one bromine atom replaces a hydrogen atom, producing bromoethane (C₂H₅Br) and hydrogen bromide (HBr). The orange colour of the bromine fades only very slowly, if at all.

*Ethene (unsaturated):* its reactive C=C double bond opens and bromine atoms add across it — an addition reaction that happens immediately, with no light needed. The orange colour turns colourless at once, and the single product is the addition compound dibromoethane (C₂H₄Br₂).

So the differences to state: substitution vs addition, UV light needed vs not needed, decolourising very slowly vs immediately, and two products vs one.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about atomic structure and the Periodic Table.

Which particle is a proton?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — X is the proton.**

X is drawn inside the nucleus carrying a single positive charge, and a proton is exactly that: the positive particle found in the nucleus. A (W) is the neutron — it also sits in the nucleus but carries no charge, so it cannot be the proton. C (Y) is an electron — a tiny negatively charged particle moving in shells around the nucleus. D (Z) is the nucleus as a whole — the central cluster of protons and neutrons, not one single particle.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: X

parts.problemMd: Which particle has a relative charge of 0?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — W, the neutron, has a relative charge of 0.**

Neutrons are the neutral particles in the nucleus: they add mass but no charge at all. B (X) cannot be right because X is a proton with a relative charge of +1. C (Y) cannot be right because Y is an electron with a relative charge of −1. D (Z) cannot be right because Z is the nucleus, which contains protons and therefore has an overall positive charge rather than zero.

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: W

parts.problemMd: Name the part of the atom labelled Z.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the nucleus.**

Z points to the compact cluster in the centre of the atom where all the protons and neutrons are gathered; the electrons (labelled Y in the diagram) move around it in shells. Almost the entire mass of the atom is concentrated in this tiny, positively charged nucleus.

parts.problemMd: What is the group number of this element?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — the group number is 3.**

The group number counts the electrons in the outer shell. Counting the electrons drawn in the diagram, this atom has shells holding 2 + 3 = 5 electrons altogether, so three of them sit in the outer shell and the element belongs in group 3. A (2) is wrong because two is the number of occupied shells, which gives the period rather than the group. C (5) is wrong because five is the total number of electrons (the atomic number), not the outer-shell count. D (11) is wrong because an atom with eleven electrons would be a much bigger atom with more shells than the one drawn.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: 3

parts.problemMd: What is the period number of this element?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — the period number is 2.**

The period number equals the number of occupied shells in the atom, and the diagram shows electrons filling exactly two shells, so this element sits in period 2. B (3) is wrong: three counts the outer-shell electrons, which gives the group. C (5) is wrong: five is the total electron count (the atomic number), not the number of shells. D (11) is wrong: eleven electrons would fill three shells, so it cannot describe this atom.

parts.problemMd: Give the chemical symbol of this element.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B.**

Three outer-shell electrons put the element in group 3 and two occupied shells put it in period 2; the atom carries 2 + 3 = 5 electrons, so its atomic number is 5. The element with atomic number 5 is boron — in the table of period 2 elements it falls between Be (atomic number 4) and C (atomic number 6) — and its chemical symbol is B.
