parts.problemMd: Two beakers are unlabelled. One beaker contains a solution of ammonium chloride and the other beaker contains a solution of ammonium sulfate. Describe tests that can be carried out to confirm that one beaker contains ammonium chloride and the other beaker contains ammonium sulfate.

**Answer: the missing formulae are Mg(NO₃)₂, Li₂SO₄ and AlPO₄.**

The completed set of compounds is therefore: with Li⁺ — LiNO₃, Li₂SO₄ and Li₃PO₄; with Mg²⁺ — Mg(NO₃)₂, MgSO₄ and Mg₃(PO₄)₂; with Al³⁺ — Al(NO₃)₃, Al₂(SO₄)₃ and AlPO₄.

parts.problemMd: Explain why magnesium oxide has a higher melting point than sodium chloride. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: both sodium chloride and magnesium oxide are giant ionic lattices held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions, but the attractions in MgO are stronger because its ions carry higher charges, so more energy is needed to overcome them — and that is why MgO melts at a higher temperature.**

Both substances are ionic: a giant lattice of positive and negative ions packed in a regular pattern, with every ion pulled from all sides by electrostatic attraction towards the oppositely charged ions around it. These ionic bonds act in every direction and must be overcome for the crystal to melt.

The difference lies in the size of the charges. In MgO the ions are Mg²⁺ and O²⁻, each carrying a double charge, while in NaCl the ions are Na⁺ and Cl⁻ with only single charges. The ions in MgO therefore have a much higher charge density, so the electrostatic attraction between them is stronger than the attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻.

Stronger attraction means more energy must be supplied to overcome the forces holding the lattice together, so magnesium oxide has the higher melting point.

**Answer: B — one product for propene with bromine and two products for propane with bromine.**

parts.problemMd: State what is meant by the term functional group.

parts.problemMd: Isoprene has this percentage composition by mass. C = 88.2 % H = 11.8 % Show by calculation that the empirical formula of isoprene is C5H8
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the calculation gives the simplest ratio 5 : 8, so the empirical formula is C₅H₈.**

parts.problemMd: Explain why isoprene does not have the same general formula as propene.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because propene is an alkene with the general formula CnH₂n (one double bond), while isoprene has more than one double bond, so it cannot fit that general formula.**

Every alkene contains exactly one C=C double bond, which is why its members follow CnH₂n — substituting n = 5 (2 × 5 = 10) would give C₅H₁₀ for a five-carbon alkene. Isoprene is C₅H₈: it has two C=C double bonds, so it has four fewer hydrogens than the alkene general formula allows and belongs to a different series (a diene), not the same one as propene.

parts.problemMd:
Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons.

Describe how useful hydrocarbons can be obtained from crude oil. Refer to fractional distillation and cracking in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions, and some of the long-chain fractions are then cracked to make the smaller hydrocarbons that are in high demand.**

*Fractional distillation:* crude oil is heated so most of it evaporates, and the vaporised mixture enters a tall fractionating column with a temperature gradient — it is hottest at the bottom and coolest at the top. The hydrocarbons in crude oil have different boiling points, so as the vapours rise, each fraction condenses at the temperature where its boiling point is reached: long-chain hydrocarbons with high boiling points condense low down where it is hot, and shorter-chain alkanes with low boiling points keep rising and condense higher up where it is cooler. In this way the mixture is separated into useful fractions.

*Why cracking is needed:* fractional distillation produces far more long-chain hydrocarbons than can be sold, while short-chain alkanes are in much greater demand than the fractions supply — so the excess long-chain fraction is cracked. Cracking is done by heating the hydrocarbon vapours to about 600–700 °C over a catalyst such as silica, alumina or zeolite. It splits large alkane molecules into shorter-chain alkanes, which are more flammable and make better fuels, and into alkenes, which are valuable reactive starting materials used to make polymers (plastics).

parts.problemMd: Explain how the combustion of an impurity in some hydrocarbon fuels causes an environmental problem.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: sulfur impurities in fuels burn to make sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in rain to form acid rain.**

Many hydrocarbon fuels contain sulfur as an impurity. When the fuel burns, the sulfur burns too — it reacts with oxygen in the air to form sulfur dioxide, SO₂: S + O₂ → SO₂. This acidic gas escapes up the chimney with the rest of the exhaust. In the atmosphere the sulfur dioxide dissolves in rain clouds (it reacts with water in the air), so the rain that falls is acidic — acid rain — which damages buildings, plants, lakes and wildlife far from where the fuel was actually burned.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about ethane, C2H6

Explain a problem caused by a product of the incomplete combustion of ethane.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: incomplete combustion of ethane can produce carbon monoxide, a poisonous gas that reduces the capacity of the blood to transport oxygen.**

When oxygen is limited, ethane burns without enough air to form CO rather than CO₂. Once breathed in, carbon monoxide attaches to the haemoglobin in red blood cells in place of oxygen, so the blood carries less oxygen round the body — which is why the gas is toxic. A second incomplete-combustion product, soot (carbon), is also a problem: released into the air it causes breathing difficulties such as asthma and other respiratory problems.

parts.problemMd: Explain why ethane has a lower boiling point than octane.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ethane has weaker intermolecular forces between its molecules than octane does, so less energy is needed to overcome them.**

Ethane is a small molecule with only two carbon atoms, while octane's long chain of eight carbons gives far more contact between neighbouring molecules and hence stronger intermolecular forces. Boiling means separating the molecules from one another — the covalent bonds inside the molecules are never broken — so the weaker the forces between the molecules, the less energy (and the lower the temperature) needed to pull them apart into a gas. That is why ethane boils far below octane.

parts.problemMd: Describe two experiments to show that the ⇌ symbol is correct for this reaction. Include any relevant observations.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: run the reaction forwards and backwards — add water to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate, then heat hydrated copper(II) sulfate — and use the colour changes as the observations.**

Experiment 1 (forwards): put a little anhydrous copper(II) sulfate in a dry boiling tube and add a few drops of water. The white powder turns blue as hydrated copper(II) sulfate forms, and the tube feels warm because the change is exothermic.

Experiment 2 (backwards): put some blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals in an evaporating basin (a suitable vessel — a boiling tube works too) and heat them to dryness with a gentle flame. parts.problemMd:
Fluorine is an element found in Group 7 of the Periodic Table.

Give the electronic configuration of an atom of fluorine.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2,7.**

Fluorine is in Group 7, so a fluorine atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell, with one complete inner shell of two electrons before that. Written in order the shells hold 2 then 7 — the atom is a single electron short of a full outer shell, which is what makes fluorine so reactive.

parts.problemMd: Which period does fluorine belong to?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — Period 2.**

Periods are the horizontal rows of the Periodic Table, numbered by how many shells the atoms fill. Fluorine fills two shells (2,7), so it belongs to Period 2. A (Period 1) is wrong because Period 1 elements use only a single shell; C (Period 3) is wrong because Period 3 atoms occupy three shells; D (Period 7) is wrong because it confuses the period with the group number — fluorine is in Group 7 but sits in Period 2.

markPoints.textMd: Answer B: Period 2

parts.problemMd: Describe how two fluorine atoms combine to form a fluorine molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the two fluorine atoms share a pair of electrons — a single covalent bond.**

Each fluorine atom has seven outer electrons, one short of a full outer shell. As the atoms combine, each contributes one electron to a shared pair that sits between the two nuclei; the electrostatic attraction between that shared pair of electrons and both nuclei is the covalent bond itself. Because the shared pair counts towards both atoms, each fluorine now has a full outer shell, giving the F₂ molecule.

parts.problemMd: Describe the changes in the electronic configurations of a lithium atom and a fluorine atom when they form lithium fluoride. fluorine lithium
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: fluorine changes from 2.7 to 2.8 — it gains one electron; lithium changes from 2.1 to 2 — it loses one electron.**

parts.problemMd: Lithium fluoride has a giant ionic structure. Explain why lithium fluoride has a high melting point.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions takes a lot of heat energy to break, so lithium fluoride has a high melting point.**

LiF is a giant ionic lattice built from Li⁺ and F⁻ ions. Every ion is pulled on by all of its oppositely charged neighbours through strong electrostatic forces of attraction, and those forces act throughout the whole giant structure. To melt the solid you have to overcome that attraction everywhere at once, which requires a very large amount of energy — hence the high melting point. Keep the explanation about ions: it is nothing to do with weak forces between molecules, and there are no covalent bonds in the lattice.

**Answer: the oxidising agent is the iron(II) ion, Fe²⁺, in the FeSO₄ solution.**

parts.problemMd: A student is given an aqueous solution of chlorine and an aqueous solution of potassium bromide. Explain how he can use these two solutions to compare the reactivity of chlorine with the reactivity of bromine.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Mix the aqueous chlorine with the aqueous potassium bromide — the mixture turns orange because bromine is displaced, which proves chlorine is the more reactive of the two halogens.**

Add the chlorine solution to the potassium bromide solution in a test tube. Chlorine sits above bromine in Group 7, and a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive one from its salt: the chlorine takes bromine's place in the compound and bromine, Br₂, is set free in the solution. The bromine is what you see — the colourless potassium bromide solution turns orange (any orange/yellow/brown shade counts as the bromine appearing). Ionic equation: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. The observation therefore settles the comparison: because a displacement reaction happens, chlorine is more reactive than bromine. The reverse argument holds too — if no change had been seen, bromine would have been the more reactive of the pair.

parts.problemMd: Describe how a pure, dry sample of the insoluble salt, barium sulfate, could be made from the two solids sodium sulfate and barium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: dissolve both solids in water, mix the two solutions, filter off the barium sulfate precipitate, wash the residue with distilled water, then dry it between filter papers or in a warm oven.**
*Step 1 — make two solutions.* Sodium sulfate and barium chloride are both soluble, so dissolve each solid in a little distilled water, giving a solution of each of the solids.
*Step 2 — mix.* Pour the two solutions together and stir. Barium sulfate is insoluble, so a white precipitate forms immediately while the sodium chloride stays in solution: Ba²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → BaSO₄(s).
*Step 3 — separate.* Filter the mixture. The residue in the filter paper is the barium sulfate; the sodium chloride solution passes through as the filtrate.
*Step 4 — purify.* Wash the precipitate (the barium sulfate residue) with distilled water to rinse off any sodium chloride solution clinging to it — without washing, dried crystals would carry trapped impurities.
*Step 5 — dry.* Dry the solid between fresh filter papers or leave it in a warm oven. Drying over a hot Bunsen flame is unsuitable: it can scorch the paper and spit fine crystals away, so gentle drying is what gives a pure, dry sample.

parts.problemMd: Explain why this process is carried out in the absence of air and at a temperature below 40 °C.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: air is excluded because oxygen ruins fermentation, and the temperature stays below 40 °C because heat destroys the yeast's enzymes.**

The fermentation reaction needs anaerobic conditions. In air the yeast switches to aerobic respiration: the ethanol that forms reacts with oxygen and is oxidised, so ethanol is not produced — in air it would be oxidised further to ethanoic acid (the acid in vinegar). Aerobic conditions also produce carbon dioxide and water instead of ethanol, so keeping air out is what makes the yeast give alcohol.

The temperature matters because fermentation is catalysed by enzymes in the yeast. If the temperature rises above 40 °C the enzymes become denatured — their shape is destroyed — which makes the reaction slow down and finally stop. Yeast works fastest at its optimum temperature, between 30 °C and 40 °C, so the reaction is kept just under 40 °C.

parts.problemMd: Predict the effect on the yield of CO(g) at equilibrium when the temperature is increased without changing the pressure. Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: The yield of CO(g) increases.**

When the temperature is increased, the equilibrium shifts to the right to produce more CO(g). This happens because the forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +41 kJ/mol), meaning it absorbs heat. According to Le Chatelier's principle, when a system at equilibrium is subjected to a change in temperature, the system will shift in the direction that counteracts the change. In this case, increasing the temperature favors the endothermic forward reaction, which produces more CO(g).

parts.problemMd: Predict the effect on the yield of CO(g) at equilibrium when the pressure is increased without changing the temperature. Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: There is no effect on the yield of CO(g).**

When the pressure is increased, there is no effect on the yield of CO(g) because there are equal numbers of moles of gas on both sides of the equilibrium equation. The reaction is H₂(g) + CO₂(g) ⇌ CO(g) + H₂O(g), with 2 moles of gas on the left and 2 moles of gas on the right. According to Le Chatelier's principle, changing the pressure only affects equilibria where there is a different number of moles of gas on each side. Since the number of moles is the same, increasing the pressure does not shift the equilibrium position or change the yield of CO(g).

Name the most abundant gas in the Earth’s atmosphere.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: nitrogen.**

Nitrogen makes up around four-fifths of the air — far more than oxygen, which accounts for most of what is left. parts.problemMd: Explain why potassium is more reactive than sodium. Refer to the electronic configurations of the atoms in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: The electron configuration of sodium is 2,8,1 and potassium is 2,8,8,1. Potassium's outer electron is in the fourth shell, which is further from the nucleus than sodium's outer electron in the third shell. This increased distance means the outer electron in potassium is less attracted to the nucleus and is more easily lost, making potassium more reactive than sodium.**

Sodium has the electron configuration 2,8,1, meaning it has one electron in its outer shell (third shell). Potassium has the electron configuration 2,8,8,1, with its outer electron in the fourth shell. The outer electron in potassium is further from the nucleus than in sodium. As the distance from the nucleus increases, the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron decreases. This weaker attraction means potassium's outer electron is more easily lost during chemical reactions compared to sodium's outer electron, making potassium more reactive.

**Answer: Fermentation uses renewable sugar cane while hydration uses non-renewable crude oil; fermentation operates at lower temperatures and pressures, reducing energy costs; fermentation uses natural yeast which is not harmful, while hydration uses corrosive phosphoric acid; however, hydration is faster and produces purer ethanol than fermentation.**

The fermentation method has several advantages over hydration. First, it uses sugar cane as a raw material, which is renewable and can be regrown, unlike crude oil which is finite and non-renewable. Second, fermentation operates at much lower temperatures (30°C) and pressures (1 atmosphere) compared to hydration (300°C and 60-70 atmospheres), significantly reducing energy costs. Third, yeast is a natural substance that is not harmful, whereas phosphoric acid used in hydration is corrosive and requires careful handling.

However, hydration has some advantages over fermentation. The hydration process is much faster than fermentation, which is a slow biological process. Additionally, hydration produces pure ethanol, while fermentation yields impure ethanol that requires further purification. Another consideration is that growing sugar cane for fermentation requires land that could otherwise be used for food production or livestock, whereas the hydration process doesn't have this limitation. Finally, hydration is a continuous process that can be operated constantly, while fermentation is typically a batch process that requires periodic setup and completion.

**Answer: There is no effect on the yield of hydrogen iodide.**

*Step 1 — masses from the percentages:* treat the printed percentages as masses in grams, so a sample of the compound contains 40 g of C, 6.7 g of H and 53.3 g of O.

*Step 2 — moles:* divide each mass by its relative atomic mass — never by the atomic numbers. Moles of C = 40 ÷ 12 = 3.33; moles of H = 6.7 ÷ 1 = 6.7; moles of O = 53.3 ÷ 16 = 3.33.

*Step 3 — simplest ratio:* the mole ratio is 3.33 : 6.7 : 3.33; dividing every term by the smallest gives 3.33 ÷ 3.33 = 1 and 6.7 ÷ 3.33 ≈ 2, so the whole-number ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.

That division delivers the ratio of atoms in the compound, and the ratio 1 : 2 : 1 is the empirical formula CH₂O.

parts.problemMd: Explain why molten sodium chloride conducts electricity.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because its ions are free to move.**

parts.problemMd: Explain why fermentation needs to occur in the absence of air.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: oxygen in the air would oxidise the ethanol product into ethanoic acid (CH₃COOH), so fermentation must happen anaerobically — sealed away from air.**

Keeping the vessel air-free protects the ethanol.

parts.problemMd: Show by calculation that the empirical formula of propanol is C3H8O.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: divide each percentage by its relative atomic mass, then divide every answer by the smallest — the ratio comes out as 3 : 8 : 1, which is C₃H₈O.**
*Step 1 — moles of atoms:* the division uses relative atomic masses (C 12, H 1, O 16), not atomic numbers, and the calculation is never run upside down (divide mass by Ar, never Ar by mass). So moles of C = 60.0 ÷ 12 = 5.0, moles of H = 13.3 ÷ 1 = 13.3, moles of O = 26.7 ÷ 16 = 1.67.
*Step 2 — simplest ratio:* divide each answer by the smallest value, 1.67: C 5.0 ÷ 1.67 = 2.99, H 13.3 ÷ 1.67 = 7.96, O 1.67 ÷ 1.67 = 1.
*Step 3 — conclusion:* 2.99 rounds to 3 and 7.96 rounds to 8, so the whole-number ratio is 3 : 8 : 1 and the empirical formula is C₃H₈O, exactly as the question states.

parts.problemMd: The student finds that 15.00 cm3 of sulfuric acid of concentration 0.180 mol / dm3 neutralises 25.0 cm3 of potassium hydroxide solution. This is the equation for the reaction. 2KOH + H2SO4 → K2SO4 + 2H2O Calculate the concentration of the potassium hydroxide solution. concentration = mol / dm3

**Answer: 0.216 mol / dm³.**
*Step 1 — moles of sulfuric acid:* 15.00 cm³ = 0.0150 dm³, so n(H₂SO₄) = 0.0150 × 0.180 = 0.0027 mol.
*Step 2 — moles of potassium hydroxide:* the equation 2KOH + H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O shows 2 mol of KOH reacting with every 1 mol of acid, so n(KOH) = 0.0027 × 2 = 0.0054 mol.

**Answer: a nickel catalyst has no effect on the yield of hydrogen at equilibrium.**

A catalyst speeds up the forward and the backward reaction equally, by lowering the activation energy for both directions. parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the yield of hydrogen decreases when the temperature is reduced to 600 °C.**

The forward reaction is endothermic (ΔH = +206 kJ/mol), so it takes heat in. parts.problemMd: Explain why metals are good conductors of electricity.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: metals are good conductors of electricity because they contain delocalised electrons that can move and flow throughout the whole structure.**

The outer-shell electrons of each metal atom detach into a shared mobile sea and become delocalised, free to drift around the lattice of fixed positive ions. When a potential difference is applied across the metal, these mobile electrons flow in one direction, carrying charge through the structure as an electric current. parts.problemMd: Two methods of obtaining a metal from a compound are electrolysis and extraction using carbon. Explain, without giving practical details, which method is most suitable for extracting iron from iron(III) oxide.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: extraction using carbon is the most suitable method for obtaining iron from iron(III) oxide.**

Iron is less reactive than carbon, so carbon can remove the oxygen from the iron(III) oxide, reducing the ore to iron inside a blast furnace. Electrolysis of the molten oxide would also work, but it needs huge amounts of electricity and is far more expensive; electrolysis earns its cost only for metals more reactive than carbon, such as aluminium. Because iron sits below carbon in the reactivity series, heating with carbon is the cheaper, sensible choice.

parts.problemMd: Explain why potassium is more reactive than lithium. Refer to atomic structure in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: potassium is more reactive because its outer-shell electron is further from the nucleus, less strongly attracted, and therefore more easily lost.**

A potassium atom has four shells of electrons (2,8,8,1) while a lithium atom has only two (2,1), so the potassium atom is the bigger atom, with a larger atomic radius and more shielding of the outer electron from the pull of the nucleus. Because that outer-shell electron sits further from the positive nucleus, it is less strongly attracted to it. The weaker the attraction, the more easily the electron is lost — and losing the outer electron is exactly what Group 1 metals do in their reactions — so potassium reacts more vigorously than lithium.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about elements, compounds and mixtures.

Give the name of a compound.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: water.**
Water, H₂O, is a compound because two different elements — hydrogen and oxygen — are chemically joined together in a fixed proportion. Nothing else in the box qualifies: calcium, fluorine, helium, neon and silicon each contain only one kind of atom (they are elements), and petrol is a mixture of many hydrocarbons rather than one bonded substance.

parts.problemMd: Give the name of a mixture.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: petrol.**
Petrol is a mixture: it is a blend of many different hydrocarbon compounds that are not chemically bonded to one another, and its exact composition varies from batch to batch. Every other substance in the box is pure — calcium, fluorine, helium, neon and silicon are elements, and water is a single compound.

parts.problemMd: Give the name of a diatomic molecule.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: fluorine (F₂).**
Diatomic means built from exactly two atoms, and fluorine exists as F₂ molecules. Helium and neon are monatomic noble gases with single atoms; calcium and silicon are giant structures holding huge numbers of atoms; water is a molecule of three atoms (H₂O), not two; and petrol is a mixture, not one molecule.

parts.problemMd: Give the name of a metal element.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: calcium (Ca).**
Calcium is a metal element: all its atoms are the same kind, and it shows typical metallic behaviour of a Group 2 metal — shiny when freshly cut, a good conductor of electricity and malleable. Fluorine, helium and neon are non-metal elements, silicon is a metalloid (a semiconductor), and petrol and water are not elements at all.

parts.problemMd: Name the technique used to separate crude oil into fractions.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: fractional distillation.**
Crude oil is heated so its hydrocarbons evaporate, then the vapours rise up a fractionating column and condense at different heights: each fraction collects the compounds whose boiling points fall in a similar narrow range. It is the column plus the spread of boiling points that lets one continuous process split crude oil into its useful fractions.

parts.problemMd: Explain why increasing the temperature of the hydrochloric acid affects the rate of the reaction. Refer to collision theory in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the rate increases because the particles collide more often and more of the collisions are successful.**
Heating the hydrochloric acid gives its particles (the H⁺ ions, and the magnesium atoms at the surface) more kinetic energy, so the molecules move faster.
Faster particles collide more often — there are more collisions per unit time (more frequent collisions).
Most importantly, a greater proportion of the colliding particles now have the necessary activation energy, Ea, so a bigger share of the collisions are successful collisions. The rate of reaction increases for both reasons together: more collisions in total, and more of them energetic enough to react.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: isotopes are atoms with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.**

parts.problemMd: Which of these compounds is an insoluble solid?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: B — calcium sulfate.**
Most sulfates dissolve in water, but the sulfate of calcium is one of the few insoluble exceptions (with barium and lead sulfates), so calcium sulfate is the compound that settles out as an insoluble solid. The other three choices are all soluble, which rules each of them out: calcium nitrate (A) dissolves because every nitrate is soluble; magnesium nitrate (C) is soluble by the same nitrate rule; and magnesium sulfate (D) is a soluble sulfate — magnesium is simply not one of the metals whose sulfate is insoluble.

parts.problemMd:
The table lists some substances and shows which substance conducts electricity. Substance Conducts electricity? water no solid magnesium chloride no aqueous magnesium chloride yes Explain these observations. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.

![table — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.10)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2025-06/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_3_d_table.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: water is a covalent molecular liquid with no charged particles free to move; solid magnesium chloride is an ionic solid with its ions locked in fixed positions; aqueous magnesium chloride conducts because its ions are free to move.**
Water is covalent — its molecules are held together by shared pairs of electrons. It contains no ions and no delocalised electrons, so there are not enough charged particles and none are free to move and carry a current: water cannot conduct electricity.
Magnesium chloride is an ionic compound: a giant lattice of alternating Mg²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions. In the solid the ions can only vibrate about their fixed positions in the lattice — they cannot move through it — so solid magnesium chloride does not conduct.
Dissolving the solid in water breaks the lattice apart: the ions separate and move freely through the solution, so aqueous magnesium chloride conducts well. It is the moving ions that carry the current in the solution, not electrons.

parts.problemMd: Give the half‑equation for the reaction at the positive electrode.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.**
At the positive electrode (the anode) chloride ions are discharged: two Cl⁻ ions each give up one electron, forming one molecule of chlorine, Cl₂, and releasing two electrons into the circuit. parts.problemMd: A sample of bromine atoms contains 42.0% bromine‑79 and 58.0% bromine‑81. Calculate the relative atomic mass of this sample of bromine atoms. Give your answer to three significant figures. relative atomic mass =
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 80.2.**

*Step 1:* Calculate the contribution of each isotope to the relative atomic mass by multiplying the percentage abundance by the mass number for each isotope:
Contribution of bromine-79 = 42.0 × 79 = 3318
Contribution of bromine-81 = 58.0 × 81 = 4698

*Step 2:* Add these contributions together:
Total mass contribution = 3318 + 4698 = 8016

*Step 3:* Divide by 100 to find the weighted average (relative atomic mass):
Relative atomic mass = 8016 ÷ 100 = 80.16

*Step 4:* Round to three significant figures as required:
Relative atomic mass = 80.2

parts.problemMd: Explain why the probability of a molecule having an Mr of 72 is not 0.1875
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 0.1875 is the probability for only one combination (35Cl37Cl), but there are two possible combinations that result in an Mr of 72: 35Cl37Cl and 37Cl35Cl. The correct probability is 0.1875 × 2 = 0.375.**

The probability of a molecule having an Mr of 72 is not 0.1875 because this value only accounts for one specific combination of isotopes. Since chlorine molecules are diatomic, there are two distinct ways to form a molecule with an Mr of 72: either the first chlorine atom is 35Cl and the second is 37Cl, or the first is 37Cl and the second is 35Cl. These are two separate molecular combinations, so their probabilities must be added together. The probability of each combination is 0.75 × 0.25 = 0.1875, so the total probability for an Mr of 72 is 0.1875 × 2 = 0.375.

parts.problemMd: Explain how displacement reactions involving halogens and halides provide evidence for the trend in reactivity in Group 7 of the Periodic Table. Include examples of reactions in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Reactivity decreases down Group 7 (from fluorine to iodine), with fluorine being the most reactive. Displacement reactions occur when a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide from a solution containing its ions. For example, chlorine displaces bromine from sodium bromide solution (Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂), showing a color change from colorless to brown. Conversely, bromine does not displace iodine from sodium iodide solution (Br₂ + 2NaI → no reaction), demonstrating that less reactive halogens cannot displace more reactive ones.**

The reactivity trend in Group 7 is demonstrated by displacement reactions, where a more reactive halogen can displace a less reactive halide from a solution containing its ions. This happens because the more reactive halogen has a greater tendency to gain an electron to form a halide ion. For instance, when chlorine gas is added to sodium bromide solution, chlorine displaces bromine, producing sodium chloride and bromine, with the solution turning from colorless to brown (Cl₂ + 2NaBr → 2NaCl + Br₂). This color change provides clear evidence that the reaction has occurred. Conversely, when bromine is added to sodium iodide solution, no displacement reaction takes place (Br₂ + 2NaI → no reaction) because bromine is less reactive than iodine and cannot displace it. This lack of reaction further confirms the reactivity trend down the group.

parts.problemMd: Steel is made from iron and carbon. Explain how the difference in malleability of pure iron and high-carbon steel affects the uses of these materials.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: pure iron is more malleable than high-carbon steel, so pure iron is used where a material must be bent or beaten into shape, while high-carbon steel is used where hardness matters.**

High-carbon steel is an alloy. Its carbon atoms are different-sized atoms sitting among the iron atoms, and this disrupts the regular arrangement of the structure, so the layers of atoms (metal ions) can no longer slide over each other easily. That makes high-carbon steel much harder but far less malleable. In pure iron every particle is the same size, so the neat rows of atoms stay in regular layers that can slide over one another — this is why pure iron is the more malleable of the two.

This comparison of malleability between pure iron and high-carbon steel decides their uses. Malleable pure iron can be hammered into shape or drawn out, so it is used for gates, railings, nails, wires, chains and car bodies. Very hard high-carbon steel keeps a sharp edge and withstands heavy loads without denting, so it is used for cutting tools, knives, blades, springs, hammers and rail tracks.

Keep the whole explanation in terms of atoms and sliding layers: bringing ionic bonds, covalent bonds or intermolecular forces into a metallic structure would break the model the explanation needs.

parts.problemMd:
The table gives some bond energies. Bond C H Cl Cl H Cl Bond energy in kJ / mol 414 242 431 Using information from the equation and the table, calculate the bond energy of the C Cl bond. C Cl bond energy = kJ / mol

![table — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.19)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2025-11/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_6_b_table.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 338 kJ / mol.**

*Step 1:* Calculate the total bond energy on the left-hand side (reactants) of the equation:
- 3 × C-H bonds: 3 × 414 = 1242 kJ/mol
- 1 × C-Cl bond: 1 × C-Cl bond energy (this is what we need to find)
- 3 × Cl-Cl bonds: 3 × 242 = 726 kJ/mol
Total LHS bond energy = 1242 + C-Cl + 726 = 1968 + C-Cl kJ/mol

*Step 2:* Calculate the total bond energy on the right-hand side (products) of the equation:
- 4 × C-Cl bonds: 4 × C-Cl bond energy
- 3 × H-Cl bonds: 3 × 431 = 1293 kJ/mol
Total RHS bond energy = 4 × C-Cl + 1293 kJ/mol

*Step 3:* Use the enthalpy change (ΔH) to set up an equation. The enthalpy change equals the energy of bonds broken minus the energy of bonds formed:
(LHS bond energy) - (RHS bond energy) = ΔH
(1968 + C-Cl) - (4 × C-Cl + 1293) = -339 kJ/mol

*Step 4:* Solve the equation for the C-Cl bond energy:
1968 + C-Cl - 4 × C-Cl - 1293 = -339
675 - 3 × C-Cl = -339
3 × C-Cl = 675 + 339
3 × C-Cl = 1014

*Step 5:* Calculate the final value for the C-Cl bond energy:
C-Cl bond energy = 1014 ÷ 3 = 338 kJ/mol

(3 x 242) OR (1 x C-Cl) + 1968 (kJ/mol)

∑ bond energies on RHS = (4 x C−Cl) + (3 x 431)
OR (4 x C−Cl) + 1293 (kJ/mol)
(1 x C-Cl + 1968) − (4 x C−Cl + 1293) = −339 ALLOW ECF calculation

parts.problemMd:
This question is about polymerisation.

The box gives some names used in polymerisation. addition alkane alkene condensation dicarboxylic acid poly(chloroethene) water Complete the table by choosing the correct name from the box that matches each description. Description Name a monomer used to make an addition polymer a monomer used to make a condensation polymer a type of polymer that biodegrades a product of condensation polymerisation

![table — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.4)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2026-06/4CH1-2C/assets/asset_1_a_table.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: alkene — a monomer used to make an addition polymer; dicarboxylic acid — a monomer used to make a condensation polymer; condensation — the type of polymer that biodegrades; water — the product of condensation polymerisation.**

Alkenes carry a C=C double bond, so many alkene molecules can open their double bonds and add together end-to-end into long addition-polymer chains. Condensation polymerisation instead joins two different monomers, and a dicarboxylic acid (a molecule with two -COOH groups) is one of the monomers used, usually linked with a diol. Condensation polymers such as polyesters can be broken down by micro-organisms, so this type of polymer biodegrades, unlike addition polymers. Every time two monomers join in condensation polymerisation a small molecule is lost, and that product is water.

The two names left over do not fit anywhere: an alkane has no double bond, so it cannot open up as an addition monomer, and poly(chloroethene) is itself a polymer — not a monomer and not a small-molecule product.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: a catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.**

Rather than forcing particles over the original high energy barrier, the catalyst offers a different route whose activation energy is lower. **Answer: raising the temperature lowers the equilibrium yield of ethyl ethanoate, but makes equilibrium arrive faster.**

*Effect on yield:* the forwards reaction (ester formation) is exothermic, so the backwards reaction is endothermic. When the temperature is increased, the system opposes that change by favouring the direction that takes heat in — the endothermic, backwards direction — so the equilibrium position shifts to the left, towards the reactants, and the yield of ethyl ethanoate at equilibrium decreases.

*Effect on rate:* at the higher temperature every particle has more kinetic energy and moves faster, so collisions become more frequent, and a bigger fraction of them involve energy equal to or greater than the activation energy — more frequent successful collisions. The rate therefore increases, and equilibrium is reached sooner even though there is less ester waiting at the end.

parts.problemMd: A 200 cm3 saturated solution of potassium sulfate is cooled from 55.6 °C to 27.4 °C. Determine the mass, in g, of solid potassium sulfate that would crystallise. mass = g
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: 10.0 g of solid potassium sulfate crystallises out.**

*Step 1 — what is dissolved at 55.6 °C:* the table gives 17.5 g per 100 cm3 of water, so a 200 cm3 saturated solution holds 17.5 × 2 = 35.0 g.

*Step 2 — what can stay dissolved at 27.4 °C:* the table gives 12.5 g per 100 cm3 of water, so in 200 cm3 only 12.5 × 2 = 25.0 g can remain in solution.

*Step 3 — mass forced out of solution:* 35.0 − 25.0 = 10.0 g.

When the saturated solution cools, the solubility falls, so the extra solid has no room to stay dissolved and forms the crystals.

parts.problemMd: A student has a beaker containing dilute nitric acid. Describe a method that she could use to prepare a pure, dry sample of magnesium nitrate crystals from magnesium oxide.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Warm the dilute nitric acid, add magnesium oxide until some is left in excess, filter, then boil down the solution, cool it to crystallise, filter again and dry the crystals.**

*Step 1 —* warm the acid gently in a beaker; warm it, do not let it boil at this stage.

*Step 2 —* add the magnesium oxide to the warm acid a little at a time, stirring as you add, until no more will react or dissolve and some solid is left at the bottom. The oxide is now in excess, which guarantees every trace of acid has been used up.

*Step 3 —* filter to remove the excess magnesium oxide; the filtrate is a clear solution of magnesium nitrate.

*Step 4 —* heat the solution so that some of the water boils away, until the liquid reaches the point where crystals form — test it by dipping a glass rod in and seeing whether small crystals form on the rod.

*Step 5 —* leave the concentrated solution to cool slowly, and magnesium nitrate crystals crystallise out as it cools.

*Step 6 —* filter the cold mixture to separate the crystals from the remaining liquid.

*Step 7 —* dry the crystals by pressing them between sheets of filter paper or leaving them somewhere warm; never use a hot oven or a direct flame, and do not wash them once they are dry, or the sample will no longer be dry.

parts.problemMd: Diamond is a naturally‑occurring form of carbon. It has a giant molecular structure. Explain, with reference to its structure and bonding, why diamond has a high melting point.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Diamond has a high melting point because it has a giant molecular structure with strong covalent bonds between carbon atoms. Many of these strong bonds need to be broken when diamond melts, requiring a large amount of thermal energy.

In diamond, each carbon atom is bonded to four other carbon atoms through strong covalent bonds. These bonds are formed by the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of atoms and the bonding electrons. Since diamond has a giant 3D structure, there are a vast number of these strong covalent bonds throughout the entire structure. When heating diamond, a large amount of thermal energy is needed to break all these strong bonds and overcome the forces holding the structure together, which is why diamond has a high melting point.

parts.problemMd: Graphite is another naturally‑occurring form of carbon. Graphite can be used in pencils because it is soft and can leave marks on paper. Graphite can also be used as a conductor of electricity. Explain why graphite is soft and conducts electricity. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Graphite is soft because its structure consists of layers held together by weak forces, allowing the layers to slide over each other easily. Graphite conducts electricity because it has delocalized electrons that can move freely through its structure.

Graphite has a layered structure where each carbon atom is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms in a plane, forming hexagonal rings. Between these layers, there are only weak forces of attraction (such as van der Waals forces), allowing the layers to slide over each other easily, which makes graphite soft and useful in pencils. For electrical conductivity, each carbon atom in graphite has four valence electrons, but only three are involved in covalent bonding within the layers. The fourth electron is delocalized and can move freely throughout the entire structure. These delocalized electrons can flow when a voltage is applied, allowing graphite to conduct electricity.

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of structure and bonding, why silicon dioxide has a much higher melting point than silicon(IV) chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** Silicon dioxide has a much higher melting point than silicon(IV) chloride because silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds that need to be broken, requiring a large amount of energy. In contrast, silicon(IV) chloride has a simple molecular structure with weak intermolecular forces between its molecules, requiring little energy to overcome. Therefore, more energy is needed to break the bonds in silicon dioxide than to overcome the forces in silicon(IV) chloride.

Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure where each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms in a three-dimensional network. These covalent bonds are very strong and must be broken for the solid to melt, which requires a large amount of energy. This is why silicon dioxide has a high melting point of 1710°C.

Silicon(IV) chloride has a simple molecular structure consisting of discrete SiCl₄ molecules. The forces between these molecules are weak intermolecular forces (van der Waals forces). Only these weak forces need to be overcome for the substance to melt, not the strong covalent bonds within the molecules. This requires much less energy, resulting in a low melting point of -69°C.

parts.problemMd: Explain why lithium chloride has a higher melting point than hydrogen chloride. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Lithium chloride has a higher melting point than hydrogen chloride because it has a giant ionic structure with strong electrostatic forces between oppositely charged ions, while hydrogen chloride has a simple molecular structure with weak intermolecular forces.

Lithium chloride forms a giant ionic lattice where lithium ions (Li⁺) and chloride ions (Cl⁻) are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction. These forces extend throughout the entire structure and require a large amount of energy to overcome, resulting in a high melting point.

In contrast, hydrogen chloride exists as simple molecules held together by weak intermolecular forces. These forces are much easier to overcome than the strong electrostatic forces in ionic compounds, requiring less energy to break. Therefore, hydrogen chloride has a much lower melting point than lithium chloride.

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of particle collision theory, how increasing the temperature affects the rate of a reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer:** At higher temperature, particles have more kinetic energy, so more particles have the required activation energy. This results in more successful collisions per unit time, which increases the rate of reaction.

According to particle collision theory, when the temperature increases, the particles in the reactants move faster. This means they have more kinetic energy. As a result, a greater proportion of these particles will have the minimum energy required to overcome the activation energy barrier for the reaction to occur. Additionally, with particles moving faster, they collide with each other more frequently. The combination of more frequent collisions and a higher proportion of collisions that have sufficient energy leads to more successful collisions per unit time. Since the rate of reaction depends on the frequency of successful collisions, increasing the temperature increases the rate of reaction.

parts.problemMd: Silicon hydride has a simple molecular structure. Silicon dioxide has the same type of structure as diamond. Explain why silicon dioxide has a much higher melting point than silicon hydride. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Silicon dioxide has a giant covalent structure with many strong covalent bonds that need to be broken when melting, while silicon hydride has a simple molecular structure with weak intermolecular forces that require less energy to overcome.

Silicon dioxide (SiO2) has a giant covalent structure similar to diamond, where each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms and each oxygen atom is bonded to two silicon atoms, creating a three-dimensional network of strong covalent bonds throughout the entire structure. To melt silicon dioxide, these many strong covalent bonds must be broken, which requires a large amount of thermal energy.

In contrast, silicon hydride (SiH4) has a simple molecular structure consisting of discrete SiH4 molecules. These molecules are held together in the solid by weak intermolecular forces (London forces). When melting silicon hydride, only these weak intermolecular forces need to be overcome, not the strong covalent bonds within the molecules. Since much less energy is required to overcome weak intermolecular forces than to break strong covalent bonds, silicon dioxide has a much higher melting point than silicon hydride.

That is why carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature, with a melting point far below that of silicon dioxide.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about crude oil.

Describe how crude oil is separated into fractions by fractional distillation.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: crude oil is heated and vaporised; the vapour enters the bottom of the fractionating column, which is hotter at the bottom and cooler at the top; the vapours rise, cool and condense at different heights; each fraction is collected where the column temperature falls below its boiling point.**

First, the crude oil is heated (boiled) so that most of its hydrocarbons turn to vapour, and this vapour enters the lower part — the bottom — of the fractionating column. The column has a temperature gradient: it is hottest at the bottom and cooler towards the top. As the vapours rise up the column they cool, and each hydrocarbon condenses to a liquid at the height where the temperature in the column has fallen below its own boiling point. The condensed fractions are then separated according to their boiling points: short-chain fractions with low boiling points condense near the cool top, while long-chain fractions with high boiling points condense near the hot bottom.

parts.problemMd: Some of the products of fractional distillation are then cracked. This equation represents a reaction that occurs during cracking. C15H32 → C8H18 + C3H6 + 2C2H4 Explain why cracking is an important process in the oil industry.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: cracking turns surplus long-chain hydrocarbons into shorter, more useful alkanes and into alkenes for making polymers.**

Fractional distillation of crude oil produces more long-chain hydrocarbons than can be used directly — demand for these thick, less flammable fractions is lower than the supply. Cracking splits them, as in C₁₅H₃₂ → C₈H₁₈ + C₃H₆ + 2C₂H₄, producing shorter-chain alkanes such as those in petrol, which are more flammable and much more useful as fuels. Cracking also produces alkenes (such as C₃H₆ and C₂H₄), which are used to make polymers (plastics). So cracking matches the supply of fractions to the demand, delivering both better fuels and valuable starting materials.

parts.problemMd: Explain why magnesium chloride has a much higher melting point than hydrogen chloride. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: magnesium chloride is a giant ionic lattice held together by strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, while hydrogen chloride is simple molecular with only weak intermolecular forces between its molecules — so far more energy is required to separate the particles in MgCl₂ than in HCl.**

Hydrogen chloride exists as simple molecules (simple molecular, with covalent bonding within each H–Cl molecule). Between one HCl molecule and the next there are only weak intermolecular forces, and it is these weak forces that are overcome when HCl melts — the strong covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken at all.

Magnesium chloride, in contrast, is a giant ionic lattice (an ionic structure) made of Mg2+ and Cl− ions. Throughout the lattice there is strong electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ions, acting in every direction. Much more energy is therefore required to break the many strong ionic bonds in MgCl₂ than to overcome the weak intermolecular forces in HCl, which is why magnesium chloride has a much higher melting point than hydrogen chloride.

parts.problemMd: Explain why diamond is hard but graphite is soft.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond is hard because every carbon atom is bonded to four others in a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice, so the strong covalent bonds need a lot of energy to break; graphite is soft because it is built of layers that can slide over one another.**
In diamond each carbon atom is joined to four other carbon atoms in a giant tetrahedral network with no weak direction. To cut or scratch diamond you would have to break strong covalent bonds, and those bonds need a lot of energy to break — that is why diamond is so hard. There are no separate molecules in diamond at all, so speaking of weak intermolecular forces between molecules in diamond would be wrong chemistry.
Graphite is the opposite: within each layer the covalent bonds are strong, but the layers are held to each other only weakly. Because the bonding between layers is so feeble, the layers can slide over one another easily, so graphite flakes and feels soft — which is why it works as a lubricant and as the 'lead' in pencils.

markPoints.textMd: A

parts.problemMd: Give the letter of the species that is an ion with a 3− charge.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: D.** Species D has 7 protons but 10 electrons — three more electrons than protons — so it carries a 3− charge. It is the nitride ion, N³⁻: a nitrogen atom that has gained three electrons to complete its outer shell.

markPoints.textMd: D

parts.problemMd: Give the letter of the species with a mass number of 19
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: C.** Mass number = protons + neutrons. Species C has 9 protons and 10 neutrons, so its mass number is 9 + 10 = 19. The extra electron (10 electrons against 9 protons) makes it a negative ion, but mass number only counts the particles in the nucleus.

markPoints.textMd: C

parts.problemMd: A sample of lithium contains two isotopes, 6Li and 7Li. In terms of sub‑atomic particles, give one similarity and one difference between these isotopes. similarity difference
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Similarity — they have the same number of protons (3 protons each) and the same number of electrons, so their electron configurations are identical. Difference — they have different numbers of neutrons: ⁶Li has 3 neutrons while ⁷Li has 4 neutrons, so their mass numbers differ.**
Isotopes of an element always share the proton count (that is what makes both of them lithium) and therefore the same electron arrangement; the extra neutron in ⁷Li is what gives it the bigger mass number.

parts.problemMd: The displacement reaction between potassium astatide and bromine can be represented by this ionic equation. 2At− + Br2 → At2 + 2Br− Explain why this is described as a redox reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because both oxidation and reduction happen at once — it is a redox reaction.**
In 2At⁻ + Br₂ → At₂ + 2Br⁻ the astatide ions (At⁻) lose electrons: each At⁻ becomes an astatine atom in At₂, so the astatide is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. At the same time the bromine molecules (Br₂) gain those electrons: each Br atom becomes Br⁻, so the bromine is reduced and acts as the oxidising agent. One species oxidised and the other reduced, with electrons transferred — that is exactly what makes the equation redox.

parts.problemMd: Describe what the student should do to the mixture formed in (c) to produce pure, dry crystals of hydrated magnesium chloride.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: filter, heat to crystallisation, cool, filter again, then dry the crystals gently.**
*Filter* the mixture from (c) to remove the excess magnesium — the residue on the filter paper is the unreacted metal, and the filtrate is magnesium chloride solution.
*Heat* the filtrate gently to evaporate some of the water, watching until crystals first start to form (that is, until a saturated solution is reached). Do not heat to dryness, or the hydrated crystals would lose their water of crystallisation.
*Cool* the concentrated solution slowly so the hydrated magnesium chloride crystallises out.
*Filter* again — or pour off / decant the excess liquid — to separate the crystals from the remaining solution.
*Dry* the crystals by leaving them in a warm place (a warm oven or a desiccator also works, or pat them dry with a paper towel).

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the covalent compounds hydrogen chloride and silicon dioxide.

Describe the forces of attraction in a covalent bond.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: a strong electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of the two atoms and the shared pair of electrons.**
In a covalent bond the outer shells overlap and a pair of electrons is shared. The attraction acts inside the molecule; it is not the intermolecular attraction between separate molecules.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the boiling point of hydrogen chloride is low.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: silicon dioxide is acidic and calcium oxide is basic — the two react as an acid with a base.**

parts.problemMd: Silicon dioxide has the same structure as diamond. Silicon dioxide is very hard and has a very high melting point. Explain these properties. Refer to the structure and bonding of silicon dioxide in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure — a rigid 3D tetrahedral lattice like diamond — and that structure, with its strong covalent bonds, explains both properties.**
Every silicon atom is bonded covalently to four oxygen atoms (and each oxygen to two silicons), so the bonding network extends in all directions through the whole crystal: one giant molecule rather than separate small ones.
The covalent bonds holding the atoms together are very strong. To melt silicon dioxide you must break those strong covalent bonds throughout the giant lattice, and breaking them requires a lot of energy — hence the very high melting point.
It is also very hard because the atoms cannot slide over each other: there are no layers of atoms (as there are in graphite), and any attempted slide would mean breaking strong covalent bonds, so the structure resists scratching and denting.

parts.problemMd: Explain why cracking is a useful process in the oil industry.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because cracking converts low-demand long-chain alkanes into short-chain products the industry needs.**

parts.solutionMd: **Answer: B.** Bromine water is decolourised when bromine adds across a carbon-to-carbon double bond, so the compound that does this must be an alkene. parts.problemMd: Give the letter of the saturated compound with the empirical formula CH2
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: E.** Saturated means the molecule has only single bonds between its carbon atoms. In E every carbon is joined by single bonds, and there are exactly two hydrogen atoms for every carbon atom, so the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms is one carbon to two hydrogens — the empirical formula CH₂. An open-chain alkane has the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (more than twice as many hydrogens as carbons), so a saturated compound whose empirical formula is CH₂ must have its carbons in a ring — E is the cycloalkane in the table.

Compounds with the same molecular formula but different arrangements of atoms, like butane and A, are isomers.

parts.problemMd: Explain why cracking is a useful process. Refer to the products of the reaction in your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: cracking converts a long-chain alkane into shorter, more flammable alkanes that are in greater demand as fuels, and into alkenes used to make polymers.**

In C₁₂H₂₆ → C₈H₁₈ + 2C₂H₄ the long hydrocarbon molecule is split into a shorter alkane, C₈H₁₈. Shorter hydrocarbons are more flammable than long-chain ones — they vaporise and ignite more easily — so they are more useful as fuels, and there is a greater demand for short-chain alkanes because they are needed for specific uses such as petrol. The reaction also produces alkenes, such as C₂H₄ (ethene), which are used to make polymers and plastics; alkenes can also be used to make ethanol. Cracking therefore turns surplus, less useful long chains into exactly the products that are needed.

parts.problemMd: A student is given 50 cm3 of dilute sulfuric acid and some zinc carbonate powder. Describe a method the student should use to prepare dry crystals of hydrated zinc sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: add excess zinc carbonate to the acid, filter, then heat, cool and crystallise, filter again and dry the crystals.**

*Step 1 — react:* add the zinc carbonate powder to the 50 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid a little at a time with stirring, until no more zinc carbonate reacts — the effervescence (fizzing) stops and a little excess powder just sits there without dissolving. Using excess powder guarantees all of the acid is used up.

*Step 2 — filter:* filter the mixture to remove the excess zinc carbonate, leaving a clear solution of zinc sulfate.

*Step 3 — concentrate:* heat the solution gently so that some of the water evaporates and the solution becomes saturated. Stop while it is still only partly evaporated — never heat it to dryness, because the crystals would spit and the water of crystallisation would be driven off.

*Step 4 — crystallise:* leave the warm solution somewhere to cool slowly. As it cools, hydrated zinc sulfate crystals grow.

*Step 5 — separate and dry:* filter off the crystals, then dry them by patting with filter paper or a paper towel, or by leaving them in a warm place (a warm oven is fine — a hot oven or a direct Bunsen flame is not, as it would cook the crystals). That leaves dry crystals of hydrated zinc sulfate.

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: graphite has weak forces between its layers, so the layers can slide over one another.**

Within a layer each carbon atom is held to its neighbours by strong covalent bonds, but the forces holding one whole layer to the next are weak. When a force is applied — a pencil pressed onto paper, for example — the layers slip over each other and stay behind as graphite smears. parts.problemMd: Explain why diamond has a much higher boiling point than C60 fullerene. Refer to structure and bonding in your answer. QUESTION 11 CONTINUES ON BACK PAGE
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: diamond is a giant covalent lattice held together by strong covalent bonds running in every direction, while C₆₀ fullerene is a simple molecular substance whose molecules are held to each other only by weak intermolecular forces — so boiling diamond needs far more energy.**

*Diamond:* every carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others, producing a giant lattice that continues throughout the whole crystal. To boil diamond you have to break strong covalent bonds everywhere in that structure, which takes a very large amount of energy, so diamond's boiling point is extremely high.

*C₆₀ fullerene:* the bonds inside each C₆₀ molecule are covalent and strong, but the substance is simple molecular — the C₆₀ molecules are only attracted to their neighbours by weak intermolecular forces. Boiling does not break the covalent bonds inside the molecules; it only has to overcome the weak forces between the molecules to separate them, and that needs very little energy.

*The comparison:* breaking covalent bonds throughout the giant diamond lattice demands much more thermal energy than overcoming the weak intermolecular forces between C₆₀ fullerene molecules, which is why diamond has a much higher boiling point.

parts.problemMd: How are the elements arranged in the Periodic Table?
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: C — increasing number of protons (atomic number).** The elements in the Periodic Table are arranged in order of increasing proton number, starting with hydrogen and building up one proton at a time. A is wrong because the table is not ordered by mass number — if it were, a few neighbouring pairs (argon and potassium, for example) would swap places. B is wrong because the number of neutrons is not the ordering principle: it rises unevenly and can stay the same between neighbouring elements. D is wrong because reactivity climbs and falls across the table and orders nothing.

parts.problemMd: Elements in the same group have the same number of
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: A — electrons in the outer shell.** Elements in the same group of the Periodic Table have the same number of electrons in their outermost shell, and it is this that gives group members their similar chemical properties. B is wrong because the number of shells is fixed by the period, not the group — going down a group adds one shell each time. C is wrong because neutron numbers can differ even between atoms of the same element (isotopes), so they are certainly not fixed across a group. D is wrong because every element in the group has its own proton number — the atomic number increases step by step down the group.

**Answer:** Crude oil is separated into fractions using fractional distillation.**

parts.problemMd: The reaction occurs because chlorine is more reactive than bromine. Bromine is below chlorine in Group 7. Explain the decrease in reactivity from chlorine to bromine.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: The reactivity decreases from chlorine to bromine because bromine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms.**

*Step 1:* Both bromine and chlorine react by gaining an electron to form a negative ion (halide ion).

*Step 2:* Bromine atoms are larger than chlorine atoms because they have more electron shells.

*Step 3:* The larger atomic size of bromine means its outer electrons are further from the nucleus and experience a weaker attraction to it compared to chlorine.

*Step 4:* Because the attraction for electrons is weaker, bromine has less tendency to gain an electron and form a negative ion, making it less reactive than chlorine.

parts.problemMd: Elements in Group 7 react with elements in Group 1 to form ionic compounds. Which pair of ions both have the electronic configuration 2.8.8?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — K⁺ and Cl⁻.**

Both ions in the pair need three full shells of electrons — the 2.8.8 arrangement. Potassium (Group 1) holds one electron in its fourth shell; when the atom loses that electron the ion left behind has exactly 2.8.8. Chlorine (Group 7) has seven electrons in its third shell; gaining one more fills that shell, so Cl⁻ is 2.8.8 as well. Now the wrong pairs: in A, Li⁺ spoils it, because a lithium ion has only two shells of electrons (2.8) and can never reach 2.8.8, even though its Cl⁻ fits. In B, K⁺ is fine but F⁻ is not: a fluoride ion fills only its second shell (2.8). In C, Li⁺ and F⁻ both fail for those same two reasons. Only K⁺ and Cl⁻ share the 2.8.8 configuration.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram represents the structure of copper metal. + + + + + metal delocalised + + + + cations electrons + + + + + Explain three properties of copper that make it a suitable metal to use in electrical wiring.

![diagram — official paper figure (qp.pdf p.9)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/Official-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2022-06/4CH1-2CR/assets/asset_4_a_diagram.png)
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: copper conducts electricity, is malleable and ductile, and has a high melting point — three properties that make it ideal for wiring, each explained by its giant metallic structure of cations and delocalised electrons.**
Conducts electricity: each copper atom releases its outer electrons, which become delocalised — a mobile sea of electrons between the fixed positive cations. Because these delocalised electrons are free to move through the structure, they carry charge along the wire.
Malleable and ductile: the cations sit in neat layers, and those layers can slide over each other when a force is applied. The bonding does not snap, so copper can be hammered into shape (malleable) and drawn out into thin wire (ductile) — exactly what wiring needs.
High melting point: the electrostatic attraction between the positive cations and the negative delocalised electrons is strong, so a lot of energy is needed to separate the particles and the metal stays solid while the wire is in use.
In each explanation the reason is linked to the correct property: moving electrons explain conduction, sliding layers explain ductility, and strong attraction explains the high melting point.

parts.problemMd: How are elements arranged in the Periodic Table?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — in order of increasing atomic number.**

Moving left to right across the Periodic Table, each element has one more proton in its nucleus than the one before, so the table is arranged by increasing atomic number. Option B is wrong: melting points rise and fall in complicated patterns across a period, so the elements are not arranged by increasing melting point. Option C is wrong: reactivity climbs to a peak in the middle of a period and then falls away, so it cannot be the organising order. Option D is wrong: relative atomic masses happen to increase broadly across the table, but the strict order is atomic number — sorting by relative atomic mass would place a few pairs of elements in the wrong slots.

markPoints.textMd: Answer A: increasing atomic number

parts.problemMd: Which statement is correct about the position of phosphorus, P, in the Periodic Table?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: D — phosphorus is in Group 5 and Period 3.**

Count the electrons in phosphorus's outer shell (5 of them) to get the group, and count its occupied shells (3) to get the period. Option A is wrong: Group 2 and Period 5 would put phosphorus among the alkaline-earth metals far down the table. Option B is wrong: Group 3 with Period 5 mixes the two coordinates. Option C is wrong: Group 5 and Period 2 swaps the true position, because Period 2 belongs to nitrogen and its horizontal neighbours, not to phosphorus.

markPoints.textMd: Answer D: Group 5 and Period 3

**Answer: xenon (Xe) is the least reactive of the four elements shown.**

parts.solutionMd:

parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: the mixture turns from colourless to brown, because iodine is displaced.**

parts.problemMd: Explain why an alloy is less malleable than a pure metal.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: in an alloy the different-sized atoms distort the regular layers, so the layers can no longer slide over one another easily — the alloy is less malleable.**

In a pure metal every atom is the same size and the atoms sit in neat, regular rows. When a force is applied, whole layers of atoms can slide past one another, so the metal bends without shattering — that is malleability. In steel the carbon atoms are much smaller than the iron atoms, so they wedge into the gaps and the regular arrangement of the atoms becomes irregular and distorted. That misfit makes it more difficult for the layers to slide, so the alloy holds its shape instead of denting.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about the insoluble salt, lead(II) bromide. Lead(II) bromide can be made by a precipitation reaction. This is the equation for the reaction. Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)

Describe how solutions of lead nitrate and potassium bromide can be used to make a pure, dry sample of lead(II) bromide.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: mix the two solutions, filter off the precipitate, wash it, then dry it.**

*Step 1 — mix:* add the lead nitrate solution to the potassium bromide solution and stir; they react and insoluble lead(II) bromide forms as a precipitate: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq).

*Step 2 — filter:* pour the mixture through filter paper. The solid lead bromide is caught on the paper and the soluble potassium nitrate stays in the solution that runs through.

*Step 3 — wash:* rinse the solid on the paper with a little deionised water to wash away any potassium nitrate solution clinging to the crystals.

*Step 4 — dry:* leave the washed solid to dry in a warm place (a low oven works, or dab it dry with filter paper). That leaves a pure, dry sample of lead(II) bromide.

Do not try to evaporate the mixture instead — evaporating to dryness would trap soluble potassium nitrate among the crystals, so the sample would not be pure.

parts.problemMd: A solution containing 0.150 mol of lead(II) nitrate is reacted with an excess of potassium bromide solution. A mass of 49.6 g of pure, dry lead(II) bromide is produced. Show, by calculation, that the percentage yield of lead(II) bromide is 90.1%. [for PbBr2 , Mr = 367]

**Answer: 90.1%.**

*Step 1 — maximum moles of lead(II) bromide:* the equation Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → PbBr₂(s) + 2KNO₃(aq) links lead(II) nitrate to lead(II) bromide in a 1 : 1 ratio, so 0.150 mol of lead nitrate could make at most 0.150 mol of PbBr₂.

*Step 2 — theoretical mass:* mass = moles × Mr: 0.150 × 367 = 55.05 g.

*Step 3 — percentage yield:* actual mass ÷ theoretical mass, expressed as a percentage:

49.6 ÷ 55.05 × 100 = 90.1%

The student harvested 49.6 g of lead(II) bromide, which is 90.1% of the 55.05 g the equation predicts — the rest was lost on the filter paper and in the filtrate.

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd: Show that the molar enthalpy change, ΔH, for the reaction is −119 kJ / mol.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: ΔH = −119 kJ/mol, and the bond energies show exactly where that number comes from.**

*Step 1 — bonds broken in the reactants:* 2 mol of H–H bonds plus 1 mol of C≡O bond: 436 + 436 + 1072 = 1944 kJ/mol absorbed.

*Step 2 — bonds made in the product:* methanol, CH₃OH, contains 3 C–H bonds, 1 C–O bond and 1 O–H bond: 414 + 414 + 414 + 358 + 463 = 2063 kJ/mol released.

*Step 3 — the difference:* 2063 − 1944 = 119 kJ/mol more energy is released making bonds than is absorbed breaking them, so the overall change is ΔH = −119 kJ/mol.

markPoints.textMd: (bonds broken) = 436 + 436 + 1072 OR 1944

parts.problemMd: Explain why this reaction is exothermic.
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: because more energy is given out when the new bonds are made than is taken in when the original bonds are broken.**

Breaking bonds always takes in energy (it is endothermic): here the 2 H–H bonds and the C≡O bond absorb 1944 kJ/mol. Making bonds always releases energy (it is exothermic): the 3 C–H, 1 C–O and 1 O–H bonds of methanol release 2063 kJ/mol. Since 2063 is the larger figure, the energy released making bonds beats the energy absorbed breaking them, so there is a net transfer of energy to the surroundings — the reaction is exothermic and ΔH comes out negative.

**Answer: circle the ester functional group, the –C(=O)–O– linkage.**

parts.problemMd:
This question is about sulfur.

Which period of the Periodic Table contains sulfur?
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: B — 3.** The period number of an element equals the number of occupied electron shells in its atoms. A sulfur atom has its electrons arranged in three shells, so sulfur sits in period 3. Option A (2) is wrong because sulfur is not in period 2; option C (4) is wrong because sulfur is not in period 4; option D (6) is wrong because sulfur is not in period 6 — six is the number of electrons in sulfur's outer shell, not the period number.

parts.solutionMd: **Answer: D — 2−.** A sulfur atom is in Group 6 and has six electrons in its outer shell, so it gains two electrons to complete that shell; gaining two negative electrons leaves the sulfide ion with a charge of 2−. Option A (1+) is wrong because the sulfide ion is negative, not positive; option B (2+) is also a positive charge and so cannot describe a sulfide ion; option C (1−) has the right sign but the wrong size — sulfur gains two electrons, not one.

parts.problemMd: The student repeats the titration without the indicator and forms a solution of sodium sulfate. Describe how the student can obtain pure, dry crystals of hydrated sodium sulfate from the solution.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: evaporate gently, crystallise, separate, then dry — never heat to complete dryness.** Warm the sodium sulfate solution so that water evaporates until crystals first start to form and the solution is saturated (roughly when the volume is about half the original volume), then stop heating at the crystallisation point. Leave the hot, concentrated solution to cool slowly so that more crystals crystallise out as the temperature falls. Pour off the excess liquid that the crystals sit in (or filter the crystals off), because that liquid carries the soluble impurities away. Finally leave the crystals in a warm place to dry — a warm oven, a desiccator, or pressing them between sheets of filter paper all work. parts.problemMd: Use the bond energies to show that the molar enthalpy change, ΔH , is about −1300 kJ / mol.

**Answer: ΔH = −1263 kJ/mol, i.e. about −1300 kJ/mol.**
*Step 1 — bonds broken (energy taken in):* C₂H₅OH holds 5 C–H, 1 C–C, 1 C–O and 1 O–H, and the 3O₂ adds 3 O=O, so from the table 346 + 5 × 414 + 358 + 463 + 3 × 498 = 4731 kJ/mol.

parts.problemMd:
This question is about aluminium.

Why does solid aluminium conduct electricity?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — electrons are free to move in the solid.**

Solid aluminium is a metal: its outer electrons are delocalised, meaning they are not attached to any one aluminium atom, so they drift through the whole lattice and carry charge from place to place. That moving charge is the electric current.

Why the other options fail: B adds neutrons to the claim, but neutrons sit inside the nucleus and are never free to move, so they cannot carry charge. C adds protons, but protons are also locked inside the nucleus and cannot flow through the solid. D claims the ions move, but in solid aluminium the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice — only the electrons flow (ions only become mobile in a molten metal or in solution).

parts.problemMd: Explain why aluminium is malleable.
parts.solutionMd: **Answer: aluminium is malleable because its layers of atoms can slide over one another.** In the metallic lattice the aluminium atoms (positive ions surrounded by delocalised electrons) are arranged in neat layers. When a force is applied, those layers can slide over one another and settle into new positions without the metallic bonding breaking, so the metal bends and reshapes instead of shattering. It is the layers that slide — not the electrons, and not any negative ions, since there are none in a metal lattice.

parts.problemMd: Why is aluminium not extracted by heating aluminium oxide with carbon?
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: A — aluminium is more reactive than carbon.**

Carbon removes oxygen from the oxides of metals that are less reactive than itself. Aluminium sits above carbon in the reactivity series, so carbon cannot pull the oxygen away from aluminium oxide — heating the two together simply gives no reaction, and electrolysis is needed instead.

Why the other options fail: B says carbon is an oxidising agent, but in these reactions carbon gains oxygen, so it is acting as the reducing agent, not an oxidising agent. C says the reaction has a low activation energy, but the opposite is true — the barrier is a very high activation energy, which ordinary heating cannot supply. D says the reaction is explosive, but nothing that dramatic happens: carbon and aluminium oxide simply do not react with each other.

**Answer: 0.00567 mol/dm³ (to three significant figures).**

parts.problemMd: This equation represents the complete combustion of 1 mol of sugar B. B + y O2 → 12CO2 + zH2O 8.55 g of sugar B is burned, producing 7200 cm3 of carbon dioxide at rtp. Use the equation to calculate the Mr of sugar B. [one mole of any gas occupies 24 000 cm3 at rtp] Mr =
parts.solutionMd:
**Answer: Mr of sugar B = 342.**

*Step 1 — amount of carbon dioxide produced:* 7200 ÷ 24 000 = 0.3 mol of CO2, because one mole of any gas occupies 24 000 cm3 at rtp.

*Step 2 — amount of sugar burned:* the equation B + y O2 → 12CO2 + zH2O shows that each mole of sugar B makes 12 mol of CO2, so the amount of sugar B is 0.3 ÷ 12 = 0.025 mol.

*Step 3 — relative formula mass:* 8.55 g of sugar B was burned, so Mr = 8.55 ÷ 0.025 = 342.

The mass divided by the amount in moles gives the Mr of sugar B as 342.
